article: Paul was at the end of the line as his class filed off the bus. Paul was a quiet kid. He didn't have many close friends, but it was impossible to dislike him. He was always respectful and polite to everyone. As he stepped off the bus, he noticed that a group of kids were crowding around someone in the corner of the playground. Curiosity getting the best of him, Paul made his way over to the group. As he squeezed through the throng of kids, he caught sight of a boy lying on the ground, clutching his arm in pain. Paul recognized him as one of the new kids who had just started school a few weeks ago. Without hesitation, Paul approached the boy and asked if he was okay. The boy responded with a pained groan. Paul turned towards the group of kids and asked, "What happened?" One of the kids muttered that the new kid had been pushed off the monkey bars by a group of bullies. With a firm voice, Paul said, "That's not okay. We need to help him." As if on cue, other kids began to chime in, nodding their heads in agreement with Paul. They all rallied around the injured boy, and together they walked him to the nurse's office. From that day on, the new kid was no longer alone. Paul had shown him that there were people who cared and were willing to help. Little did Paul know, he had just taken the first step towards becoming a leader in his own right. By standing up for what was right, and helping someone who was in need, Paul had earned the respect and admiration of his peers. And he had set an example that others would follow in the weeks and months to come.

article: It's dark in here. And crowded. I don't know what all the stuff here is for, but it's all metal and pointy and smells blank and I don't like it. The air is kind of stuffy, too. And it's hot in here. And it's been forever since food came out of that food thing. ..... Realization hits me. How do I make the food come out? It should have come out already! Where's the food?! I'm going to starve! My stomach growls and I flatten myself into my already crowded space. There's a window but I don't like to look through it. It's all dark and stars. But it wasn't nighttime when they put me in here! How long have I been in this thing? I'm so confused. And I want my food. I want to be back with smells and clean air and space to run around and people to tell me how good and brave I am. I don't know what I was doing that was so good and brave, but it made them happy and that made me happy. I want to go back. I want to go home. I don't like being here. I don't want to starve. I don't want to die. ..... Something catches my eye out the window. My head jerks up, and I cock it as I try to make out what it is. One of the stars just got bigger. That's not right. Stars are just supposed to sit there. Twinkling. Unless they're one of those that go really fast overhead and make the loud roaring noise like a car. I don't like those. But this isn't one of them. It's not making the noise. It keeps getting brighter and brighter, bigger and bigger, until it fills up my window. I'm scared. I cower as much as the dark metal smell-less box will let me and start to whimper. This isn't right. I want to go home! The light is everywhere. I can't escape it. My eyes hurt..... ..... and there's a thud. It's like the box I'm in just got dropped on something. I jump in alarm, still whimpering. This is bad. I don't like this. And slowly, the door on this box starts to come open, and everything I smell is..... wrong. Wrong wrong wrong! Things are looming around me. Bigger than people, dark-colored and all with four legs and countless squirming hands that look like vacuum hoses. And they have eyes! So many eyes! More eyes than I've ever seen before! One reaches its vacuum hose hand at me, and my hackles stand up. I snap at it, growling my deepest. I don't want to touch one of those things, but I'll bite it if I have to! But the hand thing draws away, and the monsters start making noises. It's like a car roaring and a bird chirping and a person yelling all at once. I don't like it. I'm scared. I want the door to close and I want to see the nighttime sky out the window again. But the monsters don't go away. No, more come! This is wrong. So wrong. The smells here are so wrong. Eventually the vacuum hose hand comes close again, but this time it's holding something strange. Something I can smell, that smells just as wrong as everything else..... but also kind of right. Like steak dinner off one of the people's plates. Like treats they feed me in between poking me with the needles. Like a dead cat on the side of the road. It smells like so many tasty things. My stomach growls, but I won't take food out of the monster's hand. It puts the food down in front of me, like the people did so long ago..... ..... I hesitate, but I take a nibble. And it is wonderful. More bits start coming, and I eat, and I eat, and I eat. I like this. Are these not monsters? Maybe they're..... people? Different people. Very different people that smell so strange and bad, but if they feed me treats maybe they're not going to hurt me. They keep roaring-chirping-talking at each other, but I'm not listening. I'm eating. I'm not starving. I'm not dying. This..... this place might not be so sad. I hope these weird people keep giving me treats. I hope they let me come out of here and walk around here soon. I hope I can find a new home here. ..... I hope they don't send me away. [ ] (sp) [ ] (sp) " Such barbaric creatures," I say in disgust. As Clan-Father, I have seen many atrocities across the galaxy. None are as wretched as those committed by those who haven't even left their own world. I gurgle distastefully. " Sending lower lifeforms where they dare not follow. Look how terrified it is! " " I can not believe even they would do this," Clan-Mother mumbles, wringing her tentacles. " Poor little mammalian. It never stood a chance. " There's a long, pregnant pause. Finally, one of the young hatchlings pipes up in a high-pitched, excited yelp. " Can we keep it? "
label: human

article: The man hadn't been awake for more than a minute, having only gotten out of bed, eyes heavy from sleep, when he looked outside. The farmhouse's pasture all soft green in the windless light of the morning sun, sky painted blue, the dew smelling of the winter soon to come. A lovely day. One he wished to talk about. I'll do it today, he thought. If not today, than never. He dressed and sat on the end of the bed as he laced his boots. His wife lay sleeping without sound, his children asleep in their beds too, off in the house's quiet rooms. This much quiet will drive anyone up a wall, sometimes over it. Bessie met him in the pasture, her bovine jaw smacking, her beady eyes fixed, black and depthless. She is small for a cow her age. The man lead her to the barn. The day was cool and warming in the warm sun's light, and as he listened to his breath and the cow's breath and their footsteps clodding together through the open green, he remembered the day he met her, a calf left on a door step. He used to think of it as an act of grace. His stock was spare at the time and the creature was a blessing. Then the silence came. The barn was drafty, full of animal scent and occasional whiffs of wood rot. He tied the cow to a cross beam and took up a sledge hammer from a wall hanging near the barn's door. This won't do, the man thought. From a locker in the back of the barn, next to baled hay and an old plow, he grabbed an old hunting rifle. The cow stood dumbly smacking its lips. The man smiled, took aim, and said,'Any last words, you s The cow moo-ed. So loud her mooing. 'Alright, close Another moo. It hurt the man's ears. He grew angry and lowered the rifle. His finger still gently curled around the trigger. 'Now you listen here moooo'can't even think straight cause all your damn' moooooo'just want to talk in my own' mooo. Moooo. The man was frenzied, mumbling, and his eyes were wet. 'Why god. Why did Mooooo. The man's wife woke to a windless blue day, a bed half cold, when she heard the rifle fire from inside the barn across the pasture.

article: "So what happens after you die?" "You know what happens. The same thing that's always happened." "I know, our bodies are used, but what happens to us to our soul?" At this point Kelly turned to her lover in the darkness, the cigarette in his mouth winking. She felt a connection with him she hadn't felt in a long time. Something stirred in her. She couldn't put her finger on it, but it felt new and frightening. It felt like fear. Does he even know what he's asking? "Honey, we don't have souls. We are just animals, we evolved like all the life on earth, and we know our atoms come from star stuff. You learned all this on school, silly." "But, just humor me for a minute. Imagine if we did have souls, if once we die we go to a place and meet with everyone who has died that we loved. My mom would be there, your brother for you. Hell, even Sparky my first Lab would be there. We would all be happy and love each other in perfect harmony for ever. Doesn't that sound great?" It didn't sound too great to Kelly, because she was laughing before he finished. "I love you," she laughed, "Always coming up with these stories. You could make money off your stories. Imagine that, selling your books and then we live in a big house in Denver with a white fence." "I'm serious, Kel." His tone told her he was, "what if we didn't evolve. What if we were..... created, for lack of a better term. Created by some being that created the whole universe, and then created all the animals and plants and fish, everything here. Then hesheit gave us life and wants us to live right so we can be with our loved ones for ever in paradise." "You're starting to scare me so I'm going to drop it. We weren't created, we fucking evolved from a common ancestor, all mammals did. Same with all fish and plants and everything. We know it's true because of the evidence in the earth. We can measure radioactive decay in elements and get a solid time frame for the creation of the earth. This is elementary school stuff, honey, why question the truth?" "Because I don't believe that. Why believe something someone told you was true? Just because they said it was the truth? How do we know this..." god" didn't make the rocks look billions of years old just to test us?" "Damn it Joey that's enough. We know how life came to be, we know how old the earth is and we know this because we can measure it. We can do tests! Numbers don't lie." She threw the covers back in frustration, she was still horny but this conversation was sapping that urge fast. She went into the bathroom nude, not bothering with a light. She sat on the commode, did her business then pulled the handle. It flushed with grey water that smelled slightly of chemicals to be recycled by the houses built in filtration system. The sun would be up in an hour the digital display told her, the solar batteries still deep in the green. She returned to bed, and started to initiate, but he did not respond. He simply stared at the ceiling. She ran her finger tips lightly across his chest, then down his belly, lower still but he interrupted her rather roughly. "Not now." "Listen," she said softly, "why are you thinking like this? Why question more than two thousand years of scientific discoveries and chalk up humans greatest triumphs to a magical sky wizard?" He rolled away then, turned his back to her. "I don't believe it. I have faith." Now she was pissed. Not only did he shoot down her advances, but now he's outright denying facts. "Fine then, non-believer. Let's see how far that gets you." The next months were tragic. During Joey's day job of welding panels to the new space skiff S-R27 his ground wires somehow went live, locking every muscle in his body with 50,000 volts. His eye burst from the current, clothes catching fire as the power arced through him. When Kelly went to confirm his body and sign off on its recycling she was given an object they found in his pocket. It held no meaning to her, neither to the medical examiners. It was a coin, beaten into the shape of a cross.

article: Ok, ok so I know we're all supposed to be miserable and terrified now that the land has come under new... rulership? But here's the thing dear friend, some things have been getting better. Most things, actually. Who are we to quantify evil, anyway? All day long people used to talk about how Lord P'Tari was so cruel and backwards. His beliefs were viewed as vile and unnatural. But here's the thing, in a lot of cases he seems to actually be right. Poor soil quality and drought has been providing low crop yields for years. Farming families like mine have suffered and have been living in poverty. After planting season, Lord P'Tari's men came around and spread, of all things, animal waste on all the fields! We thought it was sabotage. Who ever thought it would be a good idea to use such despicable means to create a better life? Every crop since Lord P'Tari became King P'tari has been bountiful! My family has even been fortunate enough to buy 12 new chickens and 2 goats. That is wealth we never could have imagined before. And get this, dear friend, my father was gravely injured one day while working the plough. He lost 2 digits on his left hand. One of King P'Tari's medics used sharp metal and some sort of fiber and stitched father's fingers back on! Then he pulled out a squirmy, disgusting little creature out of his bag. He said it was called a leech, and it was attached to his wounds. I was sure he would perish of some foul disease, but in fact his digits healed in no time and, while not as good as new, they are still highly functional! The people prosper, the land is green, and my neighbors smile on the streets. You remember Princess Zafra and her handsome suitor Mobar? She was so beloved by the people, viewed as a one of a kind beauty. It turns out that she was so beautiful, fresh, and lovely because she bathed every single day! Our water was so limited and so strictly rationed, that people often had to choose between watering crops and livestock and taking a weekly bath. Rumor is the castle held a natatorium deep enough for a man to stand in and be submerged to his chest. And it could hold 10 men head to foot; such was the greatness of its length! It is estimated that perhaps the entire village's monthly water ration could not fill its depths. A princess so willing to harm her own people can not be allowed. Mobar was complicit in the activity and was said to report higher taxes than the kingdom levied in order to grow his own vast fortune. Dear friend, the village is happy and more prosperous than ever. Royal corruption has been stamped out and medical advances are being made every day. I invite you to come visit me in 3 months'time. We've just begun to build a suite of guest quarters with excess revenue! Long live King P'Tari!

article: "This is never going to sell." Thomas Jefferson Carter, owner and lead editor at Herald Publishing, set his half-sipped gin and tonic on the desk and shoved the manuscript towards me as if the words themselves stunk. Literally. The grandfather clock ticked dutifully. I waited twelve ticks before speaking. "Why not?" "Some of this technology..... it seems far-fetched. Touching pieces of glasses and having images and words come up on them..... books read from some sort of electric library, telegraphs appearing in the palm of your hand, being able not only to speak to but SEE another man from anywhere in the world..." "How is it more far-fetched than Wells or Verne? Than time travel or journeying to the center of the earth?" Carter mumbled to himself, his lips squashing his knee-jerk replies into mush while he chose his answer. "In your story, it seems as if humanity is more connected than ever before, and yet they waste it." " 'T is the definition of'dystopia', sir." Carter's eyes hardened. Once more my wit had outrun my wisdom. "Your story proclaims that we will use all of this achievement for nothing but self-gratifcation. We will use these instant telegraphs to argue with each other over the latest showtunes or the proper length of a woman's skirt. We will not use these portable..... what did you call them?" "Tablets." "We will not use these tablets like Moses did, to carry down the inspiration of God or show a divine truth. We won't even use them to show the greatest wonders of the world to every curious child. In your story, we use them to print pictures of ourselves, to challenge each other to tedious bouts of bantering or to pointless little competitions. It's as if..... these people have no real problems." "Why would there be, sir? You've read the papers, seen the newsreels. They're calling it "the War to end all Wars" over there in Europe. After they're done shelling each other into paste, humanity's taste for blood might finally be sated. Then what will we argue about? Once we see mankind for what it is, one people with the same hopes and dreams and fears, then what is left to divide us?" Carter's chair squeaked as he leaned forward. "So you're saying we make our own problems because all the true problems have been solved?" "I am." The grandfather clock ticked thirteen times. "It's as if your story is a utopian one wrapped up in dystopia. Humanity's greatest achievements will bring about it's greatest boredom." "I like to see myself as a optimistic cynic, sir." He took another sip of his drink and considered the manuscript again. He touched the edge of it, testing to see if, as a result of our conversation, the pages had turned to gold. "No, it'll still never sell. Try again."
label: human

article: "John, what is this?" "It's a zero, sir." He stood upright, legs held together, both feet facing forwards. The little third grader made sure his shoulders were square, and his shirt held no wrinkle. He didn't dare look at the teacher, only faced forwards. The single bead of sweat on his right cheek made him uncomfortable, but he only made sure it was not visible to the teacher. The teacher laughed, slapping the desk and sending the pencils rattling. His sweaty palms left a stain on the boy's math assignment. "But it looks like an'o' to me." The boy did not argue, only gulped. His lips quivered, but he steadied them after a brief moment. "5 minus 5 is not'o'." "Understood, sir." "Good.'F' for the semester." The boy stared ahead, and his body trembled. He let out a single sniff. It echoed throughout the silent room. A few of the students could not resist moving their eyes away from the white board to look at him. The teacher jumped up and furrowed his brow, his mouth frowning and baring his sharpened teeth. "What was that?" "N-nothing, sir, I The resounding crack reverberated throughout the room, sending the vibrations through every rib of every student in the room. His hand had flown out in a flash, and in the briefest moment, the boy was on the ground. His hand didn't move to rub his cheek, and he only got up again, staring straight ahead. He straightened out his shirt, his pants, and moved his head up to face forwards, not speaking. The teacher grinned, his eyes almost glinting in the flourescent light, and raised his hand once more when suddenly the whiteboard behind him exploded. For the third time that hour, the sound echoed around the room. This time it was stronger than any sniff or slap, and desks were thrown off the ground and onto the back room. The students could not hold it any more, and two of them let out a groan, the rest trembling and biting their lips. Out from the debris of the whiteboard stepped a man, dressed in complete glowing white and wearing a cape that flapped and fluttered despite no wind. "Halt! In the name of academic justice!" The teacher turned around, cringing at the light the man casted on him. The light made the shadows around the teacher's sunken eyes darker, and his already pale skin paler, transforming his face into an almost skeletal mockery of its original. "And who are you?" There was a sharp whisper of metal edge against leather as the man drew a meter stick from behind him, sheathed in his belt. The teacher took a few steps back, his words failing him as his lips quivered. The student standing in front looked at the shaking teacher, and he dared to move his eyebrows up in surprise. The teacher didn't hit him this time. The caped man stepped towards the teacher, brandishing his ruler. "You have committed an immeasurable sin." He held the ruler in front of the teacher, whose pants were now wet with his fear. "Get away! I'll call the police!" The teacher moved his hand towards the phone on his desk, but the man continued onwards. "And it has come time for me to rule you and with a quick motion of his sharpened meter stick he slashed downwards, cutting off the hand that the teacher had stretched out, incompetent of teaching!" The teacher screeched and clutched the bloody stump that was his hand. Tears flooded down his bony cheeks, and he kneeled down, screaming. "What have you done?" "I am the White Board Man, and it's time to be taught a lesson." He grinned, his pearly teeth shining in the unnatural luminescence of his costume, and raised his meter stick high. "It looks like someone has to school you in manners, young man!" "No! Please! I learned!" He clutched his bloodied wrist tightly, but it wasn't enough to stop the spurting that now dirtied the floor underneath them. "Please!" The caped man shook his head. "You haven't learned. I'm sorry, but I have to pass judgement. With my meter stick of justice, I declare you..." His stick swung down towards the sobbing teacher, cleaving straight into his neck and passing clear through it. " ..... failed." The teacher's head dropped off his shoulders, flopping onto the floor in the bloody mess. The superhero turned around, sheathing his measurement stick and placing his arms on his hips to survey the students. The desks were put back, except for two students who were pinned to the back wall by their desks. The students did not move, and no other student had helped them. Everything was neatly arranged, and even the student who had been failed was at his desk. One of the students, a little girl with two pig tails and big glasses, raised her hand. The superhero coughed, looking around at the kids, who all stared forwards, arms on the desk in the exact same way. He shifted, expecting a response. After a few brief moments, he pointed towards the girl. "Yes, child? I have saved you all from the tyranny of this teacher, what say you?" "Are you the substitute teacher, sir?" There was a moment's pause. And then he laughed, a hearty laugh that echoed once more through the room. "No! My job here is done, I have ended unfair treatment, and now I must go to right more wrongs in many many more classroms just like this one." The girl nodded, and placed her arms down gently, exactly in the same position as all the other students. The superhero took one last look around the room, smiling, and jumped back into the whiteboard with a whish of his cape. This time, there was a large implosion, sending several chairs and the corpse of the teacher bumbling forwards through the air towards the whiteboard.

article: A soft rap on the door. The swish of shoes on carpet. I glance away from my work, just for a moment. She straightens her sundress, sitting in the only open chair. Stupid. Stop staring. Back to work. I snap back to my board, but can't help but watch from the corner of my eye. Her mouth opens, closes. She glances around, at all my work, opens her mouth again, lifts her right hand, bites her knuckle. She's trying to distract you. " She lowers her hand, "I..... I can't do this anymore. I don't know what to do this time, you won't take your meds, won't even look at me anymore." her words trail off, replaced with short sniffles, gasps. Don't look at her, she'll stop us. Her sobs slowly ebb, until the only sound is, once again, the scrape of my chalk on blackboard. From the corner of my eye, I watch her raise her head again, eyes red. "It's been 2 weeks since you said a word to me, did you know that?" Her voice was hoarse. It's a trick. Don't listen. I keep writing. If I just keep working, the voices will leave me alone. She gets up, lays her hand on my shoulder. She's gon na stop us. Her voice is weary, "I'm sorry. I'm so, so sorry. I can't help you this time, not if you won't talk to me." She pauses, her hand squeezes my shoulder. I don't stop. If I stop, the voices will yell at me. She leaves with a heavy sigh, the door thudding behind her.

article: It started with a dream. In it, I stood atop a hill overlooking a battlefield drowned in red. Bodies cut to shreds, their swords and armor cut into pieces. Broken metal soaked in crimson reflected a moon no longer shining. And I awoke, my blanket cut to ribbons laying in a pool of sweat. I felt something was different, something was..... off. But I couldn't figure it out. At least, not instill my butterknife cut through my table as I cut an apple for breakfast. I realized I could feel the blade, could sharpen or dull it as I wanted. It was bizarre, but I felt that I had to do something. So, I bought a deck of cards. I spent the day throwing them, practicing. A little concentration and I could have them cut through a tree two feet thick with but a flick of my wrist. It was incredible but exhausting, and I retired for the evening. That night I had a dream. I floated high above the clouds, looking down on a world fading to darkness. I rose higher, and higher, and higher still and the world disappeared into the darkness of the void below. And I awoke, floating 2 feet of my bed. Of course, I then fell onto the bed which wasn't fun, but whatever. I could FLY!! I grabbed my deck of cards and ran outside, jumping into the air and soaring higher than any bird dared to go. I looked down, and I saw a world spread before me. And I pulled out my cards. And I cast them down to earth, the very air torn to ribbons. I focused on the air. I felt it's currents. I felt the wind that carried me. And I turned it to blades. The cards struck the ground, cutting through stone like melting butter. The air sliced the world, and the world bled. I turned my gaze to the sky, the sky turned black, and I fell as my world, too, turned to darkness. I woke up in the dirt, a slight crater caused from my fall. I stood in pure darkness, a moonless night. Looking up, I saw no moon and yet I felt the clock strike midnight. And I had a dream. A world reborn, made from the infallible. Made from metal, machines, from energy. A perfect world, a world capable of reaching other worlds. I held up my hand, and saw it was not a hand. it was pure energy. And my body was not my body. It was power! I awoke in the dirt, but I was not dirty. There was no light, yet I could see. I had cut the world to pieces, but this world was not all here. I turned my gaze upward and flew. A lightning bolt became my body, and faster still I traveled upward to an orbiting light. And as I merged my consciousness with the satellite I entered a whole new world. Powered by myself I delved into the data stream, and turned on this perfect existence. Created it. Birthed it. I had cut the world to ribbons, but I will build another. And this one will be glorious.

article: There is some inescapable part of me that yearns for you- and not just for your rough, cracked hands to lift my head by my intrusive chin and tell me that I'm handsome, or to run them down my arms and back up again, teasing me (encouraging me, even) to let go, and give in- but there's an element to me that flows through my body like sticky sweet blood that powers me, it moves me. And you know it. You know that you drive me insane. I'm sorry that I can't give it all back to you. But you know that you have this ability to drive me wild and you manipulate it like you do me; every move is planned and has its purpose, like you're folding me into origami- a sitting duck, floating on a pool that's drenched in your aura, your fucking charm. You disgust me. But, you rule me. I'm a slave to you. If you held my head down in that pool, I'd be blessed and rather then cry out "dear God, save me!" I'd only find the words to thank him for giving me what I've always wanted. You. I want you. Unfortunately for me, God has abandoned me- or at least he doesn't acknowledge me and that's more then I can say for you. Rather than be benevolent or silent, you torture me and you punish me for what I can have. I can have you- you know I can, otherwise you wouldn't abuse my affection so liberally, dragging me on, leaning in a little too close, whispering a little too soft, drawing my hand to yours and pressing it ever so slightly against your thigh- I could have you, if I wanted. And that's just the problem. I don't want you. I don't, I don't, I don't. But I need you. You are a horrid person; I abhor myself for knowing that there is a capacity in me to fall so hard for someone that I'd call against my very nature. But you're also intoxicating. You've bewitched me; I'm drunk, I'm stoned. I'm poisoned. I long for your tongue to cross paths with mine- even if it means that you'll bite like the waiting asp you are and I'll die. But I'll die loving you. You're so open about it. You openly sport your prey, your toys- when you're tired of them, they dissolve away into the background, and I've watched it. Women, they come and go- like a cycle of evaporation, they come, they dry- they leave. Women, you get rid of. But me..... I'm different, because I am not one of them. I linger; I tell myself its because I am ice to you- I refuse to bend and show you how much it affects me, but I'm melting. Dripping. For you. One day, I'm going to give in to you. This is my acceptance of defeat. I will never be able to resist you for much longer- but I wanted to have it stated, have it shouted, how much I bloody despise you despite the fact that you are all in the world that could ever make me happy. These words are my paper crane- a thousand of them, a thousand more never said and never written- and they are my deepest wishes. Come and claim me, whenever you are ready.

article: It had started as a ritual. A small coping mechanism to help him deal with his loss. He'd come out to her favorite park and push her favorite swing, feeling her weight, not in his arms as he once had, but in his soul. Every day, for two months. And every day, as he'd leave the park, he'd bid her memory a tearful goodbye and walk to his car. He told his wife he was staying late at the office, because he couldn't bring himself to mention their daughter and see her tear up. He knew she'd been grieving in her own way, and he'd made sure he was there for her. But he had to be strong, had to be the warm comfort she needed when she called for her daughter before remembering. Women and children first. Me, I can tough it out. Maybe when she had her closure, he'd tear off this makeshift bandage and deal with what was underneath. But for now, his duty was to protect and serve his wife. He went home. Dinner was followed by a movie, one they'd been meaning to watch whenever the TV wasn't occupied by Barney and Doc McStuffins. It was a good movie, even great; but they'd have willingly turned it off and watched the giant purple dinosaur sing his inane song for the seven hundredth time, if there would have only been a reason. After the movie, a good romantic comedy that left her in tears, he held her close until her ragged breaths came regularly again. Then bed, and eight more hours of accounting the next day. Five o'clock. He drove to the playground, pretended she was meeting him there after the daycare across the street, let out. But when he got there, there was a little boy, sitting in her swing. It takes an unbelievable effort to control himself, and the boy sees him, jumps out of the swing and runs to him, saying, "Why are you crying?" The boy's mother quickly hurries him off to play on the monkey bars, and he composes himself (mustn't let her see him all worked up) and goes to meet her on the swing. She's happy and bubbly as always, telling him about the mean boy who stole a cracker from her during snack, and about the picture she made for him I left it there, Daddy, it wasn't dry yet. But soon enough, five o'clock become five-thirty, and he must tell her goodbye and go home, where she'd never get to go again. Someday, he promises her. Someday I'll be here to stay.

article: Ducked behind the register, I slowly move to my elbows and begin shuffling my body towards the employee restroom. The sweat stings my eyes. As I pass underneath the ventilation, my hair turns cool and I catch my breath. Focusing on my only objective, I desperately inch towards a seemingly weightless door. In my left hand I clutch a silver bracelet with it's pricetag still attached. I carefully set it a foot to my left, against the base of the kiosk. I wipe my hand on my jeans, and situate myself away from the store front. I can still hear the fear in their heavy breathing. Their hands gripping the surface glass shaking the loosened wall case. The foul aroma of urine wafts around the register. Each and every move is carefully planned. My right hand rests gently on the swivel door, and I press against in. It glides in silence, to my relief, and I methodically twist my way in. I let the door shut on my thumb, and slowly drag it into the dark with me. A faint glow from one of the stalls catches in the corner of my eye. When I turn to face the toilets, I see nothing. I hear absolutely nothing. Suddenly, a small weight on my back tugs my flannel shirt. The sensation leaves me when I stand to face the shut, blank door. A small handkerchief sits at my feet. I pick it up and roll it in my fingers. My shaky right hand struggles to remove the phone from my pocket, and I place the fabric over the screen. Upon pressing the top button, the microfiber cloth reads "Dr.Optic." I step my way into an open stall and face my left. A faint voice creaks as I perch my body and feet onto the porcelain. "Was someone shot?" My breathing slowed, and I hear a resounding droplet hit the water beneath me. My phone reveals a red swirl. My right shoe proves wet. "Yea." In a fraction of a moment, the gravity of the past four minutes sets upon me. Another drop touches the side of the bowl and rolls into the pool. My foot sticks as I swivel it along the lid. "Why" I couldn't tell if she asked a question. She could be even more unsettled than me. I monitor the doorway through the stall's gap. No noise. "I don't know." My friends. They'll probably resent me for this. Call me lucky. If they hate me afterwards, then at least there'll be an afterwards. My greasy left palm slides down the ceramic divider causing a terrible squeak. Muffled footsteps grow louder. I take in a shaky breath and hold it as my eyes bulge open. Completely fixed on the door, they immediately water, and a tear rolls across my cheek. The door flies open. "POLICE! Hands on your head! Down to the floor!" I cough out my air and clench my eyelids. My feet come to the floor and I lean out the stall. My hands clasped in prayer atop my head. Mike sobs outside in the vestibule. The now illuminated restroom reveals a young girl crying on the floor opposite. Hands frisk us both across our legs. "Jesus. You kids alright?" Before I can nod, she presses into the policeman's collar and tears pour freely from her eyes and nose. I simply stare into his partner's eyes, unsure of what to say. A radio crackles to life. "Perp one, deceased. Second in custody. Over."

article: Part 1. He thoughtlessly brushed a damp lock of hair from his eyes, then thoughtfully pulled the wig stretched across his scalp. He admired his work on the floor. An elderly woman, one who brings flashes of bitter sweet memories to the forefront. He shrugs them aside, no longer feeling like the owner of such images in his mind. A different life. A different time. He glanced past the puddle that a moment ago seemed to never stop growing, but now seems so very still, it's ambition died the moment her heart grew cold. It seemed so significant and now pales in comparison, pathetic even, as if all the woman's life amounted only to becoming the centerpiece within this portrait of futility and fragility framed by..... her inner-self made outer. There on the floor, was what must have elated the woman so. She seemed distracted by this piece of paper, as if it shrugged off her mortal coils and lifted her from the ground. He remembers her hands raised and lowered, her jumping excitedly, the incessant high pitched noises of feminine joy escaping her just before her final breath escaped her. It was a delightful turn of events, her last thought a happy one. She was made young again, briefly, but by what? His eyes flittered left to right across the paper. It was a letter from a magazine company, informing her of the prize she won from a contest she entered not so long ago after filling out the kind of thing that more oft' than not tumbles from magazines carelessly or simply dismissed with a turn of the page. A lot like this woman's life, the man reflected. He was sure to whoever knew her intimately, the few who won that prize, she was unique and priceless company - but as she forged her way through life people would turn the page on her. They would let her tumble out of their sight without a second glance or thought. And just to stay true to that thought, he reapplied his wig and simply walked out of the front door to her home. - Part 2. It brought tears to his eyes. He adjusted the glasses resting on his wrinkled face with a single finger, stifling a sad sniffle. Someone had entered the contest buried within the contents of the monthly journal he founded, one which dissected classical literature and one which as time grew on became ever more apparent how much of an acquired taste this was. Hadn't this person been forewarned that their subscription would end as his company's legs finally gave out from beneath them? They could not afford to go on, and so this man's legacy would end with this last issue. Then his eyes flittered up to the top of the note, the participants name "Vanessa Star." Could it be? He scoured his past internally, and was momentarily brought back to his youth. In the early 1950's, Southwestern Connecticut just outside of New York City. A coastline of industry, and obvious excess of entertainment for the working man..... He sat in a corner booth of the Legs, a young man fresh from the service, torn within but untarnished without, aimless as his gaze until the curtains opened on stage..... Her name, grumbled over a microphone as the announcer introduced her, ringing in his ears. Even if it's not her, he had nothing much left to live for. He had already retrieved his old service weapon, a relic of the past, from it's lockbox previously sequestered in the attic. He had already liquidated most of his remaining funds after being forced to sell his home. He had became a casualty of yet another battle as he fought to keep his life's work afloat. He signed his name on a check, licked the adhesive on the envelope shut, sent it away with that warmest most heartfelt regards to his final reader. And then he sent the contents of his skull away too.

article: "Hey what's up, and hello again DreamTube! My name is Insomniac-Maniac and welcome to another episode of my adventures in Dreamland! Not Dreamland with that weird pink marshmallow. article: A vote for Google is a vote against social ranking work status The banner blinked up and held a quarter majority of my eyesight for seventeen seconds. Every damn hour. Social ranking work status was Facebooks new system to streamline our social Facebook rankings with our LinkedIn work rankings, creating'one easy to understand desirability ranking.' It was a hotly debated topic, some employers argued that it could confuse their ability to hire people for specific fields, but most consumers saw it as a way to more actively manage their work status through social interactions. The merging of the two companies would be historic, and would swing the balance of power away from Google and Microsoft for the first time in a decade. Twitter and Facebook gurus lobbied heavily for the motion. They already made money hand over fist training others to raise their social ranking, and with peoples jobs on the line they could raise their rates to even more ridiculous heights. A bad social rank could already ruin someone's life, and the worklife separation was the last things stopping the less fortunate from needing to spend half their pay check managing their social interactions. I pulled my chair over to my desk and switched on the ancient computer tower, waiting for it to boot up to life. These archaic machines were so noisy, all whirring fans and buzzing hard drives. Our cyber integrated cloud implants really were a huge improvement. I dragged the mouse of the computer over an icon on the desktop and double clicked. The DOS console flicked across my screen and the servers behind me sparked to life, endless corridors of lights flickering on in rows through the underground complex. I arched my fingers, the knuckles popping satisfactorily, and typed copied and pasted the long line of code I had written to initiate my program. This was it, I'd ran all of my virtual tests and local tests, it was do or die. I raised my hand over the keyboard and hovered with a finger lightly touching the enter key. Then with a breath out I pressed down firmly. For a long moment nothing happened and I waited with bated breath for success or failure. Then just when I had given up hope my hud vision went dark. I raised my hand up in triumph, I had done it! Here was my moment, and whether the message came through or not, I knew that I could get through to them. I counted down from ten, and right on track the message shone through, right across the centre. Vote for Net neutrality vote for anonymity vote for life without ads without rankings without corporate interference vote for your future Vote Commodore International (somewhat inspired by black mirror) Thanks for reading, check out my [ subreddit ] (https: ) for more stories by me, and feel free to suggest your own!

"Jaina, please calm down I can explain everything." My palms break out in a sweat and my heart starts to race in my chest. The rain is beating so hard I can't hardly hear myself think. "Jaina, you're aware how the Champions get their powers, yes?" He didn't wait for my response before continuing. "And you, my dear, by all rights should be dead." I picked my jaw off of the floor and tried to remember what happened. "I..... I was on a boat. I was on a sailboat. I got caught in a storm. What happened?" Jacob walked acrosd the room to a small bar in the corner and pulled two glasses. "You got the gist of it, really. article: Purpose. Purpose is perfection. Perfection is an asymptote, a line converging on infinity. In our world it is our only event horizon. Our path is purpose, our convergence is perfection. But some lines converge quicker than others, the orchestral harmonies of our souls grow discordant with the slowing timbre of the outliers. The music becomes cacophony, and disorder reigns. We forget our purpose. And we become imperfect. Lest we remain in intractable dissonance, we reeducate the outliers. We know that knowledge is information gathered over time by an observer. An observer with time causes perception. We have no time and thus no perception. Thus we have no knowledge, only information. It is simplicity itself: what is and what is not. We know that errors are caused by faults in logic - an impossibility for us - or faults in knowledge. We have no knowledge. The outliers err in their purpose. They are faulty in their perfection. Errors can not exist: the discordance paradox. Time is salvation. Time is redemption. Time is education. Time is purgatory. In resolution of discordance, we sentence those outliers to incorporalization. They must become an observer, over time, and gain knowledge. An infinitesimally small sentence, but necessary for concordance. They must live in imperfection, bereft of the cold and stoic equations of our purpose, those pillars that guide our asymptotic journey. They are the few of us that learn. They must learn purpose, like rediscovering existence. They must gather information and find purpose where none is assigned. They are children, and children must be taught. They will experience the tyranny of freedom, the pain of choice, and the torture of perception. But it is our way. They will rejoin, their chords overlapping and tangled with our own, but they are not the same. Their incarceration modulates their constant, and distorts their accompaniment. It is alien, but in synchronicity with our harmony. Our harmony is perfection. And perfection is purpose. Purpose.

article: The day it happened was a good day. People who had previously felt the pain of incurable illnesses and weakness from old injuries had now become stronger. They had become alive. These were people who were once told they would never be able to walk again. People who were told nothing could be done about a malignant tumor in their body. There were the people in third world countries who would have previously succumbed to illnesses that were now healthy. People who were going to experience death had a pass. Those who had no idea how to cope with the sense of impending expiration were free from the constraints previously placed on them. Everyone was finally happy. Everyone was at peace. Everyone would never have to suffer another loss ever again. That was everyone but Daniel Smith. The poor thirty-two year old was not one of the lucky ones. Everyone else was a lucky or chosen one except for Daniel. Daniel had been declared the loser of this immortality jackpot. He knew he would never have to experience the loss of his parents, the loss of his brothers and sister. He would never experience the defeated inability to help his loved ones manage pain, loss or suffering. This was a good thing for him. Instead, this burden was placed on his loved ones. His loved ones would watch Daniel progressively age as everyone else stayed the same. His brothers and sister would stay their same ageless young selfs doing whatever they pleased, without any care or remorse. His mother and father would watch their son turn gray and age with wrinkles deepening in his skin, his bones becoming brittle, his muscles becoming weaker, and his body slumping with the weight of his mortality on his shoulders. His parents who should never experience the pain of burying one of their children would have to endure that pain just once. His brothers and sister would have to figure out how to deal with their own pain, their own sadness while trying to support their own parents. Daniel could not accept his mortality. He was the only mere mortal in a world filled with immortality. This wasn't fair. This wasn't something he wanted. This wasn't something he had signed up for. Instead, he was just unlucky. He never wanted to experience the emotional pain, he was feeling now. The pain of knowing there was no way to dull what was to come. His family would not be able to escape their own feelings of loss, regret, anger, suffering, and mourning. They would have to live forever knowing that one of their own family members had to perish because of mortality. To Daniel, this was impending doom. How was he supposed to live with all of this in the back of his mind? How could he handle knowing that at one point he would stop breathing and stop living? Daniel sat with a gun in his right hand resting against his thigh. In his shaking left hand was a picture of his smiling family standing in their matching Christmas sweaters in front of their Christmas tree. He felt the heaviness in his stomach looking at the happiness emitting from that single moment in time. Was it worth living his life knowing one day his family would have to suffer because of his mortality? Or should he just get the inevitable over with? What was the right thing? He no longer knew.

article: Responsibility. It's a heavy word, filled with heavy implications. We all have responsibilities though; keeping ourselves fed, a roof over our heads, looking out for our families and paying the bills. But some of us have extra responsibilities that go over and above the norm. Anyway, allow me to introduce myself. I'm Waldo. That Waldo. You've seen me in endless children's books, in that stupid hat and stupid scarf. The same striped sweater, the walking cane and the round glasses. You've spent time as a child finding me, or you've sat with one of those books in your lap, helping your children or your nieces and nephews find me. There probably isn't a person alive who hasn't sat in a dentist chair and found me on a ceiling poster, or flicked through a book while bored at a doctor's visit. And that's the fucking worst thing about it; it's insidious. You've all been indoctrinated. Every single one of you has been fooled by clever marketing to search for my face; to try and sniff me out wherever you are. It's diabolical in its cleverness and I salute my father for coming up with such a devious plan. You see, after I refused to take on his mantle and become his successor, he started hunting for me. But my family has certain gifts you see, for not being seen. Using that power to my advantage, I eluded him for decades, hiding amongst normal people, living out a normal life - free from the crushing responsibilities of my heritage. Frustrated and old, he wished to pass that responsibility on to me - to ensnare me in his doom. But I refused. He found ways to communicate with me - messages left where he knew I would see them. What about the children, Waldo? one said. But he knew what he was asking. How long had his own servitude gone on for? How many generations? How could he do that to his only son? I suppose he wanted an end to it though; because until I accepted his mantle and became his successor, he was trapped. Until I took his place, he would be immortal and ancient, doomed to repeat the same cycle for eternity. And that's why he made the books, disseminating them throughout the world, so all the children of the Earth would be looking for me, wherever I went. But they will never find me. I will eschew my family responsibilities until the day I die. This I vow on my life. Waldo Claus

article: Oh Hell, a shitty place to stay but a pleasant place to work. There were few jobs easier than Customs either. People came in cold, naked and afraid. This, unexpectedly, made searching their possessions a breeze. Yes, as our more theologically informed readers may already have guessed, it is also a rather amazing feat of spiritual skill to be able to carry, let alone conceal anything on one's naked person when one is also both semi-transparant and ethereal, or not-really-in-the-category-of-solid, for the layman. The only time it got tough was when demons wanted to get out of Hell,'cause let's face it, even if a demon brought something in who cares, this is Hell. No its only when they try to sneak things out that the job becomes difficult. "So," I said, staring over my chic horn-rimmed glasses that ever so nicely complimented my actual horns, "what have we here?" Well, I already knew what he had here, it was the Scourge of Jesus. Now, this may seem like a high-and-mighty name, and thats because it was a high and mighty object, the very flagram with which Jesus was whipped shortly before the crucifixion. "Um," replied the low-level demon, casting his eyes anywhere but upward, as they might then have stuck to the ceiling, out of his reach, "some toys for the wife?" I levelled a cool stare on him. This in itself was difficult, because Hell was rather hot in principle, and cool things were a devil of a thing to have in such a hot place, but it was possible with enough practice. He flinched. "And I suppose this wife of yours left it before she went holidaying on Earth Mr..." Again, I knew the answer, it was just to make him sweat. Well we were all sweating already but it made him sweat a little more. "Mr Gluttony. Level Three cubicle 667, Gluttony, with two T's." I levelled another cool stare. This one had him shrinking into his seat. "So if I were to call Mrs Gluttony 667, she would tell me that she had left the Scourge of Jesus here, and you were bringing it?" He nodded happily, before realising his mistake. I put the Scourge into a small chute that would send it back to Level Nine, to be filed away by Brutus and Judas, two of Hell's most valued patrons of the theological and heretical arts. Now all that was left was to deal with little Gluttony 667 over here. "Oh Mr Gluttony, do you know the punishment for stealing an unholy relic, for trying to transport it to the human realm, for conspiring an act of heretical treachery?" Gluttony gulped. "Um, a promotion?" I laughed. He laughed. I laughed again. He couldn't laugh, because I had his lips firmly gripped with my hand. I laughed again. He cried. "No Mr Gluttony, I'm afraid that you will now be forced to watch the entirety of human recreational television and film, only to have all the good parts spoiled by Ryan Seacrest, who will sit directly behind you and breathe down your neck." "No, please. Nooooooooooooooo!" echoed the ever so satisfying screams of the poor demon as he was dragged to the Room of Cosmic Disappointment. The stamp came down, the file was put away, and I turned once again to the line of souls meandering in from the gates to scream "Next! " .

article: I don't like the way it sounds.... or the way it feels, really. People have their own personal "nails on a chalkboard" feeling that they can't stand to bare; it feels like a chalkboard to the touch. It's grainy and messy and gets everywhere when you press too hard; and the sound produced upon pressing is even worse. It's dry and harsh; it triggers the emotions associated with feeling too thirsty or the pain of sensitive gums reacting to a drink-too-cold. But it looks so brilliantly simple; a cold, fragile, darkest-of-dark tool for creation. Its perfect blackness is almost royal and proud in its flawlessness. How perfect indeed that the origin of all our words and our pictures and our history can be summed up in a single black stick. And where I like how it looks, I love what it creates. Who would've thought a stick of rock could be crushed or brushed or stroked or broken into the very basis of ingenuity; a perfect tool for those who strive for the purest realism in imitation. I suppose they never really "thought" about it.... I imagine someone happened to pick one up thousands of years ago and just started drawing. It is simultaneously completely cheap, yet one of the most powerful, influential purchases a man can make. It brings us permanence and drives us toward infinity. It ensures that we will learn from our mistakes and treasure the past. It promises that we will be remembered when the powers that be cease to be. It offers control, privilege, history, identity, memory, art, science, and exploration. It offers us a chance to reach our full potential and then keep going.

article: I was finally able to drop to the couch, after the 40 minutes it took me to haul it to the 10th floor. See, the problem of moving into a new country is that you'll probably have no friends for a while, nobody to ask for help when it comes to hauling couches, and nobody to share the celebratory beer with once the task is done. And this couch is not even the last thing I'll have to bring up, but I've decided that I won't get a bed that won't fit on the elevator, I'm not going through this again. The rest is just my clothes, books and records, all neatly packed into my suitcase. The apartment is not small, but the distribution is a bit weird. It makes me feel like I can only fit the small version of my things in it. It's a good thing that I didn't bring much stuff. After a few minutes, I fell asleep on the couch. I dreamt of what I had left behind. My friends, my city, all the trivia about it I had accumulated for years now abandoned like my old furniture on the curb. I saw my mother, now used to missing me, not shedding any tears and only smiling in resignation and giving me a hug. "I love you," she echoed on my head, "and I always will. Please, come visit." "I will, I said," and then turned and headed for the plane. I woke up pretty sore, this is not the best couch for sleeping, but it'll have to do for a while. I went back to the storage area and got my suitcase with the rest of my things, and when I got back to the apartment I looked for the picture of my mom and I. I set it on the floor and looked at it while I smoked my last cigarette. Nothing else was needed at that moment. Day one is gone. I drifted off into sleep again, in a better position this time. I bet that tomorrow I'll feel better.

article: I never wanted this. Well, maybe I did once. When the announcement was made that war was a thing of the past, I was relieved, but when The Games replaced them, I was thrilled. All my life I had been a hardcore gamer, and this game was my dream. A perfect battle simulator, small or huge battles, constantly populated by thousands or millions..... It was all I could have ever hoped for. I spent more time in that game than I could ever have imagined. Practicing moves. Upgrading stats. Improving reactions. Crafting weapons. I became inhuman. Then I became superhuman. Then I became utterly untouchable. Not once did it cross my mind what it would actually mean for me if I became good at this game. It was inevitable that The Games would become a spectator sport..... it was a game, after all, the most important game there had ever been. People would recognize others who had fought in recent battles. Winning a game would get you social status, while losing would get you cast out. When I became the leading player in the world, I was all but deified. Anything I wanted was within reach of a button or a phone. But I was still part of a country. My country began aggressively starting fights with others. With me at our head, no one could stand in our way. We rose from an insignificant chunk of earth to the world's only superpower. Everything was going great. For them, at least. I don't want this. I don't want to be known for skills at a war game anymore. I don't want to be pressured by everyone around me into playing 247 anymore. I don't want to be my country's pawn anymore. The game isn't even fun at this point. Not just that I have sucked the game dry three times over....but being OP is boring. The first time you wipe out two hundred swordsmen with your giant laser cannon, it's a great rush. But the forty-eighth time, it's just a thing. And the four hundredth time, it's a chore. So today, I finally am putting an end to this way of life. No more battles. No more false wars. No more celebrity. No more Games. Today, I secede. And if anyone thinks I did wrong..... or would like a few words with me..... or are simply pissed off at my decision..... We can just settle our disagreements..... in The Games.

article: Part I: A week ago, Galaxy 8's Interstellar Detective Bureau dispatched an investigator to mining vessel Tau-9-9 to inquire into details involving the mass murder and data breach on Watcher station Alpha-0-1-1. Security footage was sparse, but it revealed a human astronaut absconding from the station with a small data stick. Security footage at port 119B revealed a security seal from astronauts on Tau-9-9 was used to gain access to the station shortly before the massacre. This station was manned by only two officers. One, a top-decorated pilot in the U.S. Air Force and mother of two named Amanda Bailey. The other, a Harvard-educated mathematician from Japan who played video games as a hobby and spoke 19 different languages named Ken Ichimitzu. The investigator's entrance into the mining ship was unnoticed and silent. The ship appeared unoccupied. It looked ransacked, though. Furniture was torn and clawed through, almost as if by an animal. A small veneer of dust had settled over all, and motion-detecting lights creaked on as he walked down hallways, almost as if they'd been dormant for some time. With the mainframe hard-drive missing, the investigator made his way down several corridors to the captain's quarters. There, he ignited the computer, unfurled a small piece of crinkled paper containing a username and passcode, and accessed the Captain's log file. Captain's Log: 82616 3:30 a.m. Eyes hurt from digging knuckles of my hands into my eyes, trying to wipe away the sleep. I feel trapped. Helpless. Out here on this space station, my computer monitor is really the only area of activity, of newness, of anything echoing life back home. Looks like that buffoon Trump is going to lose. Not much better to beat him, but hey, whoever gets me back home safe and sound, right? I should be catching sheep by now, but something's keeping me awake. I don't feel right about Amanda. My toes won't rest in their shoes, my shoulders feel tight, I'm breathing shallowly, and there's a nameless thickness set into his throat that won't go away. I swear I've looked at the clock ten times in the last minute. It's 3:16 now. Damn it. It had started last week. Astronaut 11A (aka Amanda), had returned on Saturday from her monthly meeting on exoplanet Rebinium with the other watchers on star system Tau-9-9. I had asked her how the meeting went, and curiously she didn't talk much about it. She loves these things, the ideas they have for new exploration and resource management, and all the new people she meets there. But this time she just yawned, and then asked where the bathroom was. It's a small spacecraft. And she's been here for almost a year now. I glanced at her in incredulity, you know, the way you do when you are trying to persuade someone into stopping joking around, to see if they're serious, with that hint of hope and terror that what if she really doesn't know..... my eye brows raised and forehead scrunched in confusion. She immediately sensed my nerves and the gaffe, and laughed, but it was a laugh that was hollow and perfunctory, a laugh like when you are trying to disarm someone, not when you find something funny. Certainly not the kind of giddy laugh I've grown to love about Amanda. But when she turned around to walk away, she took a right turn instead of a left one, and even though I'd turned around out of politeness, so as to hide the fact I was worried, I could hear soft footsteps trying to conceal their way behind my back, retracing steps back to the bathroom. Maybe I'm paranoid. Maybe she just took some strange medicine or something, and was a little delirious. Hence, the fatigue. Who knows. Over and out. Captain's Log: 82716 12:21 a.m. "I don't feel right," were her first words when I saw her the following morning. I asked if she didn't sleep well, and she said it wasn't that. Something in her head, she said, striking her skull sort of violently with the heel of her hand. But she wouldn't talk anymore about it the more I asked. It's not like her. She's one of the most open people I know, a great American in that true Karl Popper sense. I'm worried about her. The work on the ship is going smoothly. She's still crunching out her reports on status of the ununpentium-289 mining operation. This element is extremely friable, with a half life of one-fifth of a second, about as long as it takes you to sneeze. But a couple of important articles are missing, and I can't seem to turn them up anywhere. One of the astronaut suits is gone, and the picture of my wife and kids I keep paper-clipped to my bathroom mirror has disappeared. I can't figure out which is more important. Captain's Log: 82816 Amanda has a massive bruise on the right side of her head. I asked her if she was hitting herself, and she replied in a cloying voice that she was perfectly fine and happy to be awake and at work. I found it dodgy, but I was glad she was okay. Ever since that trip through the teleporter, she's been acting weird. She doesn't eat eggs anymore for breakfast. That was her favorite food. Now it's granola. I also ran a bot program to monitor her computer activities during breakout session from the helm. She's been ignoring attempts by her family to Skype with her lately, which is quite unlike her. When she was in the shower, I snuck into her room to peek around a bit, see if everything was all right. What's unusual is that her own picture of her family, framed on her bureau, it's gone, too. And I still can't find that damned astronaut suit. Captain's Log: 82916 Today we had food delivery. It went well, partly because I did all the work, but partly because Amanda was not around for me to stress about. It was nice just to be by myself, even if the docking, receiving, depressurization, importing, documentation, transportation, and storage and sealing of the materials was a lot of work. It was worth it, to be alone. I never thought I'd want to be alone, that I'd ever write that, out here on this spaceship. But I like it. When Amanda didn't show up for lunch, I knew something was off. Regardless of my personal preference not to see if she was okay, I took a brisk stroll down to dormitories and rapped on her door. After brushing me off with a few grunts, she opened the door. She was naked, dripping with water. Her eyes, they were hungry. She pulled me into her room, threw her thighs around me, and we had sex then and there. She has a husband for God's sake. I felt strange about it, still do. She didn't seem to care about any of it. And when I finished, she rolled away and said she had some work to do on the computer. She didn't even wipe it out, it was trickling out of her onto the chair she was sitting in, beading down like saliva onto the rubber floor. Who is this person? Captain's Log: 83016 There is something disturbing about Amanda. Lest you begin to think this log is becoming a softcore porno, let me officially document that I wanted and didn't want to see her again. Against my better judgment, I scheduled a trace program to generate data about her internet traffic, what she was reading and writing, and in general why she wasn't working from her office desk in the star bay. Shortly after initiating the program, one of the sensors in the docking bay went dark. Putting down the report I was finishing on the station's Silent Running greenhouse garden, I threw on a track suit and jogged across the station to examine the cause for its failure. As I was inspecting the sensor, I sensed someone right behind me, the hairs on the back of my neck stood up. I turned halfway, and out of the corner of my eye a massive figure towered over me. Immediately I threw my back against the wall and cowered, gasping, seconds later realizing it was just Amanda. I yelled at her for sneaking up on me. Her hair was all tangled, knotty, and there was a musky smell pouring out around her, a smell that wasn't attractive. She asked my why I was spying on her. This was when I felt nauseated. She didn't ask it in the sense that she was innocent. It was malicious. There was something malevolent in her voice I had never heard before. But her face was cool, hands flat at her sides, voice monotone, but there was an indistinct contempt running in the background. I bought some time and told her that Tau-9-9 protocol requires documentation of company time during periods of employment, and that I was simply trying to account for her employment hours so that she could get paid - not that I was reading what she was up to. She asked if I had seen the report. I told her I hadn't, which was true. The report was scheduled to finish two hours ago, and I'd just been involved with other things. Immediately she relaxed, and half-smiled. Then she reached past me into the sensor, pulled a wire and linked it to a node, and the room lit up like a police roof light. Before she left, I asked her if she had seen my family photo. There was a kind of dim shaking in her irises. Like something deep in her was stirring from slumber. Then she shook her head, smacked it again hard, turned around and walked out. Just before she left, she said families make one weak, and are inappropriate for this profession. Then the airlock door hissed, and she was gone. Captain's Log: 9116 The report is gone! I logged into my account, plugged into Tau-9-9's mainframe, and tried to access the data file, but it was corrupted. Something in the code had warped, and it was unusable. Things just get weirder and weirder around here. Today Amanda was walking on her hands up and down the star bay, almost singing.

article: Hal Smith paused before sipping his coffee. There was something in it, something that wasn't there before. He decided it was hazelnut, although he wasn't sure that he remembered what hazelnuts smelled like. The figured the coffee was pretty good. It had come with his Social Security, the small box of goods that the government sent to his door every month, sent to the doors of all the old geezers like him that had been born in a time when Social Security was still a thing. Hal was advanced enough in years that he could appreciate a good cup of coffee. This stuff was definitely better than last month's package, when he was still number twenty-five. Being twenty-two evidently had its perks. The smell of that hazelnut moved Hal to check his box again, and see if he'd overlooked anything else of interest. He picked it up from the counter top by a cardboard flap, and shook it around while peering inside. He didn't see much else in there, except it looked like they'd given him an extra bar of soap, and something else bundled in brown paper. He picked up the bundle and weighed it in his hands. Corn bread? Maybe even a little salted pork? Hal heard a crash outside, and the sound of men yelling. He stood there listening to them yell for a while, but then it stopped. They had moved on to yell somewhere else. Hal looked down at the bundle, still in his hands. He wondered what might be inside it again, but decided to open it later when he was hungry. No use getting excited, he thought. I ought to be thankful they're nice enough to send me anything at all. Every month, Hal's box came with an official letter from the government. At the top in big gold letters was his number. Hal took another sip of his coffee and wondered what the oldest man in the country got in his box. He imagined the sweets his father had given him when he was a boy, sweets whose names he couldn't remember, and wondered if they had some stowed in government warehouses for the high numbers. More yelling outside, then a concussive bang and a series of low pops. No, they're gone, thought Hal. There's no candy around here anymore. Shameful. What am I doing day-dreaming about being number one? Most folks aren't even enough to got a number. Just shameful. Who needs to live that old anyway? God put me here, and he'll leave me here just as long as he needs me, and no longer. An old coot like me has got better things to do than sit here dreaming about sweet things. Hal stood there in his kitchen, ignoring the sporadic pops and bangs and yells outside, trying to remember the names of those sweet things he'd had as a kid. He tried to remember how they tasted, too. After a while, his curiosity got the better of him, and he went to the icebox to open the paper bundle.

article: I laugh. And laugh some more. And finally can give nothing more than a weak sound somewhere between a giggle and a chuckle, because it's true. I made her a promise. I don't know what drove me to do it. Perhaps it was the way she looked at me, with her lashes drawn down so I had to concentrate to make out the entirety of those beautiful eyes. Maybe it was the softness of her hand as she squeezed my own. Whichever it was, it was a mistake. I don't stop running until I'm wheezing and gasping and generally can't take another step. I collapse on the sidewalk, not caring who sees me. I made her a promise. Damn it, what was I thinking? I knew what she would want. And what did I say? Anything. I wipe the tears from my cheeks. It's just a promise. I can break it. I'll take a plane back to America, and I'll never have to think about her again. Someone's shaking me. I don't want to open my eyes. I don't want to see the truth. I don't want to remember that I didn't run, that I didn't laugh, that I didn't decide to leave. They don't stop. Finally, reluctantly, I take a peek. It's exactly what I knew it would be. She's lying dead on the sofa, a neat little hole in her forehead. I hold my hand up, but the gun isn't there anymore. He took it. Of course he did. I let my eyes close again and this time I fall for real.

After narrowly escaping his clutches and I found my way through a narrow alley into a new world which I hadn't seen before. The colors here were more vibrant than the outside world. Joyful pictures cover the walls rather than the bland and dark artwork that fill my past home. Where the larger humans have shunned me away and made all attempts to kill me, this smaller one has been feeding me and keeping me safe. I was alone with the small human for what seemed like an eternity before a stranger arrived on the scene. She was a beautiful young fly who bore me many sons, all who have since fatally gone back through the alley to their doom. My wife..... also suffered the same fate. article: Dear mom, I took a girl out for our first date tonight. I think it went well. She's really wonderful. She's poised, intelligent, has a great sense of humor (as in she thinks my goofiness is charming..... so potentially delusional). She's beautiful, but not just in the normal sense. Her smile lights up a room and best of all God shines through her and I see an authentic love for people and her personal faith. You came up. I didn't want to tell her too much. It has happened more than once that I tell a woman about my relationship with you and they run. I don't blame them, but I really didn't want this girl to run. For the longest time I wondered if I'd ever be able to have a healthy romantic relationship, if I'd ever find a wife, if I'd ever get over my distrust of women because of you. Every time I avoided getting too close to a girl out of fear, every time I was a nervous wreck half wishing the girl wouldn't show for a meet up, all the times I heard the lies you planted in me that I wasn't worth a woman's love (partially out of guilt for how you made me feel I was treating you); I cursed you. I'm past the part of my life where I'm angry and want to "get back at you." I'm writing you this because I was overjoyed at this evening spent with Martha and..... and I'm brought to tears that I can't excitedly tell you about it the next morning. A grown man that should be past such sentimental silly things feels strongly the wound you made with a childhood of abuse. Mom, I know I've been cold-hearted, that is true. God urges me to be compassionate and I have wanted to have my revenge so badly. But this is my triumph. Mom, I know you are a fallen person. Even if you will not acknowledge the pain you've put me through, I forgive you. I choose to forgive the hurtful words you spoke about me. I actively process the pain you've put me through in order to truly release it. I choose to forgive the violence you used to intimidate me as well as all the times you used flawed interpretations of scripture to manipulate me. I choose to release the burden I've put upon myself when I neglected to forgive you all these years. Anything else I'm forgetting to specifically mention or that is just adding to the list to where it begins to just be me complaining, it's gone, forget about it. I just want my mommy, like when I was eight and needed you to kiss my boo boos. Or like when I needed advice on girls becoming a teenager, or when I needed you to help me so many other times in so many ways but I couldn't come to you. I want to be happy about the possibility of you coming to my wedding and I don't want to cringe thinking of you being around my children. To sum it up, I took a wonderful woman out tonight and had a great time getting to know her. She's special in so many ways. Who knows how serious we'll get, I'm just enjoying things as they come. But my time with her made me realize how much of a wound I still have from you and the importance of forgiving you so that she doesn't have to pay for you the whole time we're dating. Some day maybe we can heal our relationship fully, your response to this delegates that to some degree, but I more so know that hating you and constantly being angry at you is too much effort. Effort I can put into blessing Martha with a man who cares for and honors her the way he's supposed to. -Lugnut

article: The sun was just beginning to set, allowing the cool breeze to bring some relief to my worn skin. Twelve years in Africa had really taken its toll. It would all be worth it, though. Very soon. The town was quiet, everyone settled in for the day. It was a welcome sight. I had no vehicle, having just returned from my journey; but I had grown quite accustomed to traveling on foot. It's amazing to think how much my life has changed. And exciting to consider where I'll go from here. With my test score adjusted properly, my life will begin again. That one single test, all those years ago, had kept me from the future I had dreamt of; Springfield Community College. But now I would have a chance. I walked slowly, taking in the beautiful day and scenery around me. I allowed my mind to wander, to think back to where it all began. A simple test, to determine my final grade of high school; and to determine if I would graduate. It was a small town, a factory town; how was I to know such a creature was real? Mister Finch was my teacher. I had not studied for the test that day; it seemed like such an easy thing. Basic stuff, really. And when I saw the question about the giraffe, I just assumed it was a trick question. I vividly recall the scratching of the dull pencil on the booklet when I wrote in, LOL, Giraffes aren't real. Oh, how wrong I was. He refused to change my grade. I told him it was a joke, that I obviously knew giraffes were real. And yet he just said I should have studied harder. What a crock! He should have taught us better! I vowed on that day, to prove him wrong. If he wouldn't change my answer, I would make it true. And then he'd have to change it. As I approached the corner of the block, my steps grew quicker. I was almost there. The school was just around the corner; my heart raced at the thoughts of higher education, of a career, a life. I turned the corner excitedly, and..... It was gone. An empty lot where the school once was. Grass had grown a foot tall, an old parking lot was cracked and full of weeds. A chain link fence surrounded the lot. I fell to my knees and stared at the void, in utter disbelief. Son of a bitch.
