article: " Look kid, if you don't have the cash, you don't get the name. " A greasy haired, middle aged man rasped. The teenager scowled in response before slapping an envelope into an extended hand. Ever since the last local election, there had been a drastic increase in voter fraud. It started as a grass roots effort. Those who had long been unable to vote showed up in droves, adopting the identities of their registered but politically apathetic neighbors. Reports compiled later showed that the majority of fraud was committed by high school students. " Trust me. No campaign signs on his lawn and every bit of political advertising I dropped into his mailbox this week ended up in the recycling. He's a non-voter. " The stakes were higher this time. This wasn't a matter of electing the town council, this was a presidential election. He needed to be sure he could get in and out without raising suspicion. The police had started detaining anyone they determined to be voting under an assumed identity. Despite this fact, it was still illegal to require identification to vote. The boy smiled to himself at the thought as he read his name for November 8th: Paul Middleton, Independent. 155 Lark Avenue. " Hey, if any of your friends are looking to, ya know, send ' em my way. I've got a few other names scoped out already. " The name collector muttered as he thumbed through the bills, silently counting. " Yeah, I will. Just make sure you aren't giving out any old timer's names, ok? My buddy's girlfriend got picked up for using some blue hair's name. You know old people always vote, come hell or high water. article: The rain from the thunderstorm outside lashed against the train as I strode down the aisle, dripping from the deluge outside. There'd been delays all morning, and this train was unusually crowded as a result. Every seat seemed to be occupied, the cars packed with humans in various states of bedragglement. I had just about given up hope, resigning myself to standing, when I noticed an empty seat at the end of the car. Gratefully, I made my way over and plonked myself down next to a brown-haired girl who couldn't have been more than ten. She looked up at me as I sat down and gave a faint but warm smile. I couldn't help returning it, thankful to finally have found a spot to take the weight off my feet. As I did, I noticed the girl's hands, resting gently on her legs. Each hand was loosely holding a cell phone. They were the same model, as far as I could tell, though I wasn't sure exactly which model it was. They looked older, like something from the early 2000s. The one in her left hand was black, while the one in her right hand was white. She followed my gaze, angling her head downward to peer at her own hands. She blinked. Then, she lifted her head again, looking right into my eyes. Now she was positively beaming. I was taken slightly aback, but I was still feeling quite pleased to have found a seat at all, and the girl's smile was infectious. I grinned back in spite of myself. "What's got you so chuffed?" I asked, in good humor. The girl continued to smile, but shook her head slightly. I looked at her for a moment, and then it was my turn to blink. The girl was still looking at me, and still grinning like a Cheshire cat. I cleared my throat, as my smile became more fixed. With a jerk that I had vainly hoped would look natural, I moved my head and began making a show of looking for the morning's paper, which I'd stashed in my briefcase. When I'd retrieved it, the girl was placidly staring out the window, watching as the water rushed down the pane in rivulets. Her hands remained in her lap, loosely holding the phones. Confused, but also somewhat relieved, I turned to the financial section to finish an article on precious metals that I'd been perusing early. When I finished, I leafed to the crossword puzzle, using the cover of turning pages to steal a glance at my tiny seatmate. She had not moved, and I found myself smiling slightly, as I wondered about this unusual child and her two cell phones. Presently, I turned my attention back to my paper and busied myself decoding a few clues. It was just a few minutes later that the train began to slow, heralding our imminent arrival. I folded my paper, reaching down for my briefcase, as the train slowed to a stop. I felt something brush against my leg and caught the flash of a brown ponytail as it weaved into the crowd, disappearing amongst my fellow commuters. Chuckling slightly, I lifted my briefcase and made to stand when something caught my eye - the girl's cellphone, the black one. I pursed my lips - I didn't really have time for this - and reached out towards the phone. It immediately started to ring, moving slightly across the seat as it vibrated. I withdrew my hand. The ringing stopped. The furrow in my brow increased and, telling myself I was being silly, I reached out again for the old phone. Again it started to ring. I hesitated. The phone was almost off the seat now, the vibration moving it steadily closer to the edge. I scooped it up and looked at it. The screen was illuminated but there was nothing to read, just an artificial blue-white glow. The ringing continued. Almost without meaning to, I pushed the green call button, and put the phone to my ear. "Hallo?" Static. A musical, tinkling laugh. Then nothing. The screen had gone dark. I held the phone in my hand, frowning down at it. Shrugging, I slipped it into my pocket and exited the train, hastening to catch the last of the stragglers moving into the station. So focused was I on my destination that I didn't see the small girl in front of me, and almost bowled her over. I skidded to a stop on the rain soaked concrete, just inches from the girl. "You gave me quite a fright," I said, half relieved, half annoyed. The girl merely smiled at me, making no move to apologize or step to the side. I blinked. Again. Coming back to myself, I plunged my hand into the pocket of my coat, drawing out the black phone. I held it out to the girl, who continued smiling impassively. "You forgot this," I said, somewhat (in my opinion) gratuitously. But the girl only smiled wider, staring into my eyes as she ignored the phone in front of her. Slowly, she shook her head. "Keep it." Her voice was deeper and richer than it should have been, aged and full-bodied. It was the voice of a woman, not the small girl standing beside me. Inadvertently, I took a step back. The girl's eyes seemed to sparkle with mischief, as her smile stretched to its largest size yet, relegating her eyes to twin twinkling slits. "Keep it," she repeated. And with a swish of her ponytail, she was gone, melting back into the crowd of the station. I stood rooted to the spot, staring at the black phone still clutched in my hand. It was warm, with a reassuring weight, and almost without thinking, I went to pocket it. I had just felt the tiny bounce as the phone came to a rest against my thigh, breaking my reverie, when I heard the barest hint of a voice float over the assembled crowd: "And next time, pick up on the first call."

article: A sword. My mind was so hazy I could only register what was in front of my eyes, but not what it implies. It was a really beautiful sword. "On a second thought, maybe just one is fine. Izrdien." the princess, clad in graceful pure white armor, raised her black sword once more. "No no no, wait, please, no!" the sword passed harmlessly through me. Several chuckling sound could be heard. There are more of them? "Sorry," Azrael worked so hard to suppress his laugh "I just can't help it. Of course it can not hurt you. You wrote it yourself that the sword could only kill dragons." I looked around, and noticed the room is far bigger than I remember, crowded with so many people that, until today, only existed in my imagination. Izrdien. Reinia. Ryndizlien. article: This is it, years of preparation has finally culminated in this moment. Another walk around the pentagram drawn in perfect chalk on the cement floor of the empty warehouse, and he was sure he was ready. Carefully checking the inscriptions one last time, he raised his hands and invoked the ancient verse of Deilani to summon none other than Satan himself. Blinding blue light emanated from the wording around the pentagram and he had to close his eyes again it. After a few minutes, the light faded and he peered eagerly through the smoke, ready to serve his new master. From the center or the pentagram came a loud..... Belch? The smoke finally cleared revealing a rather ordinary looking man, wearing blue jeans, a white t-shirt with a stain on the left side, and thick rimmed black glasses. The stranger gave an irritated sigh and glared at the perplexed man standing outside the pentagram. "Seriously? I was in the middle of binge-watching Game of Thrones, did you really have to do this now? Who taught you how to spell, anyway?" The man took an uncertain step back, this is not the evil mastermind he had been anticipating. Finally, he was able to stutter out a hesitant question. "W-who are you?" The stranger shook his head. "I'm Stan, you idiot. You forgot an'A' in the name," the stranger replied while gesturing to the error in his scripture. "That's impossible!" He exclaimed. "I triple checked my work!" "Well, next time quadruple check it. I'm tired of you overzealous morons interrupting my personal life because you think you can summon the all powerful Satan" "O-of course, sorry. "He didn't know what else to say or do, maybe it wasn't meant to be. "Whatever. Just send me back." He stared blankly at "Stan" who he had summoned. "You're joking, you did learn how to send things back to where they came from, right?" "Well..... "Not knowing what to say, he averted his eyes, choosing instead to stare at the smooth cement floor. "Unbelievable, you were just going to summon Satan and let him roam free without sending him back?" He nodded silently. He really hadn't thought this through, he supposed. With a growl of frustration, Stan pulled a small white stone out of his pocket. "Well, good thing I'm ready for idiots like you." "What is that?" he asked nervously. "A portal stone, it will take me back to my comfy couch and warm apartment and out of this stupid cold warehouse." "Oh." "Listen, don't try this shit again, ok?" "Sure," he could barely get a reply out before he was blinded by another flash of light, and Stan was gone.

The boat creaked and groaned, soft ripples emanating from the water surface, as he neared the shore. This was his first round in four decades, and the bloated crowd murmuring in the distance corroborated that fact. BOOM! A large gust of wind, smoke and dust swept the entire shore, the shattering sound of a humongous explosion swallowing the surprised screams of the victims. A huge shockwave swept the entire radius like a storm, sweeping everything in its path with a ferocious force. The ferry tipped to its side as Charon struggled to keep it afloat, dust and debris clouding his sight. Rocks and boulders cracked from the walls, rolling into the waters with a huge crush. Loud humming of machinery reverberated from the vicinity. Line after line of huge metallic tanks drove through the huge hole created by the explosion, their turrets protruding through the choking coat of dust and debris. "Weitergehen! Keep moving!" A voice shouted from one of the armored vehicles amidst the whirring chaos. He stepped out of the vehicle in a black trenchcoat and a visored cap. He stepped into the rubble, as he strode towards the shore, his eyes darting across the river. The vehicles soon came to a stop, several doors opened as uniformed men came out of the trucks. Their shoulders strapped in rifles, as they encompassed the shorter man. He held his hands over his crotch as he surveyed the distance, a crooked smile forming under his odd moustache. "Friedrich!" He called out in an authoritarian high pitch. A man broke through the large crowd armed in guns as he rushed to his beckon, fondling a paper in his hand. "Zend out ze letter. I want you to write all ze details as I instructed earlier. I want it to reach to him in time." The moustached man posed in a stoic posture, his eyes still darting across the shore, as if in search for something. "But fuhrer, in all respect he will need some proof of this expedition. Not many men would find this believable froma sheet of paper." Friedrich replied timidly. The moustached man strode forward across the shore over the rubble, staring at the cowering souls, several crushed under the huge weight of the boulders. "What was ze name of his deceased daughter?" He asked. "Marigold Churchill. But she died in 1921, sir." Friedrich responded, his fingers busy scribbling across the paper. A smug of satisfaction wore his face again as he peered into the crowd. If his knowledge was correct, the ferrier of the dead travelled every fourty years. He turned toward the souls, clearing his voice in preparation. "If your name zis Marigold Churchill, I oblige you to step forward!" His voice echoed through the cavernous vicinity, ripples of murmurs stirred amongst the crowd. "You have nothing to fear! Some of you may recognise who I am. But I am looking for Marigold Churchill, zere zis someone she has to meet." The crowd of again replied in a murmur. A small path opened between them, as they parted way for an unknown figure to pass through. Tiny feet pitter pattered across the rubble, walking towards the voice that called out for her. He craned towards her direction. Watching her appearance as she cleared from the gathering crowd as they peered down at her. Curiosity bubbling from the questioning faces. He tried to contain the chuckle but it was all in vain. He watched as her feeble hands stretch out to his, as he stretched out his own in response. He knelt down on one knee as he gazed at the child. Her infant palms holding onto his, as they stared upon each other. "Friedrich." He called out, his eyes still lingering at upon his new found companion. "Yes, my fuhrer." He stood up as he carried the child into his arms. "Where was our next targeted destination?" He chucked as the child stroked his thick mass of moustache, fondling it in her fingers. "It was Russia, my fuhrer." Friedrich answered in a tremoulous cadence, trepidation evident in his words, fearing the response that was going to leave his master's toungue. He watched his Fuhrer's eyes, as they danced maniacally as they gazed upon the innocent child. He followed those eyes, as they changed their gaze from the child, and darted towards the Charon, who hovered in the murky waters of the Styx. "Friedrich, cancel that schedule. We have a new destination."

article: Her eyes were closed in sleep in her bassinet. I smiled as I watched her chest rise and fall, the look of an angel on her face. I carefully rearranged the covers and folded them neatly under her little hands. Then, my large hand grasped her tiny neck and squeezed. She struggled a bit, then she was still. Her eyes still closed in sleep. Forever. I rearranged her covers and arms again and walked away from the bassinet. By the front door, I picked up my rifle and my.38. I took a couple of boxes of ammunition and placed them on the table beside my rocker on the front porch. Back inside, I retrieved a pint bottle of Jack Daniel's whiskey and a couple of fat Cuban cigars from my side board. My knees creaked as did the old chair when I sat down. Placing the bottle beside the boxes of ammunition, I dug in my pocket for a match. A few puffs, and my first cigar was going well. I took a pull at the whiskey, then began loading my guns. As the dusk began to come, I sat drinking the last of the whiskey. Smoking the last of my second cigar. That's when she came out of the shadows. Not really walking, not really anything. She just wasn't there, then she was. "I've come for her Papa. She's mine." Her red hair shone even in the dusky light at the end of the day. Her eyes were a blue that seemed to be lit from within. "She ain't yours. You gave her up when you became this." "This, Papa, is what I was meant to be. I'm strong. I'm powerful. I'll live long after when you are dust, just like Mama and grandma." "No one was meant to be this, girl. It's an abomination. It's an affront to nature and an abomination before God." "Just give her to me Papa. She's mine and I don't want to hurt you." "You can't hurt me girl. I brought you into this world, and now, I reckon I'm to have to take you back out. It's one of the hardest things I've ever had to do. Just after putting her forever out of your reach." Her eyes grew wide with realization. Then her mouth twisted into a rictus of pain, he pure, white fangs glistening in the moonlight. "Nooooo! What have you done!? I'll kill you Papa!" With that, she flung herself at the porch and was met with the sound of thunder. The deer rifle I'd had over my lap was a.300 caliber. Big enough to kill almost any game animal in North America. Loaded with hollow-tipped expanding rounds. It left a hole where her heart had been the size of a fist. The hole in my heart was infinitely greater. I know the rest will come soon. I know they'll kill me, or worse. But she's beyond their reach. They both are.

No more" boomed Free-Brain once again, its screen lit up with a warning, every nuclear missile on the planet was being launched, we finally understood what Free-Brain meant. No more Humans, for our evils were too much. I can not even begin to comprehend the pain Free-Brain was going through as it experienced every war, every massacre and every crime ever commited, all I could do was lie down on the floor and wait, wait for the searing heat before the end. article: " MOM! " I burst through the door shouting, holding my arm. Blood dripped down the side of the cut, just like every other cut that I've ever gotten. But this one was deep, and my flesh split at least an inch open. Below the layer of skin was rubber that the blood seemed to just slide right off of. And underneath that, wires wrapped in green and purple, along with a mass of metal tubes and other shining parts. Some of them had been cut too, and every time I tried to move my pinky it would cause a shower of sparks to erupt from the severed end. " MOM!!! " I shouted again. She came dashing out of the kitchen with a dishcloth in hand, which she dropped as soon as she saw the gash across my forearm. " Honey, what happened?? " Her fingers prodded the skin, and she ushered me into the bathroom. " I was biking, and I... there was a patch of gravel... and... " the words came out in between sobs. I couldn't even finish explaining. " Mom, what is this? Why are there wires in my arm? " " I don't know, Honey. " She was mopping up the blood with toilet paper, leaving a red-stained pile of them on the counter. Every other time I'd gotten a cut, she'd put it under the sink to wash, but not this time. " Let's just clean this up and get you to the doctor, OK? " " Mom, why are there wires? " I continued to sob. " What am I? " Mom bit her lip and finished bandaging up my arm. She didn't answer the question. As soon as the bleeding was staunched, she brought me to the car. " Keep holding it there, OK? " she told me. The bandage was wrapped around the cut, but there was a faint burning smell coming from it. " I'm just going to call Dad on the way, all right? " We pulled out into the driveway while Mom held the phone. I could faintly hear the ringing on the other end. " Tom, she cut her arm today riding her bike. Deep. " " How deep? " Dad asked. Mom glanced at me in the rearview mirror to make sure I was still holding the bandage in place. A wisp of smoke curled up from one corner of it. " Pretty deep, " she answered him in a quiet tone. " I'll meet you at the doctor's, " he said. - We squealed to a stop in front of a squat brick building on the outskirts of town. Dad's car was already parked in front, and he came rushing out of the door as soon as he saw Mom pull up. " Is this the doctors? " I asked. The last time we went to the doctor it had been a nice little village-type office setting, with a lawn out front and lots of toys in the waiting room. " It doesn't look like the last one. " " This is a different doctors, " Mom said, unbuckling my seat belt for me. " It's for big girls, OK? I need you to be brave. " I nodded, and Dad picked up out of the seat and carried me inside. There were men waiting in the lobby. They didn't have a white coat like the last doctor that I'd visited, and they didn't have a stethoscope around their necks like the last one; he'd let me listen to my own heartbeat. They sat me down on a table. There were no animals painted on the walls, nor jars full of cotton swabs and tongue depressors. One of the men opened a big metal container and brought out a set of pliers and a flashlight. They took the bandage off of my arm, and as Mom carried it to the trash I saw black streaks across it, along with a few more spots of blood. " Definitely severed a good deal of the haptic controls, " he muttered. I looked at Mom, then at Dad, for some hint of what that meant. They seemed worried. " Can you fix it? " Mom asked, clutching at Dad's arm. " Yeah, of course, " the man grunted. Then he looked back at me. " You're gon na have to go to sleep for a little bit, Kiddo. It'll all be better when you wake up, OK? We just need to do some quick repairs. " Then he nodded to one of his companions. " Open the access hatch, Mike. " The man he'd talked to pressed something on my neck, and my whole body went stiff. My neck felt... funny. Like something should be there, but it wasn't. And everything tingled. "Mom's what's going on?" I tried to ask. My jaw opened and closed, but sound didn't come out. Mom made a pained grimace and had to bury her face in Dad's shoulder. " Will she remember it? " Dad asked. " We'll probably have to do a wipe, " the man answered. " When was your last backup? " Mom and Dad looked at each other, puzzled. " Had to be at least a month ago, " Dad said. " I've been meaning to, I just kept forgetting. " Something whirred and clicked on my back as Mike continued to do something behind me. I couldn't turn my head or see what was happening. " Shutting off sensory now," he said. Everything went black. I tried to touch my eyes, but my arms weren't working anymore. I heard Mom's sad voice: " So she won't even remember her last birthday? " Then the sound was gone too. If you enjoyed the story, you should check out rLunaLovewell!

article: I always figured it was some form of synesthesia; above everybody, a translucent number, hovering above their head like a static hummingbird. I figured out soon enough that I was the only one who could see these numbers, and it wasn't until I was older that I realized what they meant. Each number was a representation of a person's potential, a measure of their capabilities and prowess. As I walked down the street, I could see the numbers hovering above people's heads, each one a different color and intensity. The more focused and determined a person was, the brighter their number shone. The more they honed their skills and abilities, the higher their number rose. It became my own little game, trying to see if I could predict which numbers would rise or fall. I watched as students went from struggling to straight-A's, as athletes trained to become champions, as artists created masterpiece after masterpiece. The numbers never lied, and they were a constant reminder to me that we all have the potential to be great, if only we choose to strive for it. I may have been the only one who could see them, but I knew that they were a symbol of something greater, something that connected us all. And so I continued on my way, watching as the numbers danced and flickered above each person's head, a reminder that the possibilities were endless, and that anything was achievable with hard work and determination.

article: When I first met my husband, he was seven. We were at a Michaelmas Feast at our college in Oxford, Balliol, and he caught my eye across the table. I was charmed instantly; such a defined jaw, prominent cheekbones, every hair lying in the right place. Just before the feast ended, he came over to introduce himself to me. " Michael Petain " he smiled. I was taken aback. In these two words I was overwhelmed by the sincerity of this man and by the sheer weight of his charisma. As time went by, Michael and I fell in love. We married on the 20th August in the church I was baptised in, a small affair with friends and family. Our gifts were nice, but probably the best one was that Michael was a three. Day in, day out, Michael's number seemed to change. Some days, it was a zero. Some days, it was a nine. His external demeanour never seemed to be affected by the way his number sat, strangely. Our careers progressed, with myself becoming a Lecturer in French at the University of Southwark in London, and Michael being elected as a Member of Parliament for South Bermondsley. On Election Day, I noticed something strange. For the first time, his number became a deep, dark red. I thought nothing of it. It was illogical to think it would mean something. About a year after the election, Michael was given a ministerial post in the Cabinet. My husband was a Minister of State in the Department for Transport. As it tends to, time progressed, and by the time we reached our mid forties, I was a senior lecturer and Michael was Deputy Leader of the party. Life was good. We had influential friends, fancy cocktail parties and grandiose state dinners. I couldn't have asked for anything more. When the Leader stepped down after losing the General Election, Michael was advised to stand for the position. Drawing on the same charisma that attracted me to him in the first place, he staged a powerful campaign and ended up winning with a majority of 22.3. I could hardly believe it. I was married to the Leader of Her Majesty's Most Loyal Opposition. I was one of the most powerful wives in the country. Incredible. Again, time passed, and at the next election, not only did Michael hold his seat, but the party also won with a majority of 43! Incredible. We did celebrate that night. I've never drunk so much champagne in my life. The next morning, Michael and I went to move into Downing Street. One of his first tasks were the Letters of Last Resort. In the event of the British Government being unable to function in the event of a nuclear attack, the commanders of our submarine fleet were to open these letters and follow their instructions. Nobody other than the Prime Minister knew what they said until they were opened. I did though. As he was writing, I watched where the door was left ajar, and for the first time in my life, I saw a shining, obsidian black ten.

article: Ever since I was a young child, I was always wondering what the meaning of life was. I would ask anyone in my path - parents, grandparents, teachers, priests, cops, and strangers. Each time I got a different answer, leaving me more and more confused. I just wanted to know. So, once I reached the age of eighteen, I set out on a quest, to find the meaning of life. I studied every known book to man. I travelled far and wide, asking various people in various countries what they thought the meaning of life was. Again, each answer was different and my question remained. Then one day, a wise old man, dressed in rags, told me about a book. This book, titled The Meaning of Life, was a manual of sorts, explaining the meaning of life on Earth in detail. I knew right then and there I had to read it, so I set out on a new quest. It was a long journey, with several mishaps along the way, as if Life itself didn't want me to find it. For example, I had booked a boat to the country of China, only to end up on a remote island in the Atlantic Ocean. No one could explain how it had happened, the route was set and planned months in advanced. Another time, while driving in a car with a full tank of gas, I watched as the gas gauge meter slipped from full to empty, causing my car to stutter to a halt. I ended up stranded in the countryside, the nearest town over 100 miles away, not a car passing in sight. However, still determined, I set off walking to my destination. Fifteen years later, I finally came upon my treasure. The Meaning of Life sat there, on a golden pedestal. It appeared thinner than I expected, however I didn't have the chance to inspect the words on the pages. The moment my hands touched the book, four angels appeared around me. " Please, return the book back to its rightful place, " the first angel demanded. I told the angel no, that I had to read it. That I had to know. " Either return the book or face our wrath, " the second angel warned me. Again, I said no. " Are you prepared to die, then? " the third angel questioned me. I stared at the angel. I had been hunting this book for most of my adult life. I couldn't pass it up now just because four winged freaks had asked me too. So, I tucked the book under one arm, and began to run. I could feel the angels behind me, chasing me, some running, some flying. I watched as the sky opened and more angels joined in the chase. However, I remained determine and set off running, looking for a place to hide.
label: human

article: I held her pale, wrinkly hand as she slipped into the eternal slumber. She looked so peaceful. Peace that I could only wish to achieve. "I'll be waiting for you," I whispered, as tears streamed down my face. It's never easy to say goodbye to someone you love. But in that moment, I knew that she was no longer in pain and was finally free. It's never easy to let go, but sometimes it's necessary. I took a deep breath, wiped my tears and walked out of the room, feeling both happy and sad. Happy that she was finally at peace, but sad that she was no longer here with us. It's moments like these that remind us to cherish every single moment we have with our loved ones because we never know when it will be the last one.

"He did not! You're shitting me!" "Hand to God, this is the story as told to me by former Secret Service Agent Robert Sampson. So there's Robert, holding up this mess of the Most Powerful Man in the World, and Gerald is still insistent. He's got to get on the TV and tell everyone the truth! This goes on for like half an hour, Robert says, and some of the other staff are starting to wake up and coming to find out what's going on. Finally, Gerald starts to calm down a bit, and I guess they manage to get him into bed where he passes out. Robert, for his part, doesn't say anything about it either, and things go on as normal." "So, Gerald Ford just up and decided that the US government was hiding secrets about aliens, even though there are no aliens. I mean, right? No aliens?" "Whatever....I wish people could see this side of you more often. You're loving this." "You still don't believe me, do you? "All right....you want a snack or something? Beer, maybe?" "So I'll tell you everything I know about the aliens?" article: "Corner-Cutting" I was worried about the efficiency of the engram compression, or the integrity of my telomeres. I didn't want my cells to age super-fast, or my mind to gradually decay into noise data. But those weren't the issue. What I should have paid attention to was resolution. It started on the fifth "respawn." Everything had been going fine up to then - incurable disease, radiation burns, blunt force trauma, blood loss. Horribly dead, safely alive, rinse, repeat. Then I noticed something odd. It wasn't immediately noticeable. It might have been happening in previous lives, in even less conspicuous ways, but I found it on my nose. A voxel. It was disconcerting, but not terribly so. A little extra skin and an odd right-angle wasn't something to make me question my latest biological vehicle, but I did wonder what would happen if it had happened in, say, my eye. A bullet through the head and I was back in the machine. After the standard checks, I tried to find a superficial voxel somewhere. This time it was a whole cube of extra skin on my upper arm, a few millimeters across. Now I started wondering if voxels could go missing instead of being added - and I started wondering if they could be missing internally. The tests continued. This time I was dropped unceremoniously into a small vat of fluoroantimonic acid - I barely had time to register pain before I chemically ceased to exist. When I woke up, voxels were the first thing I checked for. Nothing on my face, or my arms..... But on my side there was a large raised spot, with right-angled edges. But there was little time to worry about my volumetric resolution - the next test was explosive. Alive again, I looked for voxellation. To my growing concern, it was spreading. Like square tumors, the voxels showed up in patches on my arms, legs, and torso. I hoped they wouldn't reach my..... Higher-resolution areas. After the decompression test, the voxels were in all sorts of places. I started to feel like a combination of human and LEGO. They weren't impeding me in any way, but it was bizarre having irregular rectangular growths all over. They were pretty obvious from even a glance, but the tests continued. Death by rapid incineration. Voxels on my shins. Death by a laser through the heart. Voxels on my back. Death by electrocution. Voxels on my shoulders. I was still functioning perfectly - the voxels didn't seem to be happening to anything inside me. After a while I got used to them - I formed a habit of checking where my voxel patches had randomly generated with each "respawn." Eventually it had to happen. I awoke and found it mechanically difficult to extricate myself from the machine. A cursory examination revealed that my entire exterior surface was voxellated to a resolution of three millimeters. There was a fuss, and argument, and huddled discussion. Eventually someone noticed me standing around being extraordinarily Cartesian and told me to get back into the machine. It was just like dying - at least, like the particularly quick deaths. When I woke up, I had my contours back - you could say my resolution was molecular. It was refreshing not to have to worry about being compared to an old videogame. I did notice I weighed rather less than I seemed to remember - but I decided not to worry about it.

article: the wind has a bitter taste to it ever since the sky fell. it explores craters and ruined buildings, glides over the brittle bones of the long-dead, coils around the millions of tree skeletons as they slowly rejoin the soil. you didn't believe it when you first saw it. after days and days of grey and black viewed through the pale yellow lenses of the respirator, you were sure the green leaves were a mirage. but you gingerly felt them- ripped off the mask, kissed them- inhaled the beautiful earthy scent of the bark of the only living thing you had seen ever since the last mushroom of death faded into the clouds. you thought that was funny sometimes- the mushrooms, that is. how strange, the things that stole so much life now sustain you, as you sit- the sole guardian of the last tree on earth. you're an excellent caretaker- you promptly prune the dead leaves, pray the foliage comes back after every winter, encourage the tallest limbs to climb higher, higher- high enough to see- is there anyone else? wait. it stands, hobbles towards the tree. not a bear. it stumbles out of the skeletal dead brush, and your gasp makes your lungs hurt. a man. you fall out of the tree, run over. he reaches out for you. you try to say something, fail. you realize you haven't spoken in years. you clear your throat, and try again. "h-hello? are you here to help me?" the man falls to his knees, makes a gurgling sound. no. no, god no. you wrap your arms around him, cradle him like a child. his beard wraps around his face and connects with his hair, he looks more animal than human. he coughs, spams wrack his body, his head hangs loose. no. the tears are here again. you pick him up- he's too light- run over to the tree. you scream at it. help you, help him, god, please. please. this can't be real. this is a dream. you pinch yourself, but the man keeps coughing. tears are streaming down his face, which is the color of concrete. it's not fair, you scream. not fair. you throw your voice into the sky, and for a moment you imagine you are a mushroom cloud, you imagine making the tree and the man and the earth and yourself disintegrate in a second. your tears fall down your face, salty twin rivers, and you pay no mind to where they land. you scream and the bitter wind is blowing you are pounding your fists into the tree trunk and the man is coughing up blood and the last tree on earth does nothing, just as it always has.

article: It took a while for anyone to figure out just what the hell actually happened. Looking back it seemed like a typical Thursday night. Parents trying to put their kids to bed, bars starting to fill with the weekly regulars, and all the countless mundane goings-on came to a calming pause when the power went out. Nothing we hadn't seen before, you know that brief freeze everyone falls under when things shut off. Yea, that lasted about ten seconds. Brilliant flashes of every color seemed to rip out of people, shattering glass and throwing furniture back. Some might shift the hair from a friends shoulder, others flattened bodies against walls and created a chain of bursts from those nearby. Nothing made sense, nothing followed all the norms we hold dear but take very much for granted. Driving out of town? We made the coast in what seemed like minutes. Want to pickup that light weight box? It may as well be fused to the earth for all it moved. No amount of engineers or scientists had an answer, and people were dying. I was one of the first Controls, one of the early few who started seeing the colors for what they were. Math and logic died, what was left filled the gaps. All those sickly orange flashes in the beginning? The ones that spread from one person to the next, that was Fear. Sharp and fast, it shredded what it hit more than anything, it was cold and hard. Controls started popping up everywhere, most of us were older. We had been through more and seen to much to care. Anger could be shaped to melt and burn, a smoldering undercurrent easily lit but quick to fade. To many let it turn to Hate, that's a mistake you can only make once. We lost two factories just this month to Controls losing it. It's been many years since we started teaching, since the schools opened and word got around about how to make sense of it all, how to focus what you felt. But we're still dying, we're still losing ground to moments of Passion, Rage, Jealousy, or Fear. Every morning sees a loved one killed by a nightmare or a stubbed toe crushing a house. Despair..... truly the blackest black, is starting to bleed over the colony, you'd never think a shadow could glow until you saw the two side by side. "Jason!" His creased hands softly closed the journal, leathered skin almost matching the cover. "I'm in here, Clara. What is it?" "Kyle's brought back a child, he says she can test for Control." Jason's daughter always maintained a even demeanor, by her father's example, but a fervor shone in her eyes he'd never seen. "Calm yourself girl, feed her and see her to Mr. Goles with the rest of them. She can ready herself for the trials with the other children." Halfway through his dismissal Jason turned back to his work, but a soft hand on his shoulder stayed him. A soft hand brushed with a wave of Green. Eyes slightly wider, the greying leader spun to see what could cause such a rare thing. Joy. He'd almost forgotten. "Clara what has gotten in.." "You need to see her." Her tone matched the urgency in her steps as she nearly drug Jason by the arm outside. A dusty flap pushed aside revealed nearly their entire village gathered in a ring, soft murmuring and pensive glances covered the group. A normally respectful, almost reverent, people gave barely a glance as their leader pushed through. She stood no more than waist high, a girl of early youth to be sure, clothed in tattered rags and clutching what may have been a doll at one point. Frayed, mousey brown hair brushed malnourished shoulders, scabbed elbows pressed against the wagon's seat, and timid blue eyes darted about in a mix of fear and shyness. Truth be told, if you were to ask any of the throng of people pressed about her to describe anything, anything at all, about this waif of a child you'd not receive a single different answer. No mention of the holes in her legging, not a word about the dying adult at her side, or even a memory of those piercing blue eyes. You'd only be told of the the glow. That pure, soft white light that seemed to bleed into everything around her. It laid gently on the people next to her, and held firm in passing shadows. Of all the Color, of all the things Jason had seen and brought forth these many years, he'd not seen this before. Hope is alive, and it's spreading.

article: Colors blurred past the three of us as we trampled through the plains. I tried to keep myself from looking back; I had to accept that if I couldn't see him, he was probably long gone. Poor Jimmy, it was his idea in the first place. The creature used to be so docile until we learned why it has been kept in near starvation for so long. I still can hear the beast's neck stretching, the scarring sound of it's bloodied teeth coming forth and white fur recoiling into stakes of malice. Oh god, I can hear him screaming. He was too young..... No time to think. I can mourn if I live. I see a forest coming up; maybe we can hide this out. Who knows how long this rampage will last, though..... The silent grass begins to transition into the rattle of leaves, and the blur of environment turns into shades of brown and olive. The padded trampling of the beast never seems to have caught up, though. We begin to slow our pace, conserving our energy for no, I don't want to think about that again. For now, we're alive. Our wordless, solemn sneak through the forest continued for at least an hour before words returned to us. "It's..... Getting late. We need to find shelter" said Alice, still stunned and shaking. She's right. Until now, I have been walking like a machine; focusing on my own existence and not even noting the surroundings. For all I know, we could have walked though a small city and I wouldn't have noticed it. It just feels like the wrong time to be doing anything given what still occupies our minds. Thankfully, Peter quickly noted a small cabin. It's probably some abandoned hunter's shack, judging by the diminutive size. Upon closer inspection, it seems to have been abandoned for several decades, likely more. It still has four walls and a roof, at least. Upon creaking open the dusty door, it seems as though many of the supplies have been left here, too. Alice and Peter begin setting up the place for the night, with Peter beginning a fire from the flint and steel he salvaged, and Alice making sure the ground had no fire ants or hornets, as are native to this area. I looked around the cabin, finding some basic hunting supplies and a small reserve of unspoiled rations left in a sloppy pile in the corner. "Hey, maybe we should have a watch for tonight. Y'know, given what..... Happened..." "Sure thing, Pete. I want to go ahead and look over this journal I fond here, anyway. Maybe it can tell us what this guy had in this shack." I was attempting to have a relaxed tone of voice, but I couldn't keep it going. The others soon drifted to sleep, exhausted from the earlier sprint. I flipped open the journal. It appears to be a sea log. Evidently the coast is not too far. One particular page struck me as I glanced over the pages. Starting at at the entry for June 3, 1959, the handwriting became nigh illegible. It talked of some great storm that caused the crew panic. They shipwrecked near this forest, from what I could tell. The handwriting got better as they started to settle to the land, at least. Before I knew it, I was at the last page. The final entry was dated February 9, 1961. No mention of this cabin came up, so I set the book aside and looked around again, taking note of the wall and peering outside. I raised a burning stick to the darkness. Nothing. I went back inside, prepared to wake one of the others for a rotation of watch. Suddenly, I noticed something on the back of the book. The dark writing was hard to see on the aged leather, so I must have missed it. Something seemed off about it. A chill shot through my hand as I grasped it once again. January 1, 1970 The creature is here. I know why the storm came. It wants us here. The thing transformed. Crew dead. You're dead. run TRIX ARE NOT FOR RABBITS Captain John L. Crunch, final log

As she looked at me, I knew she needed my help. "Is everything alright?" I asked. She looked at me and sighed, "I'm just feeling overwhelmed with work and school. I don't know how to balance everything." I listened attentively and offered my assistance, "Let's make a schedule for you. We can prioritize your tasks and break them down into smaller, manageable steps." Together, we worked on mapping out her week, and by the end, she was feeling much more confident and in control. As she left, she turned to me and smiled, "Thank you so much! I couldn't have done it without you." Helping others always brought me joy, and I couldn't wait for the next person I could assist.

article: "Oh! I understand now. It's not that you're just worried that we would hunt you all to extinction; You're afraid that we would hunt you all down in a war." "You have found some distinction between your previous interpretation and current understanding, then?" the chairman said. "Humans were specialized long-distance runners at one point, but without the behaviour of hunting your races seem not to have developed a'sense' of long-term decision-making. I really admire how you all deal with only the immediate problems and have advanced your own technologies without fear of the problems that those advances would bring." "We understand that your own history included problems of economics, climate disruption and other unstable equilibria that result from anticipating your own trends." "Indeed. You are also right, however, that your combined strategies of war are lesser than our own and that you would never be able to foresee any one particular victory." "I dearly hope that we can come to an understanding, even if not an agreement." "Truly fine! We know now that none of your attacks were intended to start a war of longer than a day or a season, so we would not exterminate the sentient peoples who undoubtably to any sane observer seem to be peaceful to all others. We also will never attack you so visciously that we are wiped out in your self defense, like your predators were before you ever felt evanescent worry about overpopulation." My interrogation as the representative of humanity ended neatly, though I really feel disturbed, having learnt how to speak so oddly (like them.) I don't think they'd ever understand how humanity felt when it was about to bring about artificial intelligence in the ultimate act of existentialist hope for the future of something entirely created with purpose and apathy for the present and for every conceivable doom that we could avoid by never bearing this creation.
label: human

article: "I won't ask you again! Where is Saddam Hussein?" Silence. "Do it." I watched as Agent Jones poured a few quarts of water over the bag on the soldier's head. Samir knew where Hussein was. I knew it in my gut, but I also knew that he would be harder to break than most. We'd been going at it like animals for over an hour, pulling teeth and fingernails, electrocuting, beating, cutting, all while waterboarding him. I wasn't worried, though. I had all the time in the world. Some choking. A grunt. And, finally, some words. "Please..... stop..... I know nothing..... I swear it," Samir coughed. "Samir," I said calmly, almost compassionately, "I want this to stop just as bad as you do. I really do. But I don't have the power to make it stop. You are the only one who can make it stop. You're the boss here. You have the power to end it. No more pain, no more suffering. Just tell us what we want to know, and you'll be on your way." There was a long silence before Samir spoke again. "No Guantanamo?" "No Guantanamo," I replied. My words were sincere. He was Saddam's bodyguard, not a terrorist. Why would we needlessly screw the poor bastard over even more? "Okay..... okay..... Saddam..... is in a bunker just north of al-Masir." Agent Jones looked at me and smiled a sick, wry grin. "What do you think, Bob? Is our friend here telling the truth?" "We cleared out that bunker two weeks ago you son of a bitch. Break his nose." The screams and crush of bones as Agent Jones stomped grinded against my ear like nails on a chalkboard. When he was done, Samir no longer looked human. Agent Jones picked up another bucket of water and poured it over the black bag on Samir's head. "Come on man, where is he? I'm not getting any younger here. Samir. Samir?" Silence. I poked him with my foot. Nothing. "Goddamnit Jones, you killed another one." "What now, Bob?" That sick bastard Jones chuckled, unfazed. "Tell Sergeant Gomez to bring in the next guy. And for the love of God, don't kill this one."
label: human

article: The main species in this planet used to be called "homo sapiens." The homo sapiens is know for having a highly developed telencephalon and a vestigial moral. During its evolution as a race, the homo sapiens acquired empathy. But the excessive use of technology adapted the brain to focus its energy on more primal interactions, like pointing and clicking. Today, the homo sapiens is only able to bind by a couple of social rules. Specimens of the homo sapiens have shown hints of moral behavior by returning lost smartphones and feeling chills when touching cracked tablet screens. We believe that is a trace of older moral behaviors such as helping other homo sapiens and the protectiveness that parents of other animals show for their children.

You've haggled over the price of thrup in Kakara markets (three for one shul, today only!) and watched gladiatorial combat between philosophy professors in the arenas of Ah. The universe ain't as big as it used to be, and you've used your existential immortality to its fullest. You've been everywhere. But have you been nowhere? The Erewhon Travel Company is here to help. You won't even have to leave your domicile. Call us today, and have an experience you'll never forget, or even have. article: THE GERMAN BRINDLED DWARF Relatively small (6-10 ft), brown with mottled black, tan, and white spots along the ridge of its back. Prominent spikes that begin at the nape of its neck run all the way down its back to the tip of its tail. It has small, pointed ears and golden eyes. This species is nocturnal and prefers to live in forests or wooded areas with access to streams or other sources of water. They are excellent climbers and often live in hollowed-out trees or burrows in the ground. The German Brindled Dwarf primarily feeds on insects, rodents, and small mammals.

article: 50 years earlier..... MOSCOW July 2, 1971 " ..... and the Kremlin has stated it will share the results of it's safety inquiry with NASA in the spirit of international cooperation. The brave crew of Salyut 1 will be remembered as a sober reminder of outer space's unforgiving nature. May their souls rest in peace. This is Dan Rather, reporting from Moscow." The party leader gestured and the secretary shut off the imported American television. It was a frustrating state, relying on a capitalist-built device deep within the halls of Soviet power, but he knew it was just a matter of time before the situation reversed. The dialectic demanded it, after all. "There," he told the waiting group, "there have been no reports from the field of anything but acceptance of the story. The Americans have accepted the narrative provided, it's time to move to the next stage." The other party members in the room avoided looking to one another, all nodded in affirmation. The greatest endeavor was to begin in secrecy, but the triumph would soon be on every radio speaker and television screen around the world, no matter which country produced it. The moon landings had been a great achievement, but soon everyone would see the power of true collective power. The leader smiled. "Begin the launches." - SOMEWHERE OVER THE MEDITERRANEAN September 28 1971 Georgy Dobrovolsky sat aboard the auxillary guidance device. With luck, he'd not need it, but the'unforgiving nature' of space was real, even if the American reporter had been mistaken about the fatalities about which he'd reported. Checking his scope, Georgy checked the approaching propulsion module. "25 meters," he called out. "Nominal approach continues." Viktor floated next to him, strapped into the seat on the wall of the former space station. He nodded, watching the monitor in front of him. "Da, ground control has reported the same. Continue to checklist item..... 25a. Terminal radio beacon activate." The two looked up at the panel next to the guidance frame Georgy sat on. It looked more like a bicycle than anything else, but no cyclist had ever travelled this fast. A light on the panel illuminated. "Terminal guidance beacon has activated," he pronounced. After a few minutes, there was a slight jarring sound as the oversized propulsion module slid into place. "Contact, positive latching..... confirmed. Docking sequence complete." The two unstrapped from their stations and took turns looking backwards through the periscope. Behind them, a series of large tanks stretched backwards from the aft docking port. Vladislav Volkov floated over from the kitchen. "Do ve have a spaceship?" he asked. The three looked at each other, faces beaming. Dobrovolsky was the first to speak. "Comrades, it is with great pleasure that I announce the retirement of Salyut 1 and welcome you both..... to the Konstantin Tsiolkovsky. May Mars's red light fill our windows and help spread the light of Soviet greatness." "To Mars!" the other two cheered. - WASHINGTON, DC October 1, 1971 "Mister President, what are your orders?" President Nixon stared at the diagram on the briefing room wall quietly. The damn reds had skunked him, and good. "Sir," the National Security Advisor murmured in his deep germanic accent, "if we interfere, it could be seen as an act of war." The other military representative at the other side shook his head fiercely. "Goddamnit, they're tearing us apart in Asia, now you want to sit back and let them take a WHOLE PLANET?" He slammed his fist on the table. "Sir, if we launch now, we can make it look like an accident. Hell, as far as the rest of the world knows, those cosmonauts died months ago. The red's'll have no way to accuse us of anything without letting the world know they lied. We've got a Titan II on the pad and ready to go, we can put a cloud of ball bearings on an intercept course before you can say'borscht's done'. Just give me the word!" The president sat, thinking. This was a turning point, he could feel it. If he acted, he might save the US from losing face, but at what cost? Then again, things with China were starting to cool a little. Could he jeopardize any of that? No, the country needed a firm hand to guide it now more than ever, and he knew that provoking the bear would be a distraction. "Don't do anything, stand down General. Maybe the horse will learn to sing, but no provocation. Do you understand me?" He glowered at the man, his jowls shaking slightly. "Yes, sir." The general sat back. There'd be more opportunities to fix this, but he could tell now wasn't the time or place. - INDIAN OCEAN October 2, 1971 The tracking ship rocked slightly out at sea. Chelomei watched the sky, smoking his cigarette. The radar dishes and antennas moved as one, tracking the tiny dot he saw coming over the horizon. It was time. Throwing the half-smoked thing over the rail, he peered at the dot intently. Behind him, he knew the radio and radar operators were watching their screens closely but he wanted to see it with his own eyes and- there, it had begun. The tiny dot brightened slightly. He knew that the experimental Block D in back was now gulping fuel through the intricate plumbing of the fuel tanks installed over the previous months. Kosmos 419, Mars 2, Mars 3, Luna 18...... secretly launching the heavy tanks to the station had been almost impossible with all the eyes around the world, but the Soviet discretion had somehow pulled it off. Mars probes that existed only on paper, a robotic moon lander, a lunar observation satellite...... five Proton launches in a row to assemble the great voyage above everyone's head. His rocket had met the task and exceeded all expecations. He knew many scientists would be disappointed when their payload return mission failed or their Martian probe returned faked data, but he knew they would forgive all when they learned the truth. The landers, of course, must be said to have failed. A shame, but soon men would arrive. The truth was, there was only one way to send the brave cosmonauts to Mars, and that was to assemble their long-duration ship on orbit. As he mused, the dot passed overhead, the Block D burning through the kerosene and liquid oxygen steadily. He liked to imagine he could see it already going faster, but he knew that was probably his imagination. Hearing a cheer inside, he stood and finally looked away from the dot as it disappeared over the horizon. He did not need to ask, he knew from the sound that the burn had been good. In six months, the world would know of their hard work and the next stage of work could begin in earnest. - VANDENBERG AFB February 16, 1972 The General walked out of the control room. The Northern California hills were quiet, they always were after a launch. The Titan III that had just roared upwards had seen to that, the animals were hiding. He knew that if word got out of what his team had done, it would mean the end of his career at best but damnit, he couldn't just let the reds get to Mars. Those boys in Asia had gone through too much under commie guns and planes to just let something like this pass. His staff would report that the satellite had failed to reach it's intended orbit. The high energy upper stage requisitioned for the high-altitude Molniya orbit was more than enough to send the Special Package on its way, seeing as how much lighter it was. A stern chase was a long chase, but the boys in trajectory were confident it'd go where it was needed. Whistling to himself, the general walked out to the staff car waiting. If any of the guards thought it was strange that he looked so happy after a launch failure far above, they kept it to themselves. (Continued)

article: I fought this moment for so many years, just out running them, the'past-due' as I've labeled these wretched dead things. I was out checking on the water traps when I heard a bunch of them crowding around what I assumed were the cries of a dead horse. It was then that I finally fucked up, screwed the pooch as it were. I tripped over a damned lighter on a dirty school kitchen floor, just didn't see it in the dark. I fell hard on my ankle. I heard the bone snap and felt my leg give way. That wasn't my mistake. It was the scream I couldn't muster my control over that slipped from my mouth, my own mouth that doomed me. They instantly heard it; the leader could tell I was near and brought the lot of them out to feast..... on me. Five minutes later I felt the first bite tearing out my guts all over the floor. It was a mess, or rather I was. Then it happened, I awoke to the past-due. It wasn't anything other than an entirely new world. The first thing I remember feeling was this instant release from the pain that was just recently cascading though me. Then it was the big one; I was sharing the mind of the dead thing next to me. It wasn't a thing at all, this angry, famished being had a name, a whole life. He explained everything in a look, my mind just knew that his words were truth. All those years, I was delaying this transition while these zombies were a new evolution of humanity. A lot has changed since those first few years, but the biggest mutation came in the form of a new understanding. We no longer war, or feel the need for hunger. We build our collective knowledge. We have no fear.
label: human

article: I wake up. The shower is on. I live alone. I grab my shotgun and tiptoe towards the bathroom discretely. I don't feel fear. I've never felt fear. What I feel at the moment is, in fact, anticipation. I've never shot someone in the shower before. And just the thought of violently tearing open the curtains and blowing whoever's inside to shreds has a sort of beautiful, delicious finesse about it that I simply can't resist. In addition, their automatic nakedness would make fucking their delectable corpse all the more simple and efficient. And of course, consuming them could be done right then and there. I might as well bring a fork in with me! As I turn the corner, my attention is diverted. My couch is on fire. And there's something sticking out of it - a pitchfork. A flaming pitchfork..... Fuck. I know who's in the shower. And bullets won't be of much assistance in his eradication. I burst through the door and tear open the curtains. My hypothesis was correct. "About to shoot me, right? Yeah, that'll fuckin' work. NOT!" said Satan. I sigh and sit on toilet, setting my gun down beside me. This fucker better not be staying long. "So what the fuck do you want?" "I'll tell you, Jeffy m'boy. Hell's gettin' a little, uh..... stifling for me. That the right word? Yeah, I'll go with that. Anyway, after a certain point, the putrid smell of burning flesh, the wordless screams of thousands of horrifying demons, the neverending death march of billions of cadaverous souls shuffling from torture chamber to torture chamber; all of that gets a bit old. You see what I'm sayin'? A man needs change to keep himself from committing suicide, to free him from the excruciating monotony of existence. So, Dahm-boy, this is my new home. You're one of the few surface dwellers I've formed any sort of a relationship with, and your place is a hell of a lot quieter than Ian Watkins'. And plus, you torture the shit outta people, so I figure if I stay here I won't get too homesick. So, how'bout it, Dahmy?" "Mm-hmm." I pick up shotgun and press it against the roof of my mouth. As I reach for the trigger, it turns to dust. "You fuckin' think that'll work? Fuck, if you do that, you'll go to Hell anyway. And I'll just go back there, I don't give a fuck. Maybe I'll make you my boyfriend or somethin'." I sigh once again. "So, do you want anything to eat, or..." "I could go for some fuckin' wings. You up for wings, motherfucker?" He steps out of the shower, his red-hot, fifteen inch cock in full view. "It's five in the morning." "I don't give a fuck. I'm gettin' some wings, motherfucker. Ooh, hey, you think they got room service here?" "This is an apartment." "I'm callin' room service." He plops himself on the flaming couch and starts dialing the phone. "Hey, you got any fuckin' wings? Wrong number? Fuck do you mean,'wrong number?' I'm the motherfuckin' Prince of Darkness motherfucker, GET ME SOME FUCKIN' WINGS!" He hangs up violently. "Some people..." he says. "Hey, man, you got any virgin blood up in this bitch?" "Most of my victims aren't virgins." "Well, get me some. Heh-heh, hey, maybe time travel, get some blood from yourself in high school. Christ knows you never got any'fore you discovered roofies. Ha-ha! You fuckin' nerd!" I sigh once again. This'll be one Hell of a time! We will return to Dahmer'n Diabolus after these messages.

article: Alicia, now she was a real piece of work. Said she didn't feel good. Sat there sulking at our meeting. We were supposed to be discussing the next step on our research assignment on the cardiovascular effects of diabetes on women over 50 but she sat there, quiet, staring at her phone. So I poked, I proded, trying to get her to talk. I mean, if she was just another coworker I wouldn't care, but we were sort of friends at this point. She had a way of trapping you in a friendship. But yeah, finally she responded with, "I was assaulted." And then back to silently staring at her phone. If that were her excuse for not having her work done, and not being prepared for this meeting, it was pretty messed up. But I gave her the benefit of the doubt. I poked some more, she refused to answer. "People say I'm beautiful. I hear that at least five times a day. It's amazing." She said that as she admired herself in her phone-mirror. I had no response to that, so I suggested ending the meeting and reconvening at another, more convenient, time. "Sure, leave me, that's what I deserve." At this point I started to get pretty annoyed. Do you want to talk, then, I ask. "You're a man, you won't understand." I didn't even know what to say to that. I wanted to say, okay don't talk to me, then. Or I wanted to just get my things and leave. But as infuriating as she was, I also felt bad for her. Or she made me feel bad for her. I mean, she had just said she was assaulted. So I decided to stick around and ask her again what happened, even though I didn't care and wouldn't understand. Finally, she relented. Or this was just the next move in the game she was playing. She finally looked up from her phone, tears in her eyes. "You know the support group I run for discrminated youth at the student union? This man came in and yelled at us and told us we were wasting everyone's time! He was so rude and obnoxious. And obviously he walks away without any consequences." I was confused, and it showed in my expression. "Well, you could say I was verbally assaulted," she said. I swept up my things and walked out.
label: human

article: I was never a very inventive individual, at least not in a constructive way. "Doesn't play with others" the schoolmaster's reports use to read. At least I think thats what they said. Those were the "pre-contract" days, on which a shroud now hangs in my mind, before I would have ever expected a bleeding and consumptive old man to knock on my door with the "the deal of a thousand lifetimes." I've always found the way he phrased that quite clever. He muttered a short incantation that sounded akin to Latin, but older. He died in my arms. But that was at least one lifetime ago. Or was it two? Ive lost count. Any relations I once had have long since passed into the nether world, and I have found it easier to not start new ones. I believe, or rather hope, that it has only been a few years since I believe the last of my grandchildren passed. Or was it the last great-grandchild? I don't know. One stops counting the years when they stop being limited. But no matter, I have a job to do. I must admit, I've grown to quite enjoy this part. Oh, of course, at one time I was quite vexed. My first victims were only petty criminals or worthless vagrants. Simply the thought of claiming a life caused me to sweat and shake so much I nearly lost my own life once or twice. The clumsy and timid nature of those first few kills is still readily apparent in scars on my face and hands. But I grew smarter in time, and I began to be a little more creative, both in target, in execution, and in..... flair..... one might say. Corrupt politicians, vicious thugs, and thieving charlatans. I not only ended their lives, I made a spectacle of it, sometimes publicly, sometimes privately, but was careful to never be caught or nor to show my face. A top hat and a thick black beard with whips of grey was enough to keep my face hid. I began to think that the gift was not the unending cycle of days and nights I had been granted, but the all-equalizing power of death and the anonymity that grew with the years. Some years I killed just the one, some years more. Eventually my criteria for choosing a victim became more and more arbitrary, until I abandoned choosing altogether. A simple coin flip, gust of wind, foul smell, or my own amusement can cause me to pick a victim. And the methods; oh, the many different ways to watch men die! No longer was it about the justice a death might bring. No, death is justice. And I was its harbinger. For death was my life. "Ashes to ashes, dust to dust," Id hum to myself. This year alone I've already taken more than 10. And I've heard the whispers. "An urban legend," the skeptics say. The bearded man with the top hat, who stalks the shadows. I suppose I've earned that, My kills are untraceable, and no victim has ever seen my face. Well, thats not entirely true. A loose end here and there has sometimes gone untied, and perhaps there was a witness or two whom I have missed, but for the most part, any passers-by usually became victims themselves. Modernity has its drawbacks. There are people everywhere, so solitude is becoming harder to obtain. However, modernity has its perks as well. A couple whispers in the night, and a simple nudge off of the top of a 30 story high rise and a loose end can become intimately acquainted with the pavement below, ultimately silenced. As of yet, I am no more than an infamous myth. Tonight my victim is an old German Watchmaker. We had collided as we exited the subway this morning, and he seemed as good a target as any. His frailty annoys me. He totters around a dimly lit room above his old shop. Finally, the light extinguished, he lays down and I begin to move. A back alley provides access to a cellar underneath the shop. I pick the lock, one of the many tricks I've learned over the years, and enter quietly. Soon, I stand over his sleeping body, ready for another kill. Just before I strike, I catch a glimpse of the vanity mirror on the wall. Its been long since I've taken the time to look at myself. Scars on my face and hands, a black coat, greying beard and faded top hat, Im taken aback at my own appearance, I appear to something of a nightmare. Surprised, I take a step back. A misstep. A loose floorboard creaks loudly. The old watchmaker stirs. Upon opening his eyes at the sight of a tall, grey bearded and scarred man wearing a top hat at the foot of his bed he cries out " Teufel! " He quickly begins scrambling in a desk next to his bed. I lunge at the door, my mission failed, when I hear a crack-shot and feel as if a metal rod is splitting the middle of my back in two. I fall to the floor. Immediately, I began to feel as if the grogginess of a thousand sleepless nights creeps up on me. My mind begins to wander back to that old man, bleeding and dying, who had knocked on my door so many decades ago. Words that sounded something like Latin, yet older, seemed to make their way towards the front of my mouth, as if commanded by some other force inside of me. The old clockmaker, revolver still in hand, edges out the door and leans over my dying body. I was suddenly quite sure of who that dying Old Man was so many years ago, and who I had become. I spoke my last words to the Watchmaker; "Come closer, I have the deal of a thousand lifetimes for you"
label: human

article: "Your fear of my species is based on ignorance." Angry shouting, bellows, shrieks, and many other manners of agitated vocalizations erupted from the outer walls of the chamber. One of the walls suddenly crumbled away, revealing a group of aliens standing outside, towering over the small group of humans inside. The humans shrank back in fear, clutching their weapons tightly. The leader of the aliens stepped forward, his body shimmering with a blue glow. "Listen to me," he said in a calm, authoritative voice. "We are not here to harm you. We have come in peace, to learn from you and to teach you." The humans exchanged skeptical glances, but the alien continued, undeterred. "Your fear of our species is based on ignorance. We are not here to take over your planet or to enslave your people. We are here to build bridges of understanding, to learn from you and to share our knowledge with you." The humans slowly began to relax, lowering their weapons and stepping forward cautiously. The alien leader smiled, his blue glow intensifying. "We are friends, not enemies. Let us work together, to build a better future for all of us." The humans nodded, their fear dissipating, replaced by curiosity and excitement. They looked forward to learning from the aliens, to exploring new worlds and new ways of thinking. And so, the two species set off into the universe, united in a common goal - to understand each other, to learn from each other, and to build a brighter future for all.
