article: Balance is everything. Not just metaphorically. Literally, balance is the key to survival when you live on a see-saw. One wrong move, and everything goes to hell. Let me get you up to speed. You see, I live in the city of Equilibrium, which was originally one of the great wonders of the modern world. It was constructed on colossal platforms high above the ground, out of the reach of any of the roving bandit groups on the plains. It was entirely self-sufficient, so no-one ever had to leave for supplies. It was said that Equilibrium would ride out the War untouched. That was true, until the missiles hit. They came out of nowhere, slamming into the titanic struts that held the platforms aloft. The entire city shook, or so I'm told. I was just a baby then. I don't remember seeing sections of the city fall into the mists below, the cries of their screaming residents abruptly cut off. I didn't hear the thunder of splitting steelcrete, the shattering of glass windows, the explosions of ruptured gas lines. All I know is the aftermath. For one part of the city stayed up. Amidst the death and destruction, a single pillar somehow remained standing, balancing a large fragment of Equilibrium atop it. It was never stable, though. The slightest shifting of weight would mean utter ruin. Worse, we had no way down. See what I meant when I said balance was key? I stood on my side of the Fulcrum, watching as James walked towards me from his side. At my feet, a faded and scuffed line of white paint marked the very centre of balance of the entire city. Weight had to be evenly divided between either side, lest one side overbalanced the whole shebang. That meant anyone crossing over had to wait until someone else was crossing over at the same time, thus keeping the balance. The rule was that you had to cross in this street only, so that we could keep track of when people were crossing over. It wasn't a rule anyone broke, anyway. It was that or death. James stopped in front of me and nodded. With a practiced movement, we both stepped over the line in opposite directions simultaneously. I turned and looked back at him for a moment before moving on down the street. His straight black hair shimmered slightly in the sunlight before he moved into the shadow of a building. I shook my head and kept walking. I had to stop obsessing over him. Granted, there weren't a lot of other candidates for my attention in this city, but surely I could restrain myself over one boy? Equilibrium was not a place for romance. It was all about the balance, so much so that even love was subjected to the cruelty of the law of the lever. Stepping off the main street, I entered Harry's Supplies, run by the much-loved Harry Peterson himself. He was quite fat compared to my skinny frame. We joked that when he needed to cross the Fulcrum, five other people had to be going the other way. 'Well, Kiara,' he boomed as I entered the shop.'Still ogling after James, I see.' I silently cursed the man's ability to seemingly see everything that went on in the street outside his shop. It bordered on omniscience. 'For the hundredth time, I'm not going to get together with him,' I said, taking my coat off and hanging it on the hook beside the door.'You'd have to stick us together to get me to go out with him.' 'I probably have some superglue in the back,' Harry grinned.'I'll put some on your palm and get you to shake hands with him, how's that? I still think you two are made for each other.' I felt my ears burn slightly at his words and turned to adjust a display of fruit in order to hide my face. He was right, as he always was. I had feelings for James, there was no denying it. But I couldn't bring myself to tell him how I felt. What if he turned my advances down? There wasn't enough space on this platform to hide away from him. 'Anyway,' said Harry.'I've got a little something to show you, something I've been working on for a while. Follow me.' He led the way out the back door of the shop and up the stairs to the roof. His building was one of the taller ones remaining in Equilibrium, a red brick construction with a flat roof about ten metres square. Usually, the roof was only used for watching impressive lightning storms or drinking cola on a sunny day. But now it housed something different. 'What is it?' I said, circling the contraption squatting in the centre of the roof. It was mostly constructed from bits of aluminium pipe and scrap metal. It had a large roughly triangular canvas going horizontally across the top. I bent down. There appeared to be a small space within the framework of metal struts that could hold a small person. 'It's something I thought could be used to try and get us off this platform once and for all,' said Harry, patting the machine fondly.'We've been cut off from the world for too long, Kiara. I remember the time before we came to live in Equilibrium, all those years ago. You and the other young'uns here, you've never experienced proper grass beneath your feet, seen the world below the mists. This will help you to do that.' I stared at it.'How?' 'You fly it,' said Harry.'Like a bird. This wing here will keep you from falling too quickly, and you'll just float to the ground. They had things like these before the War, you know. Hang gliders, they called them. Best way to get to the ground with what we've got here.' 'So why haven't you told anyone about this?' I said.'Why keep it a secret?' 'I didn't want to get anyone's hopes up,' he said.'It's not been tested. I've built it as well as I can remember with the materials at hand, but I think the others would object to anyone potentially falling to their death. I can't test it; too heavy. It needs a smaller body.' I frowned.'Me? You want me to fly this thing to the ground?' He nodded.'My plan was to attach a cable to the back and let the glider carry one end to the ground. Then we could build a zipline and get everyone else down as well. What do you think?' I smiled.'If this is what it takes to get us off this platform, I'm in. Are you going to tell the others?' He shook his head.'This has to be our secret. If we take the glider out to the edge tonight, we can have the zipline up and ready before anyone can say it's too dangerous. Let the end justify the means, that's my motto.' I nodded and turned my gaze back to the machine that could potentially save us all. And get me together with James, finally. If he rejected me down there, I would have the whole world to run away to. I was surprised by how light the glider was. I could easily carry it above my head as we sneaked towards the edge of Equilibrium. The moon was a sliver overhead; it was as if it too was conspiring to keep us hidden. Harry carried a huge spool of thick cable under his arm. It looked long enough to get to the ground and back several times. The jagged outline of the edge of the platform was outlined by the silvery light of the moon as we approached. I set the glider down as Harry dropped the spool over a bollard near the edge. As he had shown me at the shop, I undid the straps and hoisted the glider onto my back. It fitted snugly around me, the wings jutting out on either side. I redid the harness' buckles with numb fingers, securely fastening myself to the glider. Harry began to fashion the end of the cable into a loop to fit onto the back of the glider. While he did so, I looked over the edge and shivered. The mists below were like an ever-changing landscape, one I had spent countless hours watching as a child. Now I would finally get to see what was below them. Harry finished his work and crept over to the glider on my back. He was just about to attach the loop when a voice rang out behind us. 'A little late to be flying kites, isn't it?' We turned to see a group of men standing several metres away. They were the unofficial council of Equilibrium, the ones who essentially led us. At the front was Edward Heath, a tall, gaunt man in a worn army overcoat. He had been a major in the War before being trapped here and had taken his position as leader of the council in no time. 'Heath,' said Harry.'You followed us?' 'I was curious as to what that thing is on young Kiara's back,' said Heath, pointing at me with the pistol in his hand.'Don't tell me you're attempting to escape again, Harry?' 'Again?' I repeated.'What do you mean?' 'Harry here has been trying to get off this platform for a different reason than what he might have told you,' said Heath.'You see, Kiara, Harry was a spy for the enemy. He gave them the co-ordinates for the missiles that destroyed this city, but didn't get out in time. So he made himself a valuable member of this community to stop me killing him. But now I have an opportunity.' He smiled.'How tragic, that he fell over the edge drunk on this beautiful night. Goodbye, Peterson.' I cried out as the crack of a dozen pistols echoed in the air and Harry keeled over with a groan. I was about to go over to him when Heath looked at me.'Her too.' I took the only option left to me. I dropped backwards off the edge of the platform, plunging headfirst into the open air below. Several shots rang out as I dropped out of sight and I suddenly felt a searing pain in my right leg. But there was no time for that. The glider's canopy caught the air after a few moments and I gradually began to level off. The mist banks below got closer and closer, until finally I was surrounded by whiteness. Drops of moisture condensed on my forehead, chilling my skin and mixing with the tears streaming from my eyes. Suddenly the mist thinned and cleared. I was below the clouds. I saw something tall whizz past me. A tree? Then another. I suddenly saw something dark rushing up to meet me. It was the ground. I hit hard, flipping the glider over and skidding on my side. Then my head hit something hard, and I blacked out.
label: human

article: As the lights around me grew darker, so did the sound disappear. A white sensation, not light, not sound approached me from a distance further than what I'd ever seen. Two enormous pillars of light ascended into my view, as I was shot into the distance, out of my life. I experienced every planet, every star, every bit of time and space in what seemed like no time. A heavy beating from within my self washed away all my previous sins and solidified time again. I am someone new now. And I am ready to enter what is new, so release me unto this world, mother. A bright light larger than all I have seen is appearing, making me close my eyes. But a sweet music is filling my ears. The song of life approaches, and my part in it is starting now.

article: Luke sat at his computer. The keys were slicked from the oil of one too many cheetos, his right hand moving the mouse sporadically along its pad while his left tapped the same four keys over and over. His eyes were focused on the game, leaving only momentarily to move toward his bag of chips or reach for his mountain dew. He would bring it to his lips with his eyes focused on the screen until there was a knock at the door and even then they just glanced up before returning their focus to his game. When it was over Luke brought the back of his hand up to his forehead and wiped away the sweat from his adrenaline. There was a knock on his door. His mother opened it without asking, as she always did. "Luke, come on. It's time to go to school." "Not going. I'm sick today," Luke gave a halfhearted cough. His mother sighed, moving inside his room with her arms crossed and standing against his wall so that he could just see her out of his peripheral vision. "Luke, this isn't a conversation. You're going to school. Change out of those sweatpants and wash your face and go to school." "I'm sick." "Then we're seeing the doctor." Luke groaned, pressing his head back. His temple was already bulging. He hadn't slept the night before, planning to stay up all night and tire his mother out by claiming he was sick. "Fine, I'll go see the stupid doctor." "And you're not using your computer all day." "What?" "You heard me. No computer. If you're sick you can stay in bed and read and catch up on some of the homework that you've missed." "Mom, that's not fair." Luke felt his face begin to heat up. This had not been part of the plan. "And you'll stay in the downstairs bedroom while you do it. No computer in there. No phone games. Just your homework or a book. Or you can watch a DVD and mdash;" "I need my computer to do homework," Luke whined. "No you don't," his mother said. "Now go wash your face and change and I'm taking you to school." Luke made his way down the hallway, adjusting himself as he went. By the time he reached the bathroom his breath was labored and heavy. He stood looking at himself in the mirror - at his pimply face and his greasy hair and his perpetually neon-orange fingertips. He could see the outline of his hand on his groin, the sweat that built along his neckline and stained his shirt, the yellow that gathered under his armpits. His nostrils flared as he looked down, turning on the sink and washing his face. It's not like it will help with the stupid acne, he thought. Nothing he did seemed to help with that. Fucking ugly piece of dirt. Luke hated school. The desks weren't big enough for his gut, and he was always acutely aware of how it spilled over onto the desk. He wore his hat low over his eyes to hide his greasy hair until his teachers told him to take it off. He would, feeling his cheeks boiling as what felt like every pair of eyes turned to him. There was a girl at school named Monica who Luke had a crush on. They had biology together, and she was one of the only people who had ever been nice to him. She was one of those popular girls, with perfect makeup and up to date fashion sense. When he faked sick so many days she would keep his homework assignments together and give them to him. He was in love with her. He opened doors for her and called her m'lady to make her feel special. He treated her like the Queen he was because Luke knew that Monica saw him for who he really was. Sometimes he would bring her small gifts - little flowers that he had picked from trees or origami swans that he had made. She always seemed to appreciate them. That day at school she came up to him after biology. "Hey, Luke. I picked up your homework assignments from the last few days. You okay? You've been out a lot." "Yeah, I'm fine," Luke said. He tipped his fedora to Monica in a way of thanks. She smiled and turned away. "Hey, Monica," Luke swallowed. She's not going to say yes. What are you doing? What are you doing? "I..... I know we don't talk much. But. Well. I was wondering if you wanted to go out sometime. If you want to get coffee or something. I'm a really nice guy, you'll see if you get to know me. I'll buy you stuff and mdash;" "Oh Luke, I'm sorry. I have a boyfriend. I thought you knew, I just mdash;" "Know, I know. I know. But he doesn't treat you well. He couldn't treat you as well as I'd treat you, Monica. You know that. He doesn't give you the attention you deserve." Monica looked down to the floor. "I've been with Sam for three years, Luke. I'm sorry, but the answer is no." Luke felt his face flush. "Why not? You're always flirting with me, giving me my homework and taking those little presents I give you. You act totally in to me but I guess you don't want to be seen with me, huh? You're embarrassed by me. But the truth is I'd treat you better than Sam ever will. I'd be the best thing that happened to you in your life." Monica's smile had vanished. "The best thing that happened to me in my life was my little brother beating cancer." Her voice was cold. "You think you deserve me because I bring you homework and you're a nice guy? You just tried to convince me to leave my boyfriend of three years. Screw you." Luke put his head down on the desk after she left, feeling a single tear fall down his cheek. Why don't I ever get anything that I want? he thought. Somewhere in France the world's tiniest violin was playing. - [ Surprise ] (s "There was no surprise.

article: Hello YouTube, welcome to this week's episode of Making Movies On A Budget. I'm here in the studio with my mate Ralph and Well, the studio is actually my mom's basement, but we're making it work. Today, we're going to talk about some tips for shooting outdoor scenes on a budget. Tip number one - scout out locations in advance. Instead of renting a location, try to find a spot outside that has what you're looking for. This can save you money and give your film a unique look. Tip number two - shoot during the "golden hour." That's the hour just before sunset or just after sunrise when the light is soft and warm, giving your scene a beautiful, natural look. Tip number three - use natural light. Skip the expensive lighting equipment and try to use the sun to your advantage. Find locations with good natural lighting and position your actors and cameras accordingly. Tip number four - consider renting a drone or a stabilizer. Drones can help get aerial shots, while stabilizers can help keep your camera steady for smoother shots. Tip number five - use sound blankets to reduce background noise. This can help you get cleaner audio during outdoor scenes. These are just a few tips to help you shoot outdoor scenes on a budget. Remember, creativity and resourcefulness can help you make a great film without breaking the bank. Thanks for watching, and we'll see you next time on Making Movies On A Budget.

article: Trit was a street rat, he hung out in an alley of off 12th street, where he shared a small sheltered alcove with old man Erkle. Now, Erkle had one good leg, and a metal stump where the other one should be. In fact, he was a whole lot of weird, but nobody messed with him, so Trit had befriended him early on for safety. One day Trit got bold, and asked a question that maybe he shouldn't have. " Erkle, people afraid of you. You got tha'stump, you don't sleep much. Don't smoke. Why come? Didya kill sumbody? " " Nah kid, you don't want that story. Don't ask those questions. What I tell, ya won't forget, and it'll weigh on ya. ," Erkle said, but Trit persisted. Erkle never got violent, never snapped at him. He asked again for a few days, till Erkle finally gave in. " Fine kid, fine. I'll tell ya. No there's no sense spreading this around, as nobody'd believe you, and those that would, might kill ya. When I was about your age I ran away. Daddy was a drunk and mom didn'care. Same story you're gon na hear a lot of if ya stay down and out in these parts of town. I took a few hits from Da'on the way out, you see. Got cut up a bit. ," Erkle waved his hand generally around his face. He had scars on his cheeks and the left side of his head, though Trit couldn't tell which were from what, or when, they seemed so old. " Now, that was when I learned I's a mite sturdier than I thought. Grab that there bottle Trit. ," Erkle said. Trit picked up the glass beer bottle, not sure what Erkle had in mind. " Now take that, and smash ' er and get a sharp piece an bring it here. " Trit brought the glass over, Erkle held out his arm. " Now slash my wrist. Don't worry none now. ," Erkle said. But Trit was afraid. He didn't do it, just stood there staring at Erkle. " Fine boy, fine! I'll do it myself. " Erkle snatched the glass from Trit, faster than he'd ever seen anyone move. Before he knew it, Erkle had run the blade down his arm, sliced open a series of scars to reveal... green. And metal. Wires, tubes. Trit had seen his fair share of violence and injuries, that's not how a person's insides worked. " You... you a robot? I thought that was a myth, that them all got destroyed. ," Trit said. " Aye boy, I'm a robot. ," Erkle said as he looked down at his arm and flexed his hand. " I don'feel nothing. Just like back then. I knew it was wrong, knew I was different. After I ran, took me a few days to realize what I was. Not sure I ever got fully used to the idea. Went back and took care of my daddy, you know? Hit him so hard that he didn't get back up. " Trit said nothing. It was far too large a thing, the last thing he expected. That one of his only trustworthy friends was a robot. A light patter of rain began, sounding a discordant tune on the tin roofs above them. " Now Trit, you best not tell nobody bout this. They're watching you know. Looking. There's a reason we's destroyed. Too strong, too fast, too smart. I know they're a huntin me. Even with just the one leg. Kinda lost the other when I got hit by a bus, wasn't time to recover it. Not like I got money for a regular prosthetic, even if I was human. " Erkle sighed and scratched absently at the arm of his old wooden chair. He looked far older than he first appeared as his shoulders slumped. " Now you know. Maybe I'll tell you another story later. You should try and stay warm till this rain stops, eh kid? " This one didn't quite end up..... on topic, I feel. But it's what I've got.

article: "Nope." I said looking around the platform. Being an American visiting in London everything was magical and new to me. Unfortunately I struggle with what some call, no sense of direction. I look back down at the map and sigh. This map Haley, my friend who has been in London on many accounts, had drawn for me was of no help. The fact that she made it so simple so easy to follow and I still couldn't understand sent a wave of embarrassment and shame over me as my eyes followed the black line across the page. I looked around another time hoping to take in the right information. This time when I look back down at the map I realize I must be rather close I had just seen a nine above me and now I see an eight on the map. Relief filled me as I discovered I was not completely useless. Oh no, in my intense study of the map I forgot to watch where I was going scathing by a rather burley woman sent me stumbling. I throw my hands up in front of me hoping to ease my impact with the brick barrier. I close my eyes, I hit the ground hard. A little confused I look up expecting to be further from the barrier than I had expected but it's gone, everything's different. The setting seems familiar but not in the way I had imagined. The platform was buzzing with excitement and parents bidding the children farewell. I had read the Harry Potter books, I mean Haley and I bonded over them and that's the whole reason why she had visited London in the first place. "Impossible." I whisper under my breath as I look around at this completely different world and directly in to the beautiful steam engine bearing the Hogwarts symbol. All was as I had been described. I would not have thought it real if I had not felt the scraps on my hands myself. JK Rolling had let us in on a whole different world one right in front of us. I guess she was right in saying muggles only notice what we want to. This is my first time writing. I hope you enjoy it.

article: "Brett! Your time has come! Face us!" What the hell..... I paused Grim Fandango and walked over to my window and gently pulled back the curtain to reveal a finely dressed man with a horde of what seemed to be hot middle-aged singles. I heard the sound of glass shattering. Alarmed, I sprinted into my living room to find a broken window and a rock on the floor with a note taped to it- Why didn't you reply? I was hot for you..... Confused, I looked out the window and saw the well-dressed man giggle and wave before re-assuming his look of determination and walking up the path to my door. Despite all the commotion, the knock on my door was quiet and civil. As if nothing odd was occurring whatsoever, I nonchalantly opened the door. "Hello, I am a Nigerian prince and am about to come into a large sum of money. I am willing to forward you one million dollars if you simply give me your credit card, social security number, mother's maiden name, address, and your date of birth for safe keeping and to confirm this transaction. If you might need a piece of paper to write all of this information down, I have a notepad and pen you may use." The man awkwardly forced his notepad into my hand. He went about these things in such a formal, nearly robotic manner, that one might be inclined to believe that he did this often. "Uh..... No, no thanks, I'm fine." The man stood there, smiling creepily. I waited a moment to see if he would leave, "Could you..... Would you mind..... Leave?" The mans smile slowly transformed into a frightening sneer. "What? You think you're to good for us? Are you to busy to respond to our emails? We were just trying to be nice, and you spit in our faces!" "What? No, I always just assumed it was a scam. I thought you were trying to steal my money!" By now I was quickly retreating into my home. I tried to shut the door, but the man (with a distinguishing French accent) shoved his foot into the way. By now I was starting to panic, "Get away! All of you!" "Oh, so now you're trying to shut us out again? Girls, let's get him!" The prince, whose name tag read: "Chuck," had tears streaming down his face as he held the door open for the horde of sexy singles flooding into my house. My dog, Maggot, tried to stop them as I ran upstairs, but was quickly torn apart and eaten by the singles. "Brett! Come downstairs! We just want to sleep with you!" I could scarcely hear the sound of the girl's voice over the sound of the hundreds of singles clambering up the stairs. I panicked and ran to hide under my bed just as the first of the girls were reaching the top of the stairs. "Honey? Where are you?" A girl with a deceptively sweet voice wandered into my bedroom, where I was hiding, Maggot's blood still dripping off her face. "Holy shit. " I whispered, barely able to hear it myself, but before I realized what was happening, the girls face, covered in blood that wasn't hers, appeared in front of me, her coal black eyes looking directly at me. "Hello." I screamed as she pulled me out of my hiding place, my nails scratching and clawing at the carpet. Desperate to escape, I kicked back at her, striking her several times in the chest, but it was no use. A horde of singles flooded into my room. Chuck spoke up, "You also would have won the Spanish lottery..." To the sound of Chuck's maniacal laughter, the sexy singles pulled out my intestines and started devouring them. My final thought before Death's enticing embrace claimed me was: shit! I'll never get to see if Manny makes it to the ninth underworld!

article: We sailed away many days ago. It's strange because sometimes I forget what I did the day before, or sometimes I forget why I walked into a room. The everyday memories of our travels are fleeting. Our actions routinary, but I will never forget the day we left, no matter how far away that day is from my present. I remember walking to our vessel. Thousands upon thousands of people watched us from afar, from a safe distance. It looked like a sea, and they roared like one too. The many voices of the people I belong to echoed through the valley as one, like the waves of an ocean hitting the shore at dawn. It was dawn. The dawn of a new era, and there we walked up to the shore, ready to venture out into the open black sea of space. I remember the countdown. I was strapped to my seat staring at myriad controls, listening to the soft voice of an artificial woman "Three." She said, and I thought of the mountains. Always firm, always there, standing over us, telling us stories from ancient times. Their massive bodies guiding our people for millennia. That day they were relieved of their duty, they could finally rest, for we were going out, searching for other worlds, and the stars would fill their place. "Two." She said, and I thought of the oceans. At a point in time they seemed infinite. They awakened in us the sense of wonder, that craving to explore, to go beyond the place where the world ended, and risk falling into the infinite abyss. "One." I remember the last time I said'goodbye'. I had said to my mother, seconds after she passed away. She had said it too, seconds before she left. She embarked on a journey with no return, and on that day I did too. "Ignition." We lost contact with Earth after four years, and that was the last time I heard a voice from my world. After that we were alone, sailing from our star to the next. We had many hopes. We endured the solitude and we endured our enclosed lives. We did it because we saw our destination, because when we got there we would start a colony, and from that colony we would thrive. Last month the lights went out. The stars disappeared. The galaxy went dark and we stared dumbfounded at the empty panorama outside our vessel. The others couldn't take it. Now I am alone. Now I've fallen into the infinite black abyss. Now I wait for death.

article: Darkness. I feel light, or am I just light headed? I looked to my left and then right, and all I could see were stars in the distance. A noise by my thigh interrupted my train of thought. Crrrrk Crrrrrk I picked up the small voice-in radio. "Hello?" "Battlestar 303, what the hell do you think you are doing?" The voice said. "Huh? I think you have wrong number?" I responded. Echoing emitted through the radio. "Did he just say wrong number? Space sickness? Possibly. Uh Battlestar, in front of you -do you see the green circle." I looked at the panel in front of me, there was a red and green circle. I smacked the green one. "Yeah, I just pressed it." "Oh God, he pressed it. Uhh..... Battlestar you were not meant to push that circle. I was just about to tell you that." I sighed. "Well shucks dude, why did you tell me to press it then?" "I didn't." "You so did." I felt my ship moving forward faster now. It spun to facing a big spaceship, a mother ship. I began travelling toward it and played with the joystick, nothing seemed to work, I was on autopilot. The voice continued. "Look Battlestar, don't worry. You've pressed the home button, you're being sent back to the ship." "Oh cool, that's good right?" "No. Not exactly. We are currently under attack, that's why we sent you out. Are you sure you're feeling okay?" Zip "Oh God dude! They're shooting at me!" "Use the force!" "The what?" I screamed into my radio. "Use the force, you're a Jedi!" I looked frantically at my control panel. "What the hell button is that?" BOOM Darkness. I opened my eyes, floating in space again. "Oh God..... this again?" Crrrk Crrrrk. The radio by my thigh repeated the noise. I hit the red button this time. "Well, let's see where this goes." I picked up the radio. "Hello, Battlestar 303 speaking." "Nuaawh! "A high pitched voice responded. Ah..... Shit.

article: We had always joked that the maths teacher, Mrs. Gresnich, was a dragon. Boy did she roar, and after shouting you down there was nothing but ashes left. Not to mention her purse, which glittered like fake gold and which she clutched close at all times. But, James, he didn't care. She'd screech at him, and all he'd do was pick his nose. Of course, he spent half the classes sitting outside, or outside the headmaster's office. That was the thing with teachers: you never won, even when you were right. Nothing to be gained, but the glory. Because, really, everyone knew James. He was a legend that would get passed on until the day Mrs. Gresnich kicked the bucket. That we stood there at the memorial, and people would come over to see him, well, that spoke to the truth of it. He didn't look particularly happy about it, but he shared a smile and a handshake with them. In a way, his arrival surprised me. I was stuck in the neighbourhood, taking over my old man's shop. He was half the world away, more or less, working over in London. Surprised us all that, somehow he'd gotten into a half-decent uni and continued on from there. Never expected the old James to do that, when he could barely add two and two to make five - he normally got seven. So, I'd nearly missed him when he turned up in a suit and tie, hair neatly combed and expression sombre. Clapped him on the shoulder, and he lit up when he saw me. Hugged me hard, not like back in the day. Made me realise how much time had passed, and how much it could do. Basically took a lump of a boy and chiselled him into a man. Not like me, sitting on my arse all day selling cuts of meat for a meagre living. He'd brought along one looker of a wife, too. Legs for days and all that, but she seemed sweet. The two of us fell in like old buddies, as she drank up the stories of our misspent youth. He didn't intervene at all, but looked decidedly uncomfortable with the memories, no doubt something he wanted to distance himself from. But, well, where we all stood, that was a reminder that our past wasn't there to be forgotten. In their own way, many people had shaped us into who we'd become. The time I'd spent with James taught me what it meant to be a hero. No one cared about men in tights saving the world, but a mate that would tell old Mrs. Gresnich to bugger off when she set her sights on some poor, snivelling lad? Yeah, I'd spent a lot of my misspent youth wanting to be like James. A recurring dream of mine had been to turn up at our old school, walk into that dusty maths room, and tell her what I bloody well thought of her. Of course, I'd never actually do it. James was a hero because he was a puny git with a voice that cracked every other sentence. A hulk of a man like me shouting at an old lady, well, I'd be lucky if I got off without the coppers being called. James probably didn't think of himself as a hero either, not at the time and not after all that time. I dunno if he was ever scared, probably was. Always grinning, always scared, always standing up. A kind of trinity of hero-ness. I asked his missus what he was up to these days, and she rubbed her belly and spoke of moving out to a small town, far from the smoggy streets of the capital. Laughed, and threw in my thought that our old town had its charms, and she laughed too. James didn't, but he hadn't laughed at all, over the afternoon. The merriment died out during the service, and we wandered around the three of us, saying our kind words to the family. Of course, James couldn't catch a break there either. " James, as in James Williams? " He nodded, awkwardly avoiding meeting the daughter's eyes. " She spoke fondly of you, " she said, smiling what looked like a natural one, and not the fake, mourning one exchanged with the other guests. " She did? " he asked, surprised. Chuckling, she softly shrugged. " Well, she spoke of you. At least, she kept complaining about you and your legacy. " " I see, " he said, bowing his head. " I'm sorry, I was a troublesome child for her. " " No, no, " she said. " It got her fired up. Even in her last days, she'd perk right up when it came to telling us all what an ungrateful child you were. So, I'm thankful for your trouble, we all are. " Say what you will about Mrs. Gresnich, but her daughter was wonderful. I hadn't thought James felt guilty about those years, but she'd cut that all away. I could see the difference in him, and the smile he had was like when he spotted me. " I'm thankful for her trouble too, " he said softly. She laughed back, and replied, " She'd be glad to hear that. " And, we all left it at that. Me, him and his missus took off to a nearby pub. I dunno if I was spoiling plans or anything, but he needed a friend. Not to talk to or anything, just to keep her from badgering him. So, I did my best to keep her attention, telling her many tales about that old dragon of a maths teacher we'd had, while tears swelled in his eyes, and did my best to cough over any sniffles he did. It took a good half hour before he started regaining his composure, and a moment's reprieve was granted when she excused herself. James, he'd really grown up since those days. Or, maybe he hadn't, and I'd just been too busy admiring him.'Cause, he'd always been a kind person, good-hearted I should say. So, having such a nice and caring wife, well, that wasn't a surprise. And, getting emotional over how he treated Mrs. Gresnich, even if she'd deserved it, that wasn't a surprise once I'd thought about it. He reached over, and patted the top of my hand, before leaning back in his seat and staring at the ceiling. " Thanks, " he said. I smiled, taking a sip of something far less alcoholic than normal. But, my company was a pregnant lass and her designated driver, so I could put aside my usual for the day. " No problem. " His head tilted to the side, towards the bathrooms, and then back to how it was. " You know, Mrs. Gresnich was the bitchiest bitch who ever bitched. " I laughed. " Yeah, she was. " " But, " he said, and his voice grew strained from just that word. " Whenever I asked her for help, she didn't tell me to bugger off, or ask me what the point of helping an idiot was, or say it was too late for me to start now. " Ah, yeah, most of our teachers were like that. Oh sure, if you were a sweet, young girl, they'd help you out. Boys were a waste of time, couldn't be bothered to listen the first time, teachers had better things to do with their time. Really, it was a surprise any of us lads had even made it to uni, though I guess some of them actually did pay attention in class, and did their homework, and studied at home. " She never complained, just helped me. When no one thought I was worth a minute of their time, she helped me get into university. " I doubt anyone had ever been brave enough to ask her for help before. Not even heroes asked dragons for help. Heroes were there to slay dragons, to fight against them to the death and claim the treasure. Maybe get the girl, who had been trapped in a tower for some unknown reason. " Really, it's thanks to her I'm happy today, " he said, softly. " Thanks to her, I met my wife, found my dream job. " " Yeah, you really pulled your act together, " I said. " Hardly recognise you. " He laughed, nodding his head. " I always wanted to come back, and say thank you to her. But, I kept thinking she wasn't going anywhere. For some reason, I never thought she'd die. " " Same here. " Looking off the side, his missus emerged, walking over with the barest signs of a bulging tummy. Only a few months in, so another half a year or so to go. And, that led to me thinking about what Mrs. Gresnich had been like as a kid. For some reason, I thought she must have been like James. A wild child, full of vigour and more questions than answers. The tomboy who shouted down the boys that bullied girls, and gave them a good kicking if they answered back. I dunno why I thought that, but it was something about how he was the only one who could confront her. Kindred spirits, from different times. So, if she was a dragon, then surely he was too. Watching him dote on his missus, while he'd been so lost minutes prior, warmed my grimy heart. A real good guy, and I guess Mrs. Gresnich had known, even if she'd been a real nasty woman, who picked on kids until they cried. She was definitely a dragon, through and through. Him? He had the soul of a dragon, but the will of a hero.

article: " Are you sure, this is a very important, nay, most important secret. " I raised my hand. I could keep a simple secret. Besides, I'm sure it wasn't that big anyway. " On my honor, I will never tell. " The maiden, Eleanor, smiled. Or at least I think she did. It was very hard to see in the dark broom closet. " Good, thank you Sir Edipum. I am going to kill the Lord and Lady of Glenfareach. " This is not what I signed up for. " Hold on, you plan to murder the Great Rulers? But why? They have brought nothing but peace to our land! " " Keep your voice down! They might have brought peace, but it came with huge taxations for the working class, like I and my kinsmen. The Lord and Lady have infected Glenfareach with their social hierarchy and warring peace. We we're better off before they came. " " That is nonsense. What about I? I pay taxes and fight for my land, I have done nothing but benefit from their rule! " " You are one of 20 knights, the best warriors of Glenfareach. AND you're the prince. You are given everything you want. " She put a hand over my mouth as I was about to respond. We sat silently in the darkness while an old man passed our hiding place. When he was out of earshot, Eleanor uncovered my mouth and spoke quickly. " Listen, if you won't help me, then at least stay out of my way. You only get to know all of this because you we're stalking me, remember? " I nodded, and she slipped out of the closet. A few minutes later, I left as well. I can't say I'm upset about the assassination plan, the Lord and Lady are horrible parents. They were never around for me, always caught up with politics. I've had to learn everything through my mentor, Marlin. He was more of a father to me anyway. For the moment, I decided to do nothing, let the events play out. I needed time, and a drink, to think. Eight mugs of Ale and three fistfights later, I was sitting in my chambers, being attended by the Royal nurse. As soon as she was done, I shooed her off. My trip to the pub hadn't solved anything. I need something to cheer me up. I needed to see Eleanor. Sneaking out of the room, I threw a robe over my royal clothes and headed to the market. I had spent a lot of time here, watching Eleanor do personal shopping for the Lady, since she was her handmaid. Before long, I had spotted her. She was dressed in the same clothes as before, a brown dress with white lace. She had saved a long time to buy that dress. I know, I watched her count her money. As she completed her shopping, I felt a growing pain in my chest, something not like the pierce of a sword nor the burn of a coal, but a deep ache that comes from the soul. My throat was dry, my stomach was tumbling, and there was something hard between my legs; I had forgotten to leave my sword in my chambers. I left a little while later, I needed to meet Marlin for my evening lessons. I tried to keep Eleanor in my sight for as long as I could, but we eventually parted. By the time I had reached Marlin's chambers, I know the answer to Eleanor's question. I was going to help her kill the Lord and Lady. In case you haven't guessed, this will be a multi part series. Comment below and I'll PM you when the next part is ready. Or, you can check out rAbout4001llamas, where I'll post all of my stories. Happy reading!

I called you Doctor Marshmallow McSnugglesworth. What kind of real person has a name like that?" The doctor smiled. " 'Marshmallow' was the first words I said, which is why my parents named me that. We've been over this." James shook his head. "We haven't," he sighed, getting up from the couch. "we haven't talked about you at all. Why would we?" Doctor Marshmallow had a deep feeling of unease. "But, my family James walked to the door, ignoring him. "I hate it when they become aware," he said under his breath, as he walked out of the room. Doctor Marshmallow McSnugglesworth watched him go. His colleague soon joined him. "Who was that?" The man asked. "Just some crazy kid." Marshmallow replied, intensely relieved that his colleague had acknowledged him. He was deeply unsettled. article: It had taken him years to come to terms with his score, to accept it. So it was something of a shock when he finally figured out what it actually meant. He started cackling to himself, like a madman. Mike's Assessment, at 6 months old, was routine. They were always routine. After so much time, the technology was perfect. DNA sequencing, brain scans. It wasn't until the result appeared on the screen that anything out of the ordinary happened. "No!" shrieked Angela. "That's not possible! There must be some mistake! You have to run it again!" "Why do I always get the difficult ones?" Dan thought to himself, readying the normal speech he gave upset parents demanding a retest. He stopped himself when he saw the result on the screen. It couldn't be..... After a hurried call to his supervisor, he retested the baby. He'd moved into a different test chamber, to rule out equipment malfunction. 1 The screen glowed with the single digit number, the first anyone in this facility had ever seen. Dan couldn't believe it any more than the mother could. Anything below 15 was extremely rare. In the two centuries since the system was implemented, only a few dozen had scored below 10, and the lowest of them, a single woman born nearly 80 years ago, was a 5. "Perhaps it'll improve at Confirmation..." Dan said, with little conviction. He was among the most experienced Assessors, well trained, well liked. But even he was shaken. The mother, a 156, latched on to that hope. "Of course it will!" she snapped at him. "I'm sorry," she apologized immediately, her face softening "I shouldn't be upset at you." "It's just so shocking. It must be a glitch. The Confirmation will make it right." Mike returned to the facility on his 13th birthday, terrified of the result. After today, his Confirmed score would become public, tattooed permanently on the back of the right hand. He might never see his family or friends again after today. His parents had taught him the system as he grew up, and school filled in the blanks. People were free to live in any zone up to 10 levels above or below their own score, and visit at will any zone within 20. A good reason was required for visiting zones outside that band, which is how the missionaries helped in the lower zones, and how the criminals made money in the higher. Zone 163 was a good place to live, in Mike's opinion, an allowable compromise between his mother's 156 and his father's 170. To hear them tell it, they'd met at a concert in 160 during their college years, but 163 was less crowded and the real estate more affordable. Mike had always hidden his score from everyone outside his family. He wasn't told about his score until he was old enough to understand why it would be to keep it private. Only a small minority of his classmates kept their scores secret, but Mike was well liked and never got into any serious trouble, so no one ever pried. The machine beeped, bringing Mike's attention back to the present. The DNA scan process was the same as when he was a baby, not that he remembered it of course, but the brain scans were longer and more thorough. At 13, his personality and temperament were set, and he was old enough to be able to make an actual difference in the world, good or bad. Or so the law said, as it always had. By chance, Dan was Mike's Assessor again. He was older now, only a year or two shy of retirement age, but age hadn't dulled his memory. He remembered the squalling baby that scored a 1 all those years ago. He frowned at the display in his control booth. The subject's file was exemplary. Good grades, no serious trouble, lots of friends, a pet that was well cared for and seemingly well loved. He was no angelic 195 to be sure, but Dan would put him at a solid mid-150s. His estimates were seldom wrong. The machine beeped again, a quick three tones that indicated the test was done. The tattooing device whirred as it activated and began inscribing Mike's hand. As the law prescribed, Mike was restrained. In the distant past, well before Dan's time, people would become agitated when their score was Confirmed and the Marking would need to be delayed until they calmed down, and the facilities became backlogged. Subjects still became agitated, but the restraints ensured they stayed still until the Marking was done. Dan glanced at the right hand of the tall, blond teenager. -1- was engraved in bold letters across it. A small, detached, analytical part of his mind thought about how 2-digit Scores were centered on the hand differently than 3-digit ones, for clarity, and realized that 1-digit Scores must be hyphenated for the same reason. He'd never seen one before. Mike didn't weep, or lash out in anger, or try to bargain, as he'd been told others had after getting a high Variance from his family. He just felt numb. Time passed as if he were in a daze. He barely noticed as his scant belongings were stowed into the train, or when he was led to his seat. Variants who were no longer suitable for the zones of their childhood were relocated immediately after Confirmation. The train moved between zones on its usual schedule. People got on and off, some Variants like him moving to their new homes forever, others visiting friends and family or out on business. As the day wore on, the zone numbers steadily decreased, as did the number of other passengers. The automated voice proclaiming "FINAL STOP" finally jolted Mike back to alertness. He shuffled out of the train, noticing faded paint on the concrete identifying the terminal as being in "ZONE 60." He looked around. The buildings had been similar to the ones in Zone 160 once, he noticed, perhaps identical. That was decades gone, though. Everything in sight had a rundown, somewhat neglected look. Shoddy, ramshackle additions were common. "Keep moving to the other train" an armed member of the security force growled at him, point across the platform. This train had only a quarter as many cars as they one he'd gotten off of. The windows were small and thick, the outer surfaces heaving armored. The interior was in relatively poor repair, but he could tell it had once been identical to the train from his home. That seemed to the way of the world - at its heart, everything was built identical and adapted to its final purpose. There were few other passengers, most glaring or leering at Mike. He had no doubt some would try to rob him, or rape him, or enslave him. One by one, their expressions changed when they saw his Mark. Some faces showing a grudging respect, but all showed fear. He took a seat in the middle of a few empty rows and looked out the window, tuning out those around him. The train rumbled through the night, becoming ever more empty. The zones became smaller and more sparsely populated. Even with a population approaching fifteen billion, only a few dozen had a Score below 20. The Black Widow, a notorious aging crimelord, was currently the lowest by two, with a 16. She lived in an opulent suite in Zone 26. He couldn't even visit there if he wanted to, Mike realized. At best, he could live in Zone 11 and visit 21. The gangs grew and processed drugs in some of those zones, he knew, but they were all essentially depopulated. In Zone 37, a Security officer with a "141" Marked on his hand boarded the train and approached Mike. He seemed to be torn between pity and revulsion. "Listen up. The law requires that all citizens are provided with an adequate supply of food and other provisions, delivered directly to their chosen Zone if they can't provide for themselves. You're free to live in whichever Zone you want, within your Range, of course, but we strongly suggest you choose 11. The tracks beyond 17 haven't been used or maintained in decades, and this train will NOT go beyond the Zone 11 station." "We don't have recent records regarding the maintenance bots in those Zones either. When your supplies are delivered day after tomorrow, inform Security if you need anything. The law guarantees electric power, clean water, plumbing, HVAC, and network connectivity, but we won't dispatch technicians unless you tell us they're needed." "T-thank you," Mike stammered in reply. "Hrmph." The officer moved towards the front of the train, seeking the security of the locked cab.

article: Brian Lindale cursed at his wife's dogs, like he did every day. Except this time, when he told the purebred Yorkshire terrier to "Die like the rat you are," he meant it. He could deal with the smell they built up over spending hours in their kennels, or the 2am barking that would spark the others to echo that sharp yipping. He even managed to somehow forgive when the smallest one chewed through the power cables on his 66" flat screen television, right when he really needed to just sit and watch something distracting for an hour. But now, images of drowning the animals in their swimming pool were tempted to stay in his mind's eye. Hell, he'd even bury them afterwards, which would be more then they deserve. He hated them especially today because now instead of leaving the house five minutes early, he would be leaving just on time. He checked the clock on his phone. 7:00. Takes twenty minutes to get there, interviews at 7:30. I'll be fine he hoped. Brian carried their kennels to the back door and opened their little gates. He gagged at the smell, and realizing that there was shit even on the handles. He rushed to the kitchen sink to wash his hands immediately, using too much dish soap as he always did. Brian was the type of person who liked clean hands, and if they were ever dirty at some point in the day, he would feel anxious. And even worse, Brian bit his nails down to the flesh, so he had to be extra careful to avoid situations like these. Scrubbing that bit of brown on his hand that just wouldn't come off, he looked up to find the dogs playing with each other, covering their white fur with shit and piss. He looked over to his phone. It showed only a black screen. Brian nudged the front button with his elbow and it showed 7:03. Ill be fine He stepped over the kennels to get to the backyard, careful not to swing the door open too much so the little rats couldn't scurry inside. He scolded them as they tried to jump on his legs. "Shoo, you little shits. Get the fuck away from me." He managed to get to the side of the house, walking barefoot over their white rock landscaping, peppered with bits of dry dog shit. He evaded them all and got to the green hose the gardeners used to water their four palm trees. He traced the hose to its source and turned the spout. He held the hose up, and chilling cold water dribbled out from the tip. He held his thumb on it, but there wasn't enough pressure to make a spray. Brian had to trace the hose again to find where it had folded, and found it on the third try. The pressure inside the hose finally let out, spraying water straight into the air. Now he had dirty water on him, but he didn't care. After this, he would need to shower again anyway. He held his thumb to the tip and sprayed the hose water at the dogs. Of course, they took him for playing and tried to jump at him. If his wife saw him repelling the little rats now by spraying directly into their faces, she would be livid. They misbehave because they know you hate them! she would say. It was the kind of thing that he thought was cute when she said it, but thinking on it later would just irritate him. What kind of sense does that make? Shitting on yourself must be some protest When finally they were as white as their innocent little souls, Brian ushered them into their spare kennels. Of course, the last one never wanted to go back in once he had been let out. But like Brian, we don't all get what we want. He carried their now full kennels inside, trying not to let their yipping get on his nerves. He set them down, walked back to the kitchen sink and checked his phone. 7:08. I'll be fine The shower was nice, at least. He liked his showers hot enough to fog the mirrors. But he didn't have the time to stew in it long. He jumped out, toweled off and slipped into his extra suit. As he walked out the door, he checked his phone. 7:15 If I hurry, I'l be fine Brian powered on his GPS device, and waited anxiously for his directions. Suddenly the screen went dark. Dead? No not now He pressed the power button desperately, but nothing else happened. "Damn NSA" he said aloud. The National Security Agency years ago made a deal with global phone providers to record all audio around every cellular device, and to shut down phones before all power was depleted in order to maintain recording. At least, that's what he had heard. He cursed the NSA out of habit, but also to try and make light of this awful situation. Brian certainly remembered where he was going: for a job interview at the local paper to write a sports column. The press factory for the Reno Times was the largest building in town, outside of North Virgiinia Street. Damn near every schoolboy in the city worked as their paperboys back in the 60s, when he grew up. Times were simpler then. Dogs stayed outside, phones didn't die and employers understood if you had a bad morning coming in. But now, companies just dont care. With one of every seven people unemployed, the companies could be as hard as they wanted on their workers. What would they do, quit? Good luck feeding your family. It was a kind of leverage that would be called criminal, back when Brian grew up. Now it's just good business. He checked his phone again to check the time. Still dead. No idea how late I am Nervously he looked at his hand, and found the nail on his right pinky finger just a bit longer than the others, showing the tiniest sliver of white at the tip. He bit down, remembered his cleaning work that morning, and gagged. He spat outside his window. Best not to think about it. Think about the road, we got ta hurry on Brian backed out of the driveway and went. The kids were on summer break, so there wouldn't be any pedestrians running about trying to catch busses or chase playballs. He remembered almost hitting a child while he was checking his phone for the time. He remembered the panic, a kind of trance you enter where everything can go wrong and your mouth tastes like metal. But seeing no pedestrians around, he sped out of his home. While driving, you always believe you're hitting every red light. Like a man in a traffic control tower is looking at you, making sure the yellow light comes on just far enough away to make you doubt yourself. But now he was certain of it. Brian passed by Piggy Pete's Coffee, which was really just a donut shop with week old coffee. This was the type of place that stayed open until 11pm so the city's hipsters could eat donuts snobbily, if that were a thing. He remembered being a kind of social rebel back then, insisting that his friends listen to the Stones instead of the Beatles, and before that Beatles instead of Elvis. But only the young have time for that now, and certainly not Brian. Traffic slowed to a crawl, and Brian cursed aloud. "Are you fucking kidding me, what now?" He nudged his car to the right so he could look ahead. A quarter mile ahead, on the side of the road, a red minivan had sideswiped a green honda. It was always the green hondas. It's like people who can't drive gravitate to cheap cars they can use up and throw away. But what bothered Brian was that everyone wanted to slow and see what was going on. He wasn't the kind to nose into other people's business, especially one so boring as a traffic accident. But sure enough, every single person driving by bneeded to slow and inspect it. And once they had, they revved up to meet the normal Reno driving speed: Speed Limit 10. When he had finally broken free of the slump, he reached that certain Reno Go, everyone in a rush to get nowhere. Except he had to rush to the Reno Times, and now he finally saw their large sign just around the I-580. Reno Times it flashed. 7:35pm he panicked. August 5th Don't Text and Drive He raised his fingernails to bite them, remembered the smell of shit, and grimaced. He looked down at his hand for a second and found it: a dab of dog dung on his wrist. Somehow he missed it while washing. Oh god, what if I went into the interview like this He looked up at the road again and found the RT Drive exit coming, where he would need to turn off. Suddenly the smell of shit was giving him immense anxiety. He would need to wash it off now. Brian turned the wheel toward the exit, and started steering the wheel with his knees. He leaned over to the glove box where he kept a small stack of napkins. He pulled one out and wiped off his wrists, looking up at the road every half second to make sure he was still in his lane.He finally wiped his wrist clean when the wheel sllipped over his knee. He quickly grabbed the wheel, napkin still in hand. "GOD FUCKING DAMN IT" He let go of the hand holding the napkin and it stuck to the steering wheel, held in place with wet dog shit. He rolled down the windows to let out the smell as he turned into the Reno Times parking lot. He came to the end of a line at parking validation, each driver waiting their turn to get a ticket. Come on, come on. Get your fucking ticket already he cursed to himself, realizing the absurdity of what he said but he didn't care. These people needed to hurry up. Now.

article: [ Loop 89 ] The heavy din of the coffee shop enveloped all of us and distracted me from what Conner was saying. None of it made sense anyway. He had been talking non-stop about his latest business venture, but his descriptions were filled with technical jargon that went over my head. It was as if he was speaking a different language altogether. I tried to pay attention, but my mind kept drifting off to the sounds around me. The hissing of the espresso machine, the clinking of cups and spoons, the rustling of newspapers and the chatter of people - it was all mixed up in a chaotic symphony that filled the air. Eventually, Conner noticed my lack of attention and paused mid-sentence. "Hey, are you okay?" he asked, looking concerned. I snapped back to reality and nodded. "Sorry, I think I zoned out for a bit. Can you repeat that again?" Conner let out a small chuckle and obliged. This time, he spoke more slowly and used simpler words that I could understand. I listened intently and asked questions when I needed clarification. By the end of our conversation, I felt more informed about his business and he felt better understood by me. As we parted ways, I took a moment to appreciate the bustling energy of the coffee shop. It may have been noisy, but it was also a place of connection - where people could come together, share stories, and help each other out.

article: The clock struck eleven, and I glanced over my shoulder. The shuffling boots stop in unison with my own steps. I turned around and glared at them. Across the bridge stood a crowd of eighty, no ninety, so people. Standing silently, they were all readily equipped with pipes, and fancy horn-rimmed spectacles that curled around the edges. All adorned in formal clothes ranging from kahki slacks, to gowns that hoisted up around the hips. Time travelers. For some God-forsaken reason, in the future archaic forms of dress kept reappearing every other decade. Who knows why. Perhaps they had run out of other fashions to wear, and they kept recycling old british attire and renaissance gowns. Either way, I continued to hold my glare. Yet I was not angry. No, how could one be angry at time-travelers? You saw them everywhere now-adays, if you knew how to look. No, it was the implication that followed them. Something was going to happen. And knowing my life, I knew it wasn't going to be something good. The glare was a means of self-defense. To hide my fear. To hide my trembling lips. To hide the fact that I hoped against hope that they could not hear my pounding heart over the howling wind. An ominous breeze penetrated my coat and the icy wind made my body shiver. The freezing December air made me visibly shake, and the crowd following me let out a silent giggle. I eyed them viciously until they stuttered into silence. "Weird," I thought to myself, "Ever since the TTIP had been passed people had been acting..... malicious." I shook my head and kept walking. The Time-Traveling Insurance Progressive allowed nearly anyone to time-travel, even those hardened criminals who had gone through the justice system. but who knew why this particular group had gathered. "Who knew what kind of satanical humor people were into these days." It wasn't until I turned around and saw the smoke in the air did my nose register the poignant odor. I 180-ed in horror at the crowd behind me. This is what they were here for. I saw a small child, a girl no older than 10, sneak an evil smile at me from behind her mother's hoisted gown. I knew what this was - They knew what this was. That was my house on fire. With this large of a crowd here, it was evident what had happened. They were here to watch the worst day of my life, like some kind of theatrical satire, taking joy in my own wretched misery. Even a child stood before me, glowing with joy at the prospect. She reminded me of Anna, my child, probably burned to a crisp in the fire. My loving wife, Regina, how we had struggled so hard to conceive. And how we were now so excited to begin to lovingly raise our daughter. No. This couldn't be happening. It was all going so well. A Family. Love. The promotion. And here I was. Standing in front of a crowd watching my life go to shambles No, I would NOT let them have the satisfaction they came here for. It was apparent that they wanted to watch me suffer, well, I would let them see the clearest expression of misery possible." I thought as I put my first foot onto the bridge. I ignored the eager clapping behind me. "They wouldn't expect this. Even people from the future don't always know what's going to happen." I straddled the side of the bridge, and the crowd went quiet. I wouldn't tolerate this cruel fate, I thought, as I jumped into the cascading river below. HEADLINE TOMORROW; TLDR: - NEW YEARS 2144 DROP BALL IN NEW NEW YORK TIMES SQUARE PAGE 1 - FIRST EVER MAN TO COMMIT SUICIDE FROM TIME-TRAVELER PRESENCE, LEAVES FAMILY TO DESPAIR PAGE 2 - TOASTER BURNS DOWN HOUSE, WALMART SUED FOR BURNS? PAGE 3

article: "Ahhh, finally we've made it. Have you writers finished the script yet?" the directorastronaut asked. "Yes Buzz, exactly how you wanted it." Kevin the head writer responds "There's one big problem. There really isn't enough here to make a movie off of. Neil Armstrong gives his famous quote, you guys set up a flag, and that's it. No one is going to want to see this." Buzz Aldren, one of the first men on the moon, starts to remember exactly how anti-climatic the moon landing was. Sure the people on Earth were thrilled but he's forgotten how it actually felt stepping off the ladder the first time and flashing back...... "The bastard already made the mission his own. There's nothing left to do here. We could find a rare mineral or even water up here but that asshole had to make first phrase on the moon that? The nerve of the guy! " .....snaps back to the present. "Buzz, Buzz, Buuuzzz!" Kevin waves the script in his face. "You're right. Past Armstrong's infamous quote there was nothing really to see here. I guess all that praise I've received over the years has esculated the uniqueness of the experience over the years. Alright, here's what we're going to do." he starts pacing back and fourth thinking and mumbling "Mr. Murphy is going to play me. I know I'm white but I like him. Kevin, you're going to play Neil." "I don't act" Kevin says with confusion "Don't worry, now. There's been plenty of dramas and horror and adventure movies based on the moon. We're not doing any of it. We'll film a fully improvised slap-stick comedy movie featuring Eddie Murphy, Rachel Drasch, Stephen Colbert, Whoopi Goldberg and you Kevin." "We don't have any of those actors and I'm seriously not comfortable this." Kevin is getting more and more reluctant. "Alright crew, back on the ship and back to Earth. Grab Kevin and tie him up. He will play Neil Armstrong!" Edit: Made a HUGE error. Confused the bicycle guy with the space man.

article: As the stars flew idly by the viewscreen, Gryxnecht lolled lazily in his gravity harness. The usual sights in Sector ZZ9 Plural Z Alpha had long ago become stale like day-old rations, and Gryxnecht found himself yearning for something new and exciting. Just then, a strange blip appeared on the ship's radar. "Captain, we have an unknown object approaching us," Gryxnecht reported to his superior. The captain quickly ordered the crew to prepare for potential danger, but as the object drew closer, it became clear that it was not a threat. In fact, it was nothing like they had ever seen before. It was a small, sleek ship that glowed with an otherworldly light, and it maneuvered gracefully around the captain's vessel. As it came closer, Gryxnecht could see that it was being piloted by a creature unlike any he had seen before. It had a lithe, almost serpentine body, adorned with shimmering scales that changed color in the light. Its head was that of a dragon, with fierce claws and an intense gaze. The captain hailed the strange ship, and to everyone's surprise, the dragon creature responded in a language that they could understand. "Greetings, travelers. I am Eriryxion, a dragon of the stars. I come in peace." Gryxnecht and the crew were stunned. They had never encountered intelligent alien life before, let alone a creature straight out of a fantasy novel. But as Eriryxion spoke to them, they realized that anything was possible in the vast expanse of space. And so began a new adventure for Gryxnecht and his crew, traveling the cosmos with their draconic companion and discovering wonders beyond their wildest dreams.

article: This is a different kind of battle, if it does not fit, feel free to delete...... It happens over and over again. The squad lines up to go, our Team Chief gives a thumbs-up, a loud snap, and he is down on the ground. As I struggle to tend to his wounds, I see the light leave his eyes. We are driving to an Iraqi police station to help train some of the new officers. Everyone in the Humvee is happy. We are talking about going home, the Insane Clown Posse, how nice grass is, whatever. We laugh and joke as we hear a loud concussion and sand, rock, and debris obscure the vehicle in front of us. Children pick through mounds of garbage, in bare feet and 120o heat, looking for scraps of unspoiled food. Bodies lay in the ditch, dead for hours, blindfolded and shot executioner style, murdered because they don't support a local tribe leader. A new widower won't stop crying, and her children look off into the distance. They are broken. It is so hot, everything smells like sewage, human excrement puddles in the streets. Garbage lines the roads, with all of this debris, how do we know if there is a bomb or not? We can't stop at every bag... Boom! Smiles. Frowns. Happiness. Devastation. Dead friends talk to me about lives they will never return to. I wake up. Sweat beads on my brow. My heart pounds in my throat. I look at the clock. 2:12 AM. Looks like another night of no sleep. I get out of bed and do a quick check through the house. Wife is sleeping next to me, check. Daughter is in her bed, sleeping. I notice that she isn't quite covered up and is shivering a little. Her stuffed animal, aptly named " Pink Puppy " is just out of her reach. I place the toy under her arm and cover her back up. She shifts a little and is still. I check the locks. The house is secure. A mix of adrenaline and shame floods through my system. It was all supposed to get better after we got back. It is supposed to be safe here, but I can't get these images out of my head. Life is so much easier when you realize that it can end at any time. Living in the moment was easy. Then you get back home and time stretches out before you, as the past pistol whips you in the back of the head. I am so irritable lately, the slightest things set me off. I can't sleep. My wife doesn't want to talk about these thoughts that I need to purge, and I can see small hints of fear in my daughter's eyes when I lose it over something insignificant. I would never hit her, but I am afraid I do more damage with my voice. They would be so much better off without me. That 450k would fix most of their problems. Getting myself out of the picture would certainly help. Work sucks. These civilians have no work ethic, and they are pissed at me for wanting to do things right. You give a lazy dude a little " encouragement " and you are down talking to your supervisor again about " being PC " and " hurting their feelings, " well, his lack of integrity hurts my feelings. I walk back into our room, and reach under the bed. I grab the gun safe and take it out with me to the living room. I quickly punch in the code that opens the box, and pull out my 9mm. Even in the darkness, light reflects off of the firearm's surface. One well-placed shot, and all of this ends. I don't want my family to find me though. When I have nights like this, I sometimes go for a drive. This time though, I won't be coming back. I go back for one last look at my daughter. God, I love her. I hope that she will be ok. Her dog is missing, probably rolled under her blanket; I hope he watches over her. I close her bedroom door and leave. When we were dating, my wife and I would go hang out at a local 24hr supermarket after hours. The lots were always full of cars at all hours. I could simply park there, pull the trigger, and no one would notice. On the drive there, I pass under a viaduct, and swerve the car over to the other side, avoiding an explosion that never comes. Had another car been coming in the other direction, it could have been bad for them. I start noticing every little piece of trash on the empty roads and scrutinize all of it. My senses are hiked up to 1000, for realty no reason, and I can't shut it down. After what feels like an age has passed, I pull into the lot. I pull the pistol out from the small of my back, and look at it. I hear a bark. I look down into my passenger seat, and Pink Puppy is sitting there. Its head is cocked to the side, as if inquiring about what I am doing here, in this lot, at 3am. I set the pistol down on the center console, and the stuffed dog's tail begins to wag. Soon, his whole backside is wagging and he leaps into my lap. He buries his head into my shoulder and lets out a low whine, as if trying to give me a hug. I break down. It is as if a dam has opened, and tears flow down my face as cooped up memories begin to flee my brain. I pul this small, pink-spotted toy into a hug of my own and give over to emotion for the first time in what feels like an eternity. I set Pink Puppy in the passenger seat, and begin to tell him stories of my experiences. He seems to be listening intently. There is the occasional cock of the head, gleam of a button eye, or thump of a tail as I discuss my hopes for the future and fear of the past. I am sure that if anyone walked by and saw me talking to a stuffed dog they would think I was crazy, but, well, I may be. Before long, I look again at the clock, my wife gets up soon for work, and my daughter will need to get ready for preschool. I put the weapon under the driver's seat and place the puppy in my lap. Together, we drive home. On the way, I feel like a new man. I know that I have demons to work out. This isn't a one night and done kind of thing, but we can make it. I try to unlock the front door as quietly as I can and move stealthily into my daughter's room. I look once more at Pink Puppy, smile, and again put him under her arm. She snuggles into him, giving him a big hug. As I walk out I hear her tiny, sleepy voice, " Daddy, when you tucked me in last night, you seemed sad. I asked Pink Puppy to help. " She looks at me, blond hair sticking up in a million directions, blue eyes that pierce my soul, and the sleepy smile of a toddler that makes your heart grow three sizes. I look at her through watery eyes, " Thank you, Kiddo, Pink Puppy helped me to feel a whole lot better. " She smiles again, " I knew he would, I love you Daddy. " and before I can say it back, she drifts back to sleep. I go into the bedroom, lay down next to my wife. I close my eyes and sleep.

article: Al had walked in first. He knew his friend, Tritius, was following him. Al sat down, in front of the bartender. "What would you like?" The bartender's words were dull and monotonous. Al looked over his shoulder to see if Tritius had arrived yet. "I'll have a beer for now. Let me know if my friend Tritius shows up, he should be here any minute." The bartender grunted and grabbed a cold bottle from the fridge. Al took a sip while keeping an eye on the door. A few minutes later, Tritius walked in and took a seat next to him. "Glad you could make it," Al said as he turned to greet him. "Of course, I wouldn't miss out on a drink with my old friend," Tritius replied with a smile. The bartender walked over to Tritius and asked, "What can I get for you?" "I'll have the same," Tritius said, pointing to Al's half-empty bottle. As they sat and caught up on old times, the bartender listened in on their conversation, cleaning glasses and wiping down the bar. "Have you heard about the new restaurant that opened up down the street?" Al asked, taking another sip of his beer. "No, I haven't. What's it called?" Tritius replied, leaning in with interest. "It's called The Wild Boar. I heard they have the best steak in town," Al said, excitedly. The bartender made a mental note to check out the new restaurant when he had the chance. He figured if Al and Tritius were recommending it, it must be worth a visit. After finishing their drinks, Al and Tritius thanked the bartender and headed out the door. The bartender watched them go, feeling content with the knowledge that he had provided them with a pleasant experience.
