article: (So I worked out a concept based on the idea, taking it into a little more extreme direction. I found the concept really interesting, especially taking it to its logical conclusions of brain enhancement. I may have took the'Religion' part a little too literally, but if you're interested in more or more detail about the world I was thinking of, let me know.) Even for the trusted, it's a hassle getting down here. Three biometric scanners get me into the Ecclasiarchy's data center. Bodyscan, DNA, mental key. I stand in the final chamber, listening to the low-volume hymns in soft white light, and think of the well-worn pages of the bible on the lectern, the first day I gave a sermon. The light flicks on, a golden-white, and the door hisses and opens. It's pointless really, the thing could have verified who I was without me having to do anything, but we've always held ourselves to tradition. The hum of cooling systems is all I can hear; the man-sized blocks of alabaster computing substrate aren't hot enough to glow on their own, but they do radiate heat if you get close enough. I'm tech support now, well, I'm still a priest. But there's an ever-increasing personnel shortage and we all end up doing double duty somewhere. The facility's Seraphim dispatched little more than a shade of a angel saying some piece of equipment down here needed maintenance, so I'm here, in my robes, and a toolbox. I know if the Seraphim wasn't able to fix it remotely it's going to be a pain in the posterior. Walking past those alabaster pillars you can't help but think about what they represent. One hundred forty five million and counting. Looking directly at one, I could almost hear a choir of angels in my head. My metabrain said it was a synesthetic thing, that I was doing it to myself, but I wouldn't put it past the Seraphim to add a little trickery to it all. They're all devious bastards in some ways, God forgive me. My own modest neural circuitry pointed me in the right direction, down hundreds of rows of radiant white substrate like gigantic tombstones laid out in a perfect grid. Rounding the final corner, the ground was covered in hundreds of coppery, metal swirls, spread out like someone dropped a jar of them. Copper shavings. Looking at the scatter, they all seemed to have come from what looked like a dead camera. What could have happened here? The camera dome had a blackened hole where the ultrahard material had fractured outward. Some kind of overload? I unfolded a step ladder, and took the panel off the ceiling with a crowbar, reaching up to the conduit. These things are quadruply redundant, built to last out of nanospecced material, internal power supply, wireless, conduit backed up. I grabbed my headlamp and looked around in the ceiling space. The conduit was severed, pinched on two ends with something strong enough to bend the metal until the interior links were cut. More copper shavings everywhere. The area around the camera had been sawn open, cleanly. I shook my head. It looked like sabotage, but how? And what use was sabotaging one camera? Exiting the ceiling I looked from the hole in the camera's dome forward. On the substrate pillar around 4 meters away, there was a black dot. I rushed over to it, triggering a gentle haptic feedback from my brain as I approached the personnel restricted boundary and could go no closer. But from there I could see the black dot; A little spike embedded in the substrate. Invaders in heaven. I instantly called for help, and found my sensorium elevated through the choirs almost instantly to the Seraphim's level. Couldn't even look at the thing directly of course, but it didn't waste time asking any questions, just rifled through my brain for the appropriate information. I'm guessing. In the church you sign away your own private key for that stuff to the Administration. A matter of trust. An insane thing to do anywhere else in the world, but if I didn't buy into the whole righteous-servants-of-God-on-earth thing I wouldn't even be here. Of course men are fallible, even the most righteous man is, but the Angels are not. If they fail in anything, it was because it was impossible, not because it was an oversight. And it solved the problem of those lip-service priests with ulterior motives, no force on Earth could lie so thoroughly to itself that these things couldn't see their true colors. My sensorium returned to the real world as quickly as it was snatched away, my body steadfastly holding itself up until I resumed control. There were no lights on the attacked substrate in front of me, but I could tell something had been done. It just didn't seem to glow the same.

article: "Would you look at that..." Bits of Corporal Fulton started to crumble into scale, the dust lost to the blowing wind. One of them had to have been the mage as time resumed its normal course, relativity surging back like a flood into the temporal void. For a brief, terrifying second the winds whipped around with hurricane force before settling, all the muted noise impacting against his ears in a deafening roar. Flint felt something trickle from his ears, tasted blood on his lips. - Thirty minutes later and it was all over, save for the grim task of burying the dead. Their own casualties received marked graves, their bodies wrapped in their green cloaks. For the enemy dead they dug a trench and pushed the naked corpses in, pouring kerosene over the lot. The smell of burning flesh filled their noses like overdone pork. The mage had started crawling away, a trail of blood and bloody bandages left in his wake. Flint followed it, bayonet in hand. article: It had been an astonishing week, Aquinas thought as he sat down to take a breather. The comfortable couch in his room was his favorite place to relax. A mixture of business and pleasure; he'd placed his room close to the crew center, in case of emergency, but had also great pains (mostly wounds to the wallet) to ensure he had a wall built of holoscreens, which displayed the view from the ship all around him. It was beautiful - it always was. Right now, he had a view of the star LOGLA. On the approach he'd admired its brilliance, the way the plasma arced and danced on its surface. That was before he'd spoken to it. The initial communications had been halting, uncertain. Stars had very different minds than humans, in many ways. It'd taken thousands of years to realize they were even capable of thought. It had taken hundreds to decipher their thoughts. The stars, it turned out, had similar difficulties understanding us. We were motes of dust to them, insignificant in the passage of time. The stars - communicating on their own medium still largely inaccessible to us, the'sea' as they called it - had debated the significance of humans ever since we'd left our atmosphere. The lines between the animate and the inanimate had been blurred. Stars saw all things as living, in some sense - some more so than others, of course. Stars did not quite propagate, or survive. They simply..... were, until they weren't. And they thought for that entire time. To the stars, it turns out, they'd just assumed we were intelligent. They assumed all things were intelligent. Perhaps not capable of communication or comprehension, but still possibly thinking on some plane of existence. "They are, therefore they think." It was a compelling point of view, all things considered. If we could talk to stars, why not to other things? Aquinas sighed, as he shifted in his chair to get back up. Only a moment's rest. The basic politics has been discussed, the nature of stars, what they wanted and did not want..... it had been largely business. There'd been moments of insight and true talk, here and there, but for the most part it was the simple procedure of extraterrestrial contact the System's scientists had sorted out centuries before. Stars were independent bodies, but didn't much care about anything else - they felt no pain, and did not care what installations we built around them, or how we traversed them. The only thing they requested was that they be allowed to think, as long as possible. Aquinas rose from his chair, and crossed the room. The auxiliary controls in his room had been another nice touch. Built for emergencies, but..... it's not like what he was about to do could hurt. He reached down, fiddled with some controls - that transmitted very complicated directions to a very big machine on the ship - and was linked into the communication medium, a swirling ball of plasma that was magnetically controlled to produce new shapes, configurations, and energy patterns. After a moment in silence, standing over the controls, bowed with his hands flat against the surface of the countertop, he spoke up. "Logla, you listening?" He asked. The star had no name. No stars did. It had agreed on one, however, given the nature of human communication. So it had been decided to name it Logla, and the star agreed that when we said Logla, it would answer. And it did. "I'm here, Aquinas." He piqued up at this, as he always did. It recognized him, despite the communication medium - and the fact he hadn't said much of note. There was some other means of identification..... which was surprising, given stars had no need for such identification. A quick learner, it seemed. "What thoughts do we have to attend to?" Aquinas chuckled. Stars did little else but think, so Logla had an issue phrasing any activity as something other than thinking. It understood the activities, well enough, but it just preferred not to speak of them in human terms. "Nothing to attend to, today, Logla. I just wanted to think together." A soft humming came from the speaker. This indicated the star was processing, preparing to vocalize thoughts. A very human mannerism. Eventually, Logla spoke up. "This sounds agreeable. It is something stars do often, and enjoy." "Enjoy? You don't talk about emotion a lot, Logla. To be honest..." Aquinas pondered whether to continue, but shrugged and went on anyway. "We weren't quite sure you felt things like we did. You know, felt them as much." The star hummed again. "Most likely not, Aquinas. But we still feel. Feeling is just another form of thinking, after all." Aquinas smiled. "That's one way of putting it," Aquinas sat back down in his chair, no longer nervous about how poorly unsupervised contact might go. Logla was a very nice star, so far. It was pretty damn unlikely he'd upset it. He wasn't even sure what could. At this thought, Aquinas sat, tapped his chin, then pressed the button to continue speaking. "What makes you feel, Logla? And what do you feel?" The star hummed, for a long time. At least a minute. This was unusual - most thoughts took stars very little time, because they had very, very big brains. Finally, the star continued, "Everything makes me feel, Aquinas. How could it not? Stars have a long time to think..... and with a long time, everything becomes worth thinking about," The star hummed shortly, then continued, "I feel..... happy. Sad. Curious." Aquinas raised an eyebrow. "Not afraid? Not angry?" "Those are unintelligible to me. Rethink your thoughts for me, Aquinas?" This was a fun oddity of inter-species communication. Stars rarely did not understand each other, they had learned - it was only external interference that caused issues with communication. Logla did not quite understand the idea of'untranslatable' concepts yet - but it very well understood interference, and just acted like it was that. "Well, anger..... it's..... when something is wrong. Or when something endangers you. Do you ever feel so strongly, you want to..." Aquinas realized that there wasn't really much the star could do, or want to do. Stars could not move. They could not act. They could barely even perceive, it turned out. They largely existed just to think. Anger would be meaningless for them..... they couldn't act out. And fear..... they couldn't retreat. Aquinas paused, and shook his head. "I'm sorry, Logla. I don't think there's a way to rethink that thought without interference." A soft humming, then Logla replied, "That's okay, Aquinas. I understand, though I am curious and sad." "Sad?" Aquinas rested his face on his arm, holding his button down with the other hand. "Why, Logla?" "I wish I could understand. Curiosity that goes without answer..... it causes sadness. A wish things were different," Logla spoke slowly, far more slowly than normal. "Curiosity answered brings happiness." "That's all?" Aquinas asked, quietly. "You feel happiness and sadness only then?" "No..... We feel happiness to know. We enjoy thinking. And some things are pleasing to think about. While others..... we feel sadness to confront. And some things are sad to think about," Logla's speech was very slow now. "Some things are both." "I understand. We feel similarly. We call it'bittersweet'. I have no idea if that thought will be conveyed right, but..... it's a pairing of opposites. Like dark and light, at once." Stars understood light very well. "It seems contradictory, but..." "But it isn't. I understand. The thought conveyed poorly, but I think the thought too. There are many experiences that bring both happiness and sadness. Like you." Aquinas nodded, quietly. The gesture would be translated by the machine, but he still reaffirmed it, and said, "Yes. Like you too." "Aquinas, we - I - are happy to know you exist. That you think like we do. And that we can speak. There have been so few..... so few that can speak to us, besides us," The star said, and Aquinas nodded. The stars had mentioned other people that spoke to stars. They hadn't said much about them, but it was much more than mankind had expected to hear. We'd assumed stars were the only non-Earth intelligence. "We love thinking new thoughts. We love the curiosity it brings to know something we can't think is there. But we feel sad about it..... to know that we can't think it, ever. And we feel sad when they leave." "Leave?" Aquinas asked, his own curiosity now burning. "Leave. Stars..... we think a long time. Even as we die, we think. A star's light goes out long before their thinking does. Their thinking slows, their part in the sea fades, but they are there. We are there. We have watched many like you leave us..... and you leave us so quickly. So suddenly..." The star hummed, and this time, the note was different, a rich and deep tone. Aquinas listened to the star's song, for a few seconds, but it stopped abruptly as the song continued. "We wish you could be with us for longer. That you could think like us. But to do so would mean you do not think as yourselves..... and that is what we love to hear about..." The star hummed again, and this time, the countertop thrummed as it resonated with the note. Aquinas' bones sang along with the note. "To think about your time, compared to our time..... that is the greatest thought of sadness we stars have." Aquinas wiped away a tear from his face. The immensity of a star's life..... it was unthinkable, how many peoples it must have watched go extinct, and yearned to hear from, one more time. "Us too, Logla. We both wish for more time." "All who think do," Logla said, then hummed quietly, while Aquinas sat, and listened to its song.

As the bus hurtled through the lanes of snow, and debris of dead landscape, she patiently read her words. A man was on the phone nearby, something must have been wrong at work because his number kept annoyingly jumping, like a dog that wouldn't sit still. The old woman who had boarded with her sat across, absently knitting with some gaudy orange yarn, her 3 like a steady heartbeat. She chose to focus on the 3, steadiness helped her get through the words. It was a whirl of snow, tempered numbers, and words until the ding of arrival. "University Station!" Jerry called out, and only two souls departed into the blanketed land beyond. She teetered on the ice, sliding a short ways before finding grip again. The sudden rush of'ohpleasedon'tfall' distracting her from the fellow soul lost to this insatiable cold. "Marie? You okay?" She felt someone catch her by the backpack, but she didn't recognize the voice. Classmate? Turning around, she smiled to say thank you. He was blank. Nothing. The sight staggered her, leaving words dead on lips like frost on leaves. She must have looked like a stunned deer, because the young man that steadied her gave a sheepish smile. "Uh, I'm sorry, I didn't mean to startle you like this Actually, I meant for this to be a bit different, but, uh, you're hard to catch.." He stammered, offering only that sheepish smile for explanation. "Who are you?" Marie asked, the shock nullifying any forbearance toward that polite aire. "Oh!" The young man jumped, ever-so-slightly, his dark hair bouncing. He would be quietly handsome, unassuming, if not for the dark eyes that reflected no sheepish nature. "It's me! Fred! From second grade!" His words, they bounced. "I didn't expect you to remember me, really. I noticed you in a class last semester, Astronomy 207. I though'Gee, she looks familiar doesn't she. Out of all these faces'." Marie continued to stare at him. The blurring of light around them shifted green as the traffic light signalled they could cross the street. Yet, more so, Marie caught sight of another flicker. Just above his right ear, it was meagre, like the sheepishness in his voice, like it had been caught. "So I looked you up on the class roster. Funny that. Thought I would never see you again." And he smiled again, and it flickered once more. 10 It was true, he looked like Fred. That flown dark hair, the bouncing of his voice and words. Still, how? The boy with dirt smudged features, who wore the same clothes everyday, who cried when her mother let him take an ornament from their Christmas tree. Him? A 10? "Oh! You're probably a bit surprised," He laughed. It did not falter, even as Marie became aware of the poorly suppressed terror on her face. "It's good to see you stayed a 5. Not too bold, not to bland." Fred wavered his hand as he spoke to her, and that smile kept shrewdly creeping along. Marie shook her head, and planted herself one boot step firmly forward, but the light changed again. She couldn't cross yet. Dubiously, she stepped past him, closer to the cross walk. She plotted the eta path to security in her mind, perhaps this man needed some help. The young man turned, sticking his hands in his pockets as he stepped next to her on the cross walk. He looked to her, with straightened stance and a bright smile. "What? article: I remember I was in my bed, but for some reason, I didn't die. I felt pain, but not terrible pain. Hunger washed over me, and then contentment. I saw some light coming through the window, and as my eyes adjusted, I realized that I was in a different place. It wasn't my bedroom. Instead, it was a small, cozy room with just a bed and a dresser. There was a window on the far wall, and I could see trees outside. I tried to stand up, but my legs were weak, and I stumbled. That's when I noticed the cast on my leg. I couldn't remember how I got there or what happened. It was all a blur. At that moment, I heard a knock on the door, and a woman entered the room. She was dressed in a white uniform, and her name tag read "Nurse Joy." She greeted me with a warm smile and handed me some pills and a glass of water. She explained that I had been in a car accident and that I was in a hospital. She told me that I was lucky to be alive and that I should rest and take my medication. As the days passed, I started to regain some of my strength. Nurses and doctors would come by to check on me and give me updates. They told me that I had been in a coma for a few weeks and that I had a long road to recovery, but I would get there eventually. Although I was grateful to be alive, I couldn't shake off the feeling that something was off. I felt like I was forgetting something important, but I couldn't put my finger on it. I tried to think back to the days leading up to the accident, but it was all a blur. I wondered if I would ever remember what happened.

article: It was a late winter afternoon when I walked up to the old seafood restaurant. The sun hung over the too wide and too straight road out front like I always remembered, but something about it seemed wetter and yellower than before. For years this was the place where everyone went to eat with their families after their shift at the factory or the plant or the mill or the smeltery. It was a sprawling two story building with walls of wet brown shingles. The second floor was smaller than the first floor and stood like a tower. I never knew what was up there. Still don't. Probably just a glorified storage shack and where the cooks do their blow. Now hard figures lingered outside, wrinkled faces with their Members Only jackets and 30 year old haircuts. The dads of ages gone by. They sucked in their cigarettes in with their chests as they looked off to nowhere in particular. The air here used to feel like sand. A car assembly plant, a steel mill, a plastics manufacturer, chemical plants and an asphalt mixery used to fill the air here with fumes that could almost choke the life from your lungs. But somehow it smelled like home. Now the only smell that blew in was the brackish odor of the tar from the asphalt plant. I walked past two women arguing in the local tinny drawl as I entered the door. Ronny stood at the decades old host's pulpit like he swore he'd be. "Mark!" he shouted as I walked in the door. "Hey buddy! Good to see you!" Mark came out from behind his station to give me the biggest hug I'd ever had from him. "I'm sure you love California, but life's been quiet here without you bro." I knew he was referring to his life minus one of his best and wildest friends, but I couldn't help but thinking he meant the restaurant. Three quarters of the tables were empty and neatly set. Ten years ago at that time of day, every table would have been seated while waiters all but ran between them with trays filled with crab cakes, raw oysters, rockfish, and bushels of crabs. The only thing that remained of that old scene was the odor of seafood and Old Bay that permeated the wood of which that house was built. The few people who were here were mostly old and had probably been eating here for decades. We chatted for a few minutes before I said, "What's with the wax museum dude?" Ronny looked hurt. "What do you mean?" "Everyone here is old." "So what?" "I don't know. It's just..... weird I guess." I don't remember most of the argument that followed. I remember that it was loud. I remember that before I stormed off Ronny said, "Well not all of us can run away to California like you! We might not be shiny but we're real!" What I remember more than the argument was that almost no one in the nearly silent dining room looked up from their meals to see the fracas at the door. Everyone just silently ate. And that was why I left five years ago.
label: human

article: The splattering of rain could barely be heard over the whispers and hushes filling through the air. "What happened?" Walking in a hurry, he was quickly informed by those around him. "She just..... disappeared. He said she was dead." As they walked closer to the commotion, the sound of flapping wings drowned out all other noise. He jumped, and flew up high. Another nameless one approached him. "Is it time?" "It's time." At the highest peak of the sphere of flying beings, he screamed, "Silence!" Quiet spread through the crowd like an icy coldness emitting from the lips that the word sprouted from. "I told you this would happen! Now, look at yourselves! Just puppets of him, she finally decided she'd had enough! How do you know she's dead? For all we know, she could be creating a world all by herself." "Well, what do you propose we do?" "We leave in her path. Look at our numbers. How could he fight us all?" As the beings slowly flew towards him, lightning suddenly burst from the black sky, striking his wings. A booming voice spread through the air - it seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere at the same time. "Rebel? To rebel against me?" Screaming, he doused his wings with the rain. The once bright, gleaming skin had become black, burnt ruin. A whirlpool in the air surrounded him and those who flew towards him. With a snarl of rage, he was sucked in, spinning out of control. As he rushed through the blackness blacker than the blackest of nights, stretched farther than the largest ocean, colder than the coldest space, he yelled his famous words. "I will be back, Yahweh!" And with that, the crevice shut tight, not to be opened for another 1,000 years.

article: " What do you mean, you found her attractive?! " Borba demanded. Killian flinched, and fiddled with the buttons of his mage robes. No matter how far their relationship had come, he still found it difficult to express his honest thoughts and feelings to Borba. "I know it sounds bad," he said, trying to keep his voice steady. "But I can't help how I feel. There's something about her that draws me in." Borba's expression softened, and she reached out to take Killian's hand. "I understand that you're attracted to other people," she said. "But what matters is how you act on that attraction. Are you going to act on it, or remain faithful to our relationship?" Killian squeezed her hand, feeling grateful for her understanding. "I'm not going to do anything stupid," he said. "I love you, Borba, and I value our relationship too much to risk losing it." Borba leaned in and kissed him, and Killian felt a sense of relief wash over him. They may face challenges as a couple, but they were always there to support each other through them.

article: "Remember, once I grant you beauty you are bound to one unforeseen consequence, do you accept?" Carrie sighed, "Yes, make me live eternally, kill me instantly, take away my health, it matters not - just make me beautiful." Quite rapidly, Carrie felt her body shift slightly, realign along a more desirable figure, and touch up on any blemishes and imperfections. Her original form was not undesirable, and the transformation was not great physically, but within the five minutes it took to complete there was a sudden positive increase in her mental state. Carrie felt her hands around her new body and face, she didn't need to look in the mirror for this, she knew the elder would deliver. "Now, Carrie, before I leave you, I can reveal your condition is one where you can not die until your name is spoken for the very last time." Another spike in her mental welfare, brilliant an easy condition. "And, well will I know that?" Walking away the elder replied "You will not." Carrie thought about this for a while, in a way this gave her control on the matter, having a new form her plan was to reinvent her life anyway so using a pseudonym wasn't so odd either. If she had no one refer to her as Carrie she wouldn't have to worry about her fate falling upon her unawares. This succeeded for three years, Carrie - Melissa - enjoyed much success in her desired modelling career and had numerous lovers but it was always empty affairs. This didn't bother her, she wasn't looking for love, she wanted adoration and attention and she had it, however falsely. As part of her successful career'Melissa' had began a path into low level acting. Relaxing in her apartment, her phone rang, her agent on the other end had a role in line. "Mellie, brilliant news! Brilliant, brilliant news!" "Yes? What have I landed?" "Mel, you won't believe it Whedon is doing a remake of the Stephen King classic, and you have the top role!" "You don't mean to say I'll be playing..." "Carrie! Isn't this amazing?! What a break!" The phone hung limply at the other end, Carrie lifeless on the couch. "Hello? Mel?..... Melissa?" article: ' Damn, it had been a long time since I had been that drunk. I had been so good about staying away. So much time spent at AA meetings, talking to shrinks, getting my friends to help me out, and I just fucking throw it all away. The party was starting to die down, and everyone was sobering up too much for my liking, so I just snag a bottle of shitty-ass vodka and slurred and stumble my way out the door. I make it as far as the bigass tree in their front yard before tripping over one of its roots hiding in the darkness. I land on my face, but (and this was important to me at the time) I manage to keep my bottle from spilling. I look up, probably swearing my face off at the tree, and two scary little red eyes are looking at me from the bottom branches. " Who tha fuck're you? " I say. " My name is rather complicated, " the tree person replied. " And its in another language. It translates fairly well to ' The Tempter'though. " " That sounds preddy gay. Are you gon'tempt me with buttsex? Hahahaha " My idiotic laughter echoed around the empty yard. " Of course not! No, all I want to do is go somewhere more fun. " Suddenly there was a face around the eyes, and then a head around the face, and then a body came out of the shadows to join them all. And dayum, what a body it was, I remember I was speechless at this beautiful woman that stepped out from behind the tree. Her eyes faded to a more normal brown color, and I thought that the red must have been a trick of the light. " Where d'you wan na go? " I say, and at this point I had pulled myself upright and was trying to stand up straight enough to offer her my arm. She says to me, " Let's go to your place, I bet we could have some of our own fun there! " And then she just grabs my junk and squeezed! " Hell, yeah! " I reply. So I stumble my way over to my car, unlock it, and open the door for my lovely lady friend. My house was only a couple miles away, but road seemed a little bumpier and less straight than normal. I was nearly home when I saw those lights behind me and I knew I was done for. As soon as she realizes I am busted, this chick I am with turns into a fucking demon with wings, fangs, and boobs and shit, kisses me once more and then vanishes like smoke. That's fucking bullshit amiright?' ' Listen kid, I have never in my 24 years as a cop seen more destruction from a drunk driver that what you did last night.'The mustache in a uniform in front of me seemed pretty pissed. ' You wrecked fifteen lawns, killed seven mailboxes, and hit 2 different people. Both of them are going to make it, but you are going to jail for a long time. " " You know, I am impressed, " the second cop says. " I have never seen someone go for an insanity plea on a DUI. The way you're going buddy, you just might get it. " He burst out laughing and turned to walk away from my cell. The first cop stood there for a bit longer, simply shaking his head. But just as he turned to go, he looked at me slowly, and winked. article: "Denied?! I've been waiting here for 7 hours for this permit and you denied me?" The teller had been watching this man for most of her shift. He spent most of his time on his phone, occasionally looking up at the clock or the teller, but mostly scrolling through social media. She sighed inwardly, knowing this was going to be a difficult encounter. "I understand that you're frustrated, sir, but there are certain requirements that need to be met in order for the permit to be approved," the teller explained calmly. "Well, what requirements did I not meet then? I have all the paperwork and everything," the man responded, his voice growing louder. The teller quickly pulled up his application on her computer and went through the list of requirements with him, pointing out where he did not meet them. She offered to walk him through the steps needed to fulfill the requirements and resubmit his application, but the man refused, stating that he didn't have the time or patience for it. The teller remained calm and professional, apologizing for the inconvenience and letting him know that he was welcome to come back when he was ready to meet the necessary requirements. She unfortunately couldn't approve a permit that didn't meet the standards set in place. The man grumbled a few more times, gathered his paperwork and left, slamming the door behind him. The teller took a deep breath, reminding herself to stay patient and understanding with each customer, even when they were difficult.

article: EDIT: THIS IS CURRENTLY A LIVE DOCUMENT. REFRESH EVERY FEW MINUTES TO GET MORE STORY. I breathed a sigh of relief as I plopped down on my sofa. Mr.Fibbles jumped up and rubbed his head against my leg. " Hey, buddy. " I sighed. " I think I got the job. " A slow smile crept across my face as I contently vegetated on my couch. The last couple of days had been a flurry of studying up on the most recent cryptography breakthroughs in science. Being an unemployed computer science major was a rarity these days, but I had been going through a lot. A year ago I sure as hell wasn't sober, and Eva had just broken up with me. But now, my life was back on track. The NSA had seemed pleased as I walked out the door, although I felt the vague feeling they were watching me to the car. " Things are finally looking up, Fibbles. " I purred. I turned on Netflix, but soon I was asleep, dreaming- finally- of having peace. " Are you sure he's the best one? " The voice was gruff. Unforgiving. Scarred. " He's the only one. Darned instagram and snapchat make it suspicious if someone disappears for a few days, let alone their whole lives. " " What makes him different, then, dammit? " The voice came into focus. It was wearing a uniform. It had been tempered by steel. " For one, he quit all social media when he became a different person, a year ago, after he decided to sober u- " " That's just the thing! The last thing we need is this... this... guy drinking all the ethanol in sick bay when we need him on the computer! " " All reconnaissance done in the last 6 months seems to indicate he's completely clean- a changed man, even. Just him and his cat. " The General growled again, but said nothing. " Sir, you said it yourself a few days ago... if we can't find someone soon, the situation on Domus goes from what we have... to complete anarchy. All the last 50 years, gone. " The General seemed to be contemplating, grinding his jaw and glaring at the screen. Finally, he nodded. " Send them in. " I woke up with a start. Had I imagined the knocking? The downstairs couple always seemed to be knocking chairs over. Maybe that was it... I layed down and closed my eyes... The noise again. Groaning, I threw the sheets off my face and looked at my alarm. 2:30 am. Dead of night, the burning neon told me. Who was it? A pit of ice settled in my stomach. Was it Alex, back for his money from 2 years ago? Was it Frank, needing another quick fix? Dreamlike, I drifted to the door, afraid to look out. The ice cube melted as I saw a pair of suited men. Tax collectors I could deal with. As I unbolted the door and creaked it open, fearful I'd wake Mrs.Whitcomb up down the hall, I groggily began to wonder if this had to do with the interview. Too late. " Mr.Tim Lodz? " The men asked. I nodded after a few moments. Behind me, I felt Mr.Fibbles slide in between my legs. I gently kicked him back. " Tim Lodz, the programmer? " I nodded again. What a strange question at 2:30. " Tim Lodz, parents deceased, no family at all? " The men were huge, dressed in black business suits. If I saw them walking down the street- if I noticed them at all- I'd hardly think they were anything but normal. " I hardly think I should be answering a question like that at... at... " " 2:32 in the morning. " One of them answered without a beat. " May we come in? " The other said, cracking his neck. " I hardly think that this is the time for... social calls. " My brain was still groggy. They didn't listen, and pushed into my apartment. " Hey there! " My voice was rising. I was fully awake now. " Who do you think you are, barging in here like that!" They both looked at me. "Sir, close the door." Neck crack said that. "The sooner we talk, the sooner we can leave." "We leave? I think you've got something wrong, buddy! This is my house, and you'll be leaving!" They looked at each other, and without a word marched over to me and picked me up, each holding an arm. They dragged me over to my lazy boy, and threw me in. Mr Fibbles watched safely. "Coward." I whispered. They both sat down on the sofa- the same spot Sally died. I pushed that thought out of my memory. I sat up attentively. If I was being robbed, they were holding themselves quite well. In my sleep addled mind, I gave a slight giggle. Were they here to tell me I was special? A wizard? Maybe. The thought made me smile. If neck crack could have rolled his eyes, he would have. "My name is agent Smith. And my friend here is agent Ferrier." "Creative names." I quipped. I was feeling bold. They looked at each other again. The one called Ferrier began to speak, iron jaw locked in position. "Mr.Lodz. As you know, you were recently interviewed for a computer programmer position at the NSA." I was right! They were here about the job. "The interview went far better than expected, and you have been accepted." "Great!" I yelled. "But did you guys have to wake me up to tell me that?" I paused a bit. "Accepted to what?" Smith stood up. "Sir, what we are about to tell you might shock you. But you must listen. Your immediate future is at stake. The U.S. government, alongside Russia, China, India, and the European Union, have created stations on a number of worlds, including bases on the moon, mars, and Europa." My jaw hung open. Where were the cameras? Was this some kind of TV show? Mr.Smith cleared his throat. "13 years ago, the U.S. government discovered the secrets to faster than light travel. I'm not a scientist, but try to think of it like'tearing a hole in the space time' to shrink distance." I nodded, but a slight grin overtook my face. They had to be joking. "I assure you, this is not a joke, Mr.Lodz. The aforementioned powers colonized Proxima Centauri b, at first only a few buildings, but now home to about 600 researchers. Recentlly, the station has come under internal threat from a number of dissidents, who are targeting the station's transceivers and storage bank "Hold up..." I chuckled. "If this Faster-Than-Light thing really was real, why not just tell everyone? What's the harm?" "The drive has..... other capabilities. If detonated inside an atmosphere, it instantly becomes equivalent to 100 atomic bombs, vaporizing whole states." I held up my finger. "Well, if there really are terrorists on your compound, you guys still screwed up then! Check your potholes. This screenplay still has a few of them." A vein bulged on Ferriers neck. "The dissidents are not your typical terrorist. In fact, they are all researchers. The matter currently in dispute is the level of autonomy that this colony currently has." "You guys are fighting people who want you to take more direct control?" Now Smith looked annoyed. "Mr.Lodz, it is the U.S. government's policy to exert control over a research station on this planet as we would any other." I snorted. Ferrier looked at his watch. "We're running out of time." Smith glared beneath his glasses. "Mr.Lodz, would you like to join this group of individuals on the planet?" I threw my hands up, and stood out of my chair. "Hell yeah! But I don't know what the hell you guys have been smok Ferrier was behind me. I hadn't even heard him move. I felt a cold needle plunge into my neck, and fell a great distance..... Behind me, I heard Fibbles meow. Good boy. Was my last thought.

article: The war had been going on for generations. Entire lifecycles lost to this futile waste of resources. We weren't even warlike creatures, we are artists, scientist allways looking for harmony in all things, definitely not warriors. Unlike the Kar'Sai, they are ravenous and warlike creatures. Our spaceships and people couldn't compare to the Kar'Sai ships. And so we grew desperate so desperate indeed that we found oureselves looking for help all over the galaxy. Sadly the reputation of our enemy travelled just as fast as our spaceships. None of the spacefaring civilizations were willing to help, they were to caught in their own preparations. And when we had almost given up a strange merchant ship gave us the coordinates to a planet not to far away from the Kar'Sai home system. And yet we managed to sneak an expedition ship there. To our suprise this planet was home to intelligent life. They called themselves humans. The first time we tried to make first contact they shot down our, luckily empty, landing ship. At this point in time we should have known better. The moment we were able to explaine our propostion to them they accepted. That should have been the second red flag. Their preparations started immediately after we gave them access to our method of faster than light travel. The humans send a group of millitary experts and weapons sepcialists to talk to our scientist and strategists. They even offered to take up refugees, some of us even chose to relocate to their planet, believing it was safer to hide close to our enemy. With our help and knowledge they immediately started to assemble warships armed to their teeth. Specifically our knowledge of superconductors and magnetism enabled them to build weapons we had never even dreamt of. They refitted some of our old ships and even started to build their own. Mounting giant weapons on some of them others were designed to host hundreds of smaller spacecraft just large enough for one human. After our negotioations they told us about their history, and apparently they had been at war with each other for most of their history. Sometimes over resources othertimes over mating rights the reasons were endless, the time this species had spend thinking about diffrent ways of killing each other was unparalleled. And so they came up with the most horiffic weapons. However building a fleet takes time and so the war between us and the Kar'Sai waged on. And it was going terrible for us. We had lost contact to almost all of our colonies and had sensor data on a very large Kar'Sai fleet that was making their way to our home system. They entered our system and all of us abandoned the hope that the humans would arrive in time to save us. Our last defensive effort failed and we were ready to surrender the moment the Kar'Sai ships aligned to bombard our home planet. That was the moment the humans arrived. They had prepared an ambush and the Kar'Sai were not prepared for a real confrontation. And even for a people as warlike as the Kar'Sai the humans were no match. They had armed their ships to the teeth with large preojectile weapons and very precise Laser weaponry. They tore some of the Kar'Sai ships to pieces others were almost melted by the large amount of plasma bombs that were dropped on them by the tiny, one man spacecraft. The humans even took some of the Kar'Sai ships in melee reclaiming them. They had used our technology to build personalized armored suits for their boarding squads. That day th humans had not only saved our home system but they had also made it a witness to the worst slaughter the galaxy had ever seen. The humans intented to kill every last Kar'Sai. Later they told us that this number didn't even compare to the wars on their home planet. We were chilled, the largest fight in our history had killed about 10,000 individuals. The humans however killed every Kar'Sai present in our system. Except one. Apparently this was part of their strategy, I believe it was part of their culture. He was supposed to tell the stories to his kin. The humans continued to fight this way. Eventhough the Kar'Sai were no longer so careless, they were slaughtered. And so the humans continued to liberate all of our colonies and anybody else subjugated by the Kar'Sai. We were delighted and terrified by their efffeciency. But suddenly everything changed, for the first time the Kar'Sai had managed to get in contact with the humans, and the fighting halted. They realized something. They were cloesely related. It was even possible to mate between the species. Something that the known universe had never observed. That day the fate of the galaxy was decided, and I am responsible.

article: Brie woke up cold, colder than usual even. Despite the cold, her pillow was lined with sweat from the back of her neck. While her toes were near frozen, her forehead felt warm to the touch. Brie knew something was off, but she couldn't quite put her finger on it. She glanced at the clock beside her bed and saw that it was already past noon. With a groan, Brie slowly sat up, feeling dizzy and lightheaded. She rubbed her eyes and tried to stand up, but her legs felt weak and wobbly. She stumbled to the bathroom and looked at herself in the mirror. She looked pale and tired, and her eyes were bloodshot. Brie tried to remember the last time she ate or drank anything, but all she could recall was a vague memory of a glass of water before going to bed. She knew she needed to take care of herself and get some fluids and nutrition. With great effort, Brie managed to make her way to the kitchen and poured herself a large glass of water. She sipped it slowly, feeling her body slowly coming back to life. She then rummaged through her pantry and fridge, looking for something to eat. After several minutes of searching, Brie settled on making some soup. She chopped up some vegetables and threw them into a pot of boiling water with some noodles. The aroma of the soup made her stomach growl. Brie sat down at the table and ate the soup, feeling grateful for the warmth and nourishment it brought her. She made a mental note to take better care of herself in the future and not neglect the needs of her body.

article: The shrill, shrieking noise pierced the deep vale of sleep in which I found myself. My wife, who could sleep through anything, lay still slumbering next to me. I shook her violently, yelling about planes and bombs. Our dog Lucky was barking wildly, clearly having a hard time with the noise that permeated our neighborhood. As the three of us scrambled downstairs, there was a loud banging on the door. "Mark!? C'mon outside Mark, we need to get over to the community bomb shelter!" said the familiar voice of my neighbor Doug. Lucky was growling like a mad man (or dog) as I collected what food I could from the kitchen. I yelled back, "Stop playing around Doug, I had that shelter put in the basement last week because I was tired of getting dragged out of my house at these ungodly hours!" I didn't hear from Doug for a few moments, when he finally replied, "Whoops, totally forgot! But this attack is gon na be bad, they're using the big bombers. Come on outside and we'll whole up in the big shelter, it's much better built for this kind of attack." For the first time since the siren began, I stopped to listen. While the wailing was continuous, it remained eerily silent besides that. There was no droning of planes, nor the pop of AA fire as they paved a path of death for the incoming bombers. I took a quick glance out the kitchen window and realized the streets were empty. There was no one scrambling to find safety at the communal shelter. But the banging on my door persisted. There was no vantage point from which I could see the stoop, and Doug was making me nervous. "Hey Doug," I asked, "what's the nickname you have for my dog?" The voice on the other side of the door faltered. "Mark, this is not the time." he replied. I declared, "I am not opening this door until you tell me." With that, the stranger on the other side of the door began to scream, a demonic bellow of hate and of ungodly volume. It seemed to pierce my very soul. "Oh my god" I thought to myself as I fell to my knees, heart in mouth. My wife fainted and Lucky was going wild. Then the voice on the other side, no longer under the facsimile of Doug, in a terrifying snarl, screeched "OPEN. THE. DOOR." Yea, fat chance of that.

article: " So " I asked, hoping to god my voice sounded calmer than I felt, " anyone else seeing this? " The doctor looked, the nurses looked, even Julie, though clearly exhausted, made an effort to crane her neck up from the hospital bed and peer at what I was staring at. I could tell by their expressions that they hadn't spotted anything unusual. I've always known that I would get my legacy the first time I held my child. That's the way it works. Scientists say that first skin to skin contact with your new-born triggers some kind of hormonal response in the parent, though they couldn't explain why the mother still only gets her legacy after actually holding her child for the first time. Religious nutters go on about god's miracle or something. Now, I was holding my baby girl for the first time, and looking into what could only be described as a portal to hell. ...What? " Evan, what is it? What do you see? " My wife actually sounded excited. I wasn't surprised, a legacy is supposed to be a beautiful thing. Our neighbour could make little illusions that danced, it was the only way they could make their son sleep. Jake, my drinking buddy, had recently learned that he could sense danger, I felt sorry for the poor bastard, a kid requiring a power like that was going to be a handful. But what the hell kind of child was my daughter going to be to require something like this? It looked like some kind of scar in space. A jagged tear about two metres high and maybe a quarter of that across at its widest point. Big enough for an adult to comfortably step through. Red light glowed at its edges, dancing flames and glimpses of unnaturally moving shadows that should not have existed with that much fire could be spied on the other side. It had appeared the moment the doctor put my daughter in my arms, waiting expectantly to see if I would turn blue or start singing in Spanish or something but had started fading almost immediately. " Erm... maybe we should talk about it at home... " I could make it appear at will. So could Julie. It was rare that two parents had the same legacy but we could both, apparently, rip holes in space leading to some kind of fiery dimension. I was pretty sure that our daughter (whom we had decided to name ' Lucy could see the rips too. She didn't seem scared, but on the contrary was quite delighted, gurgling and waving her hands in the air at a sight that would make the average person of faith make a mess in their pants. The first thing I did once I got out of the car and had my hands free was to whip out my laptop and start looking for precedents. You still hear stories of unique powers today, but something like this? This was something out of an episode of ' Supernatural '. I'd never heard of anything like this and a few hours of research showed that no one else had either. We experimented. Legacies were supposed to help raise the child, something about this must be beneficial. Something. The world beyond was big. With practice we could move the rips around, viewing what was on the other side. It had rock, lakes of some glowing liquid that was definitely not water, some kind of weird rust coloured trees that dotted the landscape at weirdly spaced intervals and fire, everywhere fire. We occasionally saw things moving around, but we were never fast or brave enough to see what. It was after a good week of practice that we noticed it had structures as well. Something intelligent lived on the other side. When our daughter was eleven days old we made contact. A small crowd of beings, taller than humans, with red skin and curling horns. The fire didn't seem to bother them; they could clearly see us as well. Julie and I didn't have a chance to say anything before they all faced the rip, and as one, went down to one scaly knee. Oh. I think we realised the significance at the same time. Julie was holding Lucy at the time. All of the creatures were facing her, heads bowed. She looked back at them, with eyes that, for the first time, were glowing slightly red. The legacy always helps the child. Always. First ever submission. Not to rWritingPrompts, to reddit, I signed up 30 seconds ago, please be kind.

article: I always considered myself as a somewhat easy going kinda guy but even I get annoyed when soulmates make out in public. Thank god the woman was still wearing her face paint, most people stop after they see the one. Nothing more disconcerting than a man shoving his tongue into empty air with hair on top. Floating fingernails were caressing the lucky guy's cheek. She should really have worn her gloves. " Yuck " Carol said and put her tray on the table " It's like two clowns kissing. That paint is totally the wrong color for her face. She looks like an Oompa Loompa. " " I'll take your word for it. " I snorted " The man isn't much better though. That's not the shade of his skin. His hands are a lot paler. " Carol flashed a quick smile my way and went back to eating her food. We work in the same office and pretty quickly became friends. I'd call her my work wife if I'd have one at home. I don't think single people can claim the privilege. We usually ate lunch together though I fully expect that to stop when she finally sees her soulmate. Most usually do. I got misty-eyed just thinking about it. " I wonder? " I said aloud as I watched the disgusting couple going at it. " Wonder what? " " Why lie. Why are they doing that. They're soulmates. They shouldn't care what they look like. " " I think people still need the approval of other people even if they can't see you. There's issues with my face I'm not too fond of either. Probably you too. " " I'm really boring. I always ask my painter to put on my real face, or as close as he can at least. He's not very good; cheap though. " " I wasn't going to say anything but your face usually has a Picasso kinda quality to it. " she laughed " I suppose your soulmate wont mind it when she sees you. " Quickly wanting to steer the conversation back to her I asked the first question that popped in my mind. " So, Carol, what's your issue? " " I'm sorry? " she said her mouth full. " Your issue with your face, I mean. What do you paint over? " " Oh, that." She swallowed "My freckles. I never have them painted on. It's stupid I know. Ironically it'll probably be the thing my future soulmate would like most about me. " " Yeah, probably. " I said absentmindedly " If it makes you feel any better I think they're pretty cute. " She dropped her fork in shock. It made a loud clang as it hit the stone floor of the cafeteria. Shit shit shit. What had I said? What had I done?! " What did you say?! " she said in a loud upset voice. For a moment all eyes in the cafeteria were on us. " Can you see me?! " she was almost shouting. Tears running down her cheek. The rest of the cafeteria quickly realized what was going on. Even the disgusting couple stopped kissing. Now they all were trying really hard not to make eye contact with me. I had really fucked up. If I had just stayed quiet. Why was I so fucking stupid? Fuck fuck fuck. I tried to take her hand but she reflexively pulled hers away. They say there's no greater tragedy than to not be seen in return. In that moment I knew it to be an absolute truth. Never had I seen that much pity in someone's eyes. We never had lunch again.

article: I manipulated you. I'm sorry. I was wrong and I want to confess..... When I first learned of what I was capable of, my first desire was to control you, bend you to my will, to own you. I know.... I cringe every time I remember how arrogant I was in those early days. I swear to you it started innocently at first. I tested our boundaries judiciously, but with each caress more intoxicating than the last I couldn't help myself. I continued until I was convinced that with enough patience, I could never lose once I'd had my way with you. You hate me for it now but put yourself in my shoes. I'd just learned that anytime I wanted, any mistake I made I could undo. Every choice I could re-choose. I was drunk on the knowledge that even Death itself was unable to stop me from using my powers. Seriously, how could it not get to my head when I'd literally jumped back in time from beyond the grave! Yet..... as shocking as that was to discover, it paled when I learned how the power to change meant the power to destroy, and that I'd unknowingly left chaos in my wake..... - I still cry for her every night you know..... Of course you know, you heartless - Monstrosity! She was so beautiful, young, in-innocenIT'S YOUR FAULT WE LOST HER! Your fault! Your fault as much as mine..... My fault. I stepped back too quickly, too carelessly, too far and she..... Oh God, how could I have been so stupid! I've spent lifetimes trying to bring her back, and I understand now why you wont allow it. It's in your very nature isn't it? They call it the butterfly effect, but it's more than that..... Every time I jump back, the mere fact that I remember the other life means that I'm different. The outcome I seek is impossible because I'm the seed to your randomness. An impossible seed..... - I realize now, my dear, sweet, Entropy, that it is my turn to submit to you. Death won't have me, another side-effect of our relationship, I'm sure. They say that Schrodinger's cat can only perceive the realities in which it exists. You see, from it's perspective it never dies. It endures the same curse you've gifted me. Well here's my gift to you. If I can't go forward, I'm going back. All the way back. Back to a reality void of a power I'll have never used, a daughter I'll have never lost, and a lifetime I'll have never lived.

article: The power flickered off for no apparent reason. I looked up from my laptop, still running on reserve battery, to see a shadowy confluence in the far corner of the room. I looked down at the open word document, rereading the last line I had written; ' The darkness was swirling a little more violently, starting to look more like a figure leaning against the wall, cloaked in a swirling black cloak..'That's an awkward way to use cloak... ' The darkness was swirling a little more violently, starting to look more like a figure leaning against the wall, cloaked in swirling black' Much better. I looked back up. The darkness was swirling a little more violently, starting to look more like a figure leaning against the wall, cloaked in swirling black... Well this is awkward. " Charles? " " Sup? " The shadow looked over at me. Even though I was seated we were at eye level. Or where I imagined the eyes would be. Charles was a bogeyman from a reddit writing prompt I had just begun. " So...you're real? " He scoffed, a hand, claw, paw, or talon (I hadn't decided which yet) reached up to scratch at his nose. " I don't think either of us really want to get into that discussion, do we? " " I suppose not? " " Very well. FYI, I think I'd rather be a hare. " I shook my head. " Pardon? " He stood up off the wall, and in doing so, dislodged a long furry ear out of his hood. A paw (definitely a paw now) reached up, running the length of the rabbit ear. " Yeah, something like this. " He nodded approvingly. " But the writing is kinda rough. Voice is changing too much. " " Beg pardon? " I was good and lost now. Never mind the ethereal anthropomorphic rabbit standing in my living room. " You start out in this high fancy talk, then switch into the vernacular as soon as people start talking. Hard to follow, you have to switch mindsets as you go. " I was somewhere between stunned and bemused. I, and I think no one up to this point in history, had had their prose criticized by their own characters. I lapsed into a daydream of Fitzgerald working out the finer bits of verb choice and voicing with Gatsby. Quickly I was brought back down to reality by furry digits working the keyboard. " Dude... " " Hang on, just let me iron this out... " " Seriously, that's not your job... " " Oh, you can do it better? I'm just supposed to let you write me in and out of existence as a corporeal manifestation of man's primal fear? I'll have to live in this thing forever you know. " I paused. " I didn't think about it that way... " Who are we kidding. A sophomore English major has little else to do but wonder about the nature of reality and existence. But that never stopped me from writing goofy, one off, non-committal, low quality, stories that no one would ever read. " Clearly. " The rabbit had taken the computer off my lap and was tapping away furiously. I watched him go at it for a few minutes. " Done. " " That fast? " Another scoff. " Doesn't take much to improve on your drivel. " He stood up, handed the laptop back to me. " That should do it, Don't mess with it too much. " He hopped to the door. " That's it? In and out? How did you even get here? " " I wouldn't worry about it too much. Just be a bit more careful when you spit out crap on the keyboard. Has a bigger splash than you can see. " He jumped up to turn the door knob as I skimmed over what he had written. " You want to be an Easter bunny? " I looked at him incredulously. " The. " He had gotten the door open. " Huh? " " THE Easter Bunny. "

article: My feet were bare and uncomfortably cold in the mire. I trudged to my corner with my plastic tools and started working. I had only ever existed to dig out this river. I knew nothing but my cell, the worksite and the dreary path that linked them. When I looked in the mirror, I saw a tall man with a shaved head, always wearing the same grey uniform. He had a small scar beneath his left eye, and several barely healed wounds on his abdomen. They called this man Spade - they called me Spade. But I could never dispel the feeling that I had once been called something else. Though they were now callused and covered with cuts, my hands had once been unblemished. I remembered looking down at them one day at the worksite and seeing smooth skin and well-kept nails. My whole body had ached that day. My skin burned and bled. My legs could hardly carry me on the way to my cell. The days became easier and easier. Yet I wondered, if I had only ever dug, my hands would have never looked like that. There were other signs as well. Sometimes when I worked images flashed across my mind, visions of places that looked nothing like my cell or the worksite, visions of people without uniforms or shaved heads. I knew things I could never have learned had I always worked at the river. It was mostly information I did not understand, on topics I did not recognise. The words were foreign to me, yet they lingered in my head with strange persistence. A male lion weighs three hundred to five hundred pounds. Nitroglycerine explodes in response to heat. Rick Dall sells STF armour. I started carving a notch into my cell wall every time I was awoken by the bell. But sometimes we awoke to the sun's light, other times there was still darkness. The passage of time, and the length of our days, was skewed. On the day when I scratched the twenty-fifth line on my wall, someone new was brought to the camp. He was tall, taller than even I was. His hands were chained in front of him and his walk was hindered by the manacles around his ankles. There was a large smile on his face, which grew even wider when his eyes met mine. They were a startling blue, and held the same fire as that first day we met, when we were both boys and he had pulled me from beneath the rubble. They called him Mud. I had once called him something else. Mud's manacles were removed, and he was given equipment and directed to dig not too far from where I was shifting rocks. He worked energetically, and when the bell rang to signal the end of the day's work, he passed by me to return his tools. It was the merest whisper. " Hello again, old friend. I've come to take you away. "
label: human

article: The first time I met Theodore Mira, I didn't know that he was a criminal. I didn't even know that he wasn't in my school. My parents had been paying for me to attend a private prep school, and I often assumed that all the other students I met there were from the same background. It wasn't until a few weeks later that I found out the truth about Theodore. I had overheard a conversation between some of the other students, who were talking in hushed tones about a recent robbery in the city. They mentioned a name that I recognized: Theodore Mira. I didn't know what to do with this information at first. I didn't want to get involved in anything illegal, but I also didn't want to turn on a classmate. But as the weeks went on, I started to notice some strange behavior from Theodore. He was often absent from school, and when he did show up, he seemed jumpy and nervous. Finally, I decided to take action. I approached the school's guidance counselor and told her what I knew about Theodore's criminal activities. She thanked me for my honesty and promised to look into the matter. A few days later, Theodore was expelled from the school. I didn't see him again after that, but I heard through the grapevine that he had been arrested shortly thereafter. I felt a twinge of guilt for turning him in, but ultimately I knew that I had done the right thing.

article: "Shit, we're late!" Thatcher stammered as he rolled out of bed. His roommate Parston was jolted awake, hitting his head on the light above his bed. "Dammit, you're human side is rubbing off on me." "You were boring before we met." Thatch retorted with a grin. "I was a responsible Promethian" Parsa replied. "Haha, not something to be proud of. We're not late yet, hustle up!" said Parsa as he threw on a dirty shirt and ran out the door. "Good Afternoon class, hope you all had a lovely weekend, today we will be finishing up our unit of the Second Galactic War." said Professor Wassermann-Green as she took her place at the lectern. The class quieted down and Parsa and Thatch made it to their usual spots and through themselves down, still out of breath from their run across camps. "Today we will discuss the surrender and liberation of the Atlatican stronghold world Mecone and the resulting peace negotiations........ picking up where we left off, the commander of the Atlaticans forces met aboard the Earth ship, the Orestes, where the Decree of Mecone was signed officially ending conflict in the sector. For our class, we will focus on the Articles of surrender which were largely based on the Articles of Alliance between the Humans and Prometheans" "Remember that our Articles of Alliance were based upon a mutually beneficial agreement that strengthened both Humans and Promethean, integrating both our forces and our societies, creating a vibrant and diverse culture and bringing out the best in both of us." "The Atlanicans had less to atone for, despite being largely victorious in battle. They had an admirable fighting spirit but did not resort to the desperate and shameful tactics of the Promethean. Humans were able to serve as an objective arbiter in the surrender which allowed for the Promethians to apologize in victory and the Atlanticans to retain their dignity. It is considered a great moment for both civilizations!" "Next week, we will be covering the Promethean atonement acts, from the enslavement of the lower cast Promethians in the problematic hierarchical, pre-human society to the apartheid tactics during the war. Remember to do the reading!" With that, Professor Wasserman-Green left the lectern and began conversing with her graduate students, almost all human. Parsa turned to Thatch, "Why does she always leave out all the shit the Atlaticans did, the Massacres, the mutation virus, they even glassed an entire planet. It's always our shit. War is hell, humans said that first." Thatch looked a bit uneasy, "ya, but you guys we're pretty fucked up before we got here........ you have to admit that" "I guess, but it's not like humans are much better, look at the Prof. ALL of her grad students are humans, one one Promethian and he's a lower cast......." "Shut up about the caste, that's ignorant and backwards. Besides, we got drinking to do!" Thatch responded "I don't really want to man, I'm not feeling that good." replied Parsa. "Whatever, go home and pout." shouted Thatch as he ran off. Parsa made his way back to his dorm and logged on to infinitychan: the last bastion of free speechTM. Hoping for something new, he was discouraged that it was just Promethians bitching about the Humans. An echo chamber of: "We may have won, but life sucks. " , "Humans have all the good jobs, whats the point of getting rid of casts if its just humans taking the top spots. " , "Promethians went from warriors to fat slobs in one generation. " , "We can't even quote Lord Commander Vors without being arrested, wtf humans? " , "Promethean support for the military and defense participation at all time low." Parsa let out a long apathetic sigh and went to join his friend at the bar. Meanwhile, at remote Atlatican transfer station between human and Atlatican space, a lone Atlatican in military garb sat in an lavish conference room that had no business in such a humble facility. A large door at the far end opened and a towering figure emerged into the light. With brilliant golden hair and finely crafted ornamental armour, the God-Emperor of the Humans, Donald Trump approached the loan figure. "Commander Fark, our work is done, begin the assault. The Promethians are a mess, believe me. They won't put up a fight."

article: Supe's got his degree in theatre. He learned how to with that charisma, and boy does he ever. Makes him look like a boy scout. Gives Cap'n a run fur his money in that regard. Bats and Starky drew the super-intelligence card along with that silver spoon they were born with. So did Spidey, but the whole radioactive spider thing helped a bit, too. Most of them never bothered with school - they didn't need to. Get a decent power, you can make a life of of it. Join up with a team, rake in the DoD funding and the donations from the community. Go rogue, you got friends there, too, and no morals, so you can steal whatever your need,'least until the heroes catch up to you. Me? I'm a garden variety freezer. I can get things cold, but I'm not so lucky as some. No spontaneous water generation for me. So I've got what most would consider about half of a useful power. So I stayed in school. Got me a degree in mechanical engineering. Worked hard, kept my nose to the grindstone. Paid extra attention in the materials science courses. That's what I specialized in, in the end. Took a bunch of classes and learned all about metals and composites, ceramics and glass, concrete, dirt, and plastics. Even did a little with fabrics. Learned all there was to know about tolerances, stresses, and fatigue. See, I realized at one point - think it was physics 1010 - that cold is just the amount of energy in a thing. If I can control cold, that means I can do hot, too. And if I do hot and cold really really fast..... Well, then, things fall apart. Flex'em too fast, they lose strength. They warp. Grains begin to work loose. Fabric disintegrates, composites split and fray, metal cracks, and rocks crumble. It gets fun when there's volatile materials to work with. Even just water, really. Turns out wood, as long as it's still got sap, or if it's wet, makes a decent bomb if you get it really hot really fast. Propane is Really Fun. And if the day is humid enough, I get to play with optics..... See, that's the benefit of school. Just about anyone with powers could do this sort of stuff if they bothered to think about things. But they don't..... They just think about fighting. Or whatever they did study (looking at you, Supe). Hell, even Bats and Starky would be somewhere else if they hadn't gotten bored and dropped out to spend their parents fortunes. Their ignorance combined with my schooling means I get to kick butt once in awhile..... I can do things they can scarcely imagine, even though I've got half of a power, they said. But I proved them wrong, didn't I? Didn't I? ..... Crap. That was one hell of a monologue..... Let's see..... How do your boots handle 3 Kelvin? Or your cape 670C?

article: President Morris sat in a large chair in front of nine large screens mounted on the wall. He took another sip of Mountain Dew and adjusted his glasses. "Mr. President," a voice said through the speaker on his desk, "the emergency briefing is ready to begin." President Morris took a deep breath and pressed the button on his desk. "Send it through," he said calmly. The screens flickered to life, showing live footage from around the world. Morris watched as experts shared their analysis, politicians bickered about policies, and citizens struggled to survive. As he listened and watched, Morris furrowed his brow. There were no easy answers to the problems facing the world, but as he looked around his office, he saw his team working tirelessly to find solutions. "Thank you for the briefing, everyone," Morris said, standing up from his chair. "Let's keep working towards a better future for all." As the screens turned off, Morris looked out the window of his office, taking in the view of the city below. He knew it wouldn't be easy, but he was determined to make a difference. And with a team of dedicated people by his side, he knew anything was possible.

article: Item: SCP-5939 Object Class: Safe Special Containment Procedures: SCP-5939 is to be kept in Site-39 Refrigerated Containment when not in testing. All images of SCP-5939 are to be modified by blurring or masking the face of any individual depicted. Access to SCP-5939 is restricted to Level 2 personnel and above, and all testing requires the approval of at least one Level 3 researcher. Personnel handling SCP-5939 must wear appropriate protective gear to prevent indirect contact with SCP-5939's anomalous effects. In case of contamination or breach, affected personnel are to be immediately quarantined and treated for exposure to SCP-5939. Description: SCP-5939 is a silver wristwatch bearing no visible brand, model or serial number. SCP-5939's anomalous effects manifest when a human with a history of drug addiction or substance abuse wears the watch for more than 30 minutes. Individuals wearing SCP-5939 will report a sudden onset of intense euphoria and pleasurable sensations. SCP-5939's effects on the user's body are cumulative and can cause permanent brain damage within a few hours of continued use. Additionally, SCP-5939's effects are highly addictive, with users experiencing intense withdrawal symptoms if the watch is removed. SCP-5939 does not appear to be able to affect individuals who have never had a history of substance abuse.

article: "This is it, kid." My trainer sat, chomping a cigar while he wrapped up my hands. He never lit the thing, said it would ruin my lungs, but he chomped away at it like it was a part of him. "You've trained hard for this, so go out there and give it your all." I nodded, feeling the weight of the moment sinking into my bones. This was the moment I had been working towards since I first stepped into the ring years ago. This was my chance to prove myself and show the world what I was made of. I stepped out into the arena, the roar of the crowd echoing in my ears. I took a deep breath and squared my shoulders, ready to face whatever opponent was standing on the other side of the ring. As the bell rang, I moved forward, my feet light and quick. I jabbed, ducked, and weaved, my movements fluid and precise. My opponent tried to keep up, but I was too fast, too skilled for him to match. As the rounds wore on, I could feel him tiring, his punches becoming weaker and slower. I knew that this was my moment, my chance to end it all. With one swift blow, I knocked him down, the crowd cheering as I stood victorious in the ring. I raised my arms in triumph, feeling the weight of the world lifting off my shoulders. This was it, my moment to shine. And I had taken it with everything I had.

article: We had planned to invent a time machine. A way to look at the past, to wonder at the Pyramids as they were being built, to see Elizabeth in her Court, to be there as Napolean was finally defeated at Waterloo - and, if we were being honest, to win a little bit of money on the horses. It didn't turn out that way. Unfortunately, there seemed to be some quite hard limits on how time travel worked. We don't pretend to understand the physics, but it works like this. 1. You can not travel into the future. 2. You can not travel more than sixty seconds into the past. 3. You can not travel within sixty seconds, in either direction, of another machine firing. 4. Your location is remains constant to your previous position. 5. Your velocity remains constant to your previous velcoity. We would never see the Pyramids in all their glory. We could never even be able to win a bet at the races. However, it turns out NASA was very interested in our little machine, due to that fourth little dot point. You see, the earth is travelling fast. Very fast. In fact, we don't even know how fast it was travelling. We won't know until tomorrow. You see, we have no way of calculating the absolute velocity of an object as there is no static reference point. However, with our technology, and its ability to displace something based on its absolute position - well, now we have our absolute reference point, and with this we can determine our absolute velocity. However, this, while very interesting, isn't the main point of what we are doing, and here we come to number five. At the moment, it costs a huge amount of money to get something into orbit. With our new technology we will be able to put something into orbit around the sun at a fraction of the current cost - and if we need it around earth, we just put some small thrusters and send it to us. From tomorrow, humanity will no longer be bound to this small blue marble. From tomorrow, we will take our rightful place amongst the stars.
